## TL;DR

If you have ever looked at a trillion parameter model and wondered, “How is anyone training this without paying a trillion-parameter compute bill per token?”, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts is one of the cleanest answers.

The idea is straightforward: instead of running the full parameter set for every token, we activate only a small subset of parameters conditionally. In practice, that conditional computation is usually implemented by replacing a standard **feed-forward network (FFN)** inside a Transformer block with a bank of expert FFNs, plus a learned **router** that decides which expert(s) each token should use.

This can feel like a free lunch: far more parameters, roughly similar floating point operations (FLOPs) per token. But it is not free. We trade dense compute for routing, communication, and training dynamics that can fail in ways dense models rarely do. The upside is that the first wave of practical SMoE designs is now reasonably well understood. We have clear patterns for routing, balancing, and sharding that work at scale, although routing, balancing, and specialization remain very active areas of research.

We will follow a five-part backbone:

## Part A: The routing trick that makes SMoE work

## The one-sentence definition

***SMoE replaces a single dense FFN with many expert FFNs and uses a learned router to activate only a small number of experts per token.***

A classic reference is Shazeer et al. (2017), which introduced a practical modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) design and many of the training and systems ideas that still show up in today’s Large Language Models (LLMs).

## Where SMoE sits inside a Transformer

In a standard Transformer block, the FFN (sometimes called a multilayer perceptron, or MLP) is often the “big matrix multiply” component. Attention can be expensive too, but the FFN frequently dominates parameter count.

An SMoE layer typically swaps the dense FFN for:

![]()

## Routing in practice: softmax, then top-k

A common router computes expert scores for each token:

If we used all experts, this would be dense. Sparsity comes from selecting only the top-k experts by p:

Why does k matter?

A helpful intuition is that k is a quality-versus-cost knob:

## Capacity and overflow: routing is constrained assignment

Here is the part that surprises many first-time practitioners: routing is not only “pick the best expert.” It is also “do not overload an expert.”

In practice, each expert has a **capacity**: the maximum number of tokens it will process for a given batch. Capacity is commonly set as:

If the router sends more than capacity tokens to an expert, the extra tokens are **overflow**. Implementations handle overflow in different ways (drop, reroute, or keep but with penalties), but the key point is this:

*Capacity is a systems constraint disguised as a modeling detail.*

Why? Because experts are often sharded across devices, and they need to finish in roughly the same time. If one expert gets overloaded, it becomes the straggler that stalls the layer.

Early large‑scale MoE implementations, including Switch Transformer, often chose a “drop overflow” design where tokens that exceed capacity simply skip expert computation and fall back to the residual path. More recent “dropless” [MoE variants](https://huggingface.co/blog/NormalUhr/moe-balance) instead guarantee that every token is processed by at least one expert, using different packing, padding, or dynamic rebalancing strategies. Dropping is simple and fast but can silently degrade quality when overflow is high; dropless designs reduce this risk at the cost of more complex packing and kernel logic.

## A simple toy routing walkthrough (top-1 with capacity)

Below is an intentionally simplified pseudocode for top-1 routing with capacity and “drop overflow” behavior:

What this omits (on purpose):

Even so, the takeaway is real: SMoE routing is best thought of as constrained assignment plus learned scoring.

## Load balancing is not optional

If the router sends too many tokens to a few experts, we get:

[Shazeer et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538) introduced an auxiliary **load balancing loss** to encourage more uniform usage. [Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2022)](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume23/21-0998/21-0998.pdf) also relies on balancing and discusses practical overflow handling. There is also algorithmic balancing work like [BASE layers (Lewis et al., 2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.16716), and routing variants like [Expert-Choice routing (Zhou et al., 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09368), where experts select tokens.

## Expert specialization: what to expect (and what not to assume)

It is tempting to imagine “one expert equals one skill.” Reality is messier.

Empirically, specialization can emerge, but it is not guaranteed and may be subtle. [ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.08906) is a useful design guide here: it emphasizes stability and transfer behavior and provides techniques and ablations that many practitioners treat as baseline.

A pragmatic takeaway:

***Key takeaways (Part A)***

***· SMoE activates only a few experts per token via top-k routing (often top-1 or top-2).***

***· Capacity limits and overflow exist because routing must respect systems constraints.***

***· Load balancing is essential for both efficiency and stability. stability.***

## Part B: Making SMoE train without collapsing

So, routing works. What can go wrong during training?

Conditional computation changes learning dynamics. It is easy to end up training only a small slice of the model, or destabilizing the router so the entire run diverges. Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2022) is a strong practitioner reference here because it focuses on stability and documents what failed and what fixed it.

## Failure mode 1: expert collapse (router overuses a few experts)

The simplest failure is collapse: the router learns to send most tokens to a small subset of experts. This can become self-reinforcing:

Meanwhile, underused experts get little training signal.

## Failure mode 2: gradient starvation (some experts never really learn)

Even without total collapse, you can get a “hot and cold” split where some experts train and others barely move. You may see:

This is both a utilization problem and a quality problem.

## Failure mode 3: router instability and numeric issues

Routers can become numerically unstable, especially under mixed precision training. If router logits become very large, softmax saturates, gradients vanish, and low-precision formats can overflow.

## The standard stabilization toolbox (what practitioners actually use)

### 1) Load balancing loss

This is usually the first line of defense (Shazeer et al., 2017). Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2022) uses a balancing loss variant and treats it as critical for stable training.

In practice, its weight is a real hyperparameter:

### 2) Router z-loss (logit regularization)

ST‑MoE formalized and popularized a **router z-loss** term that penalizes large router logits to improve numerical stability (Zoph et al., 2022), and closely related formulations are now used in Switch‑style and other production MoE implementations, where router\_z\_loss is exposed as a first‑class hyperparameter. The same idea is also summarized in practitioner explainers such as the [Hugging Face MoE article](https://huggingface.co/blog/moe).

### 3) Higher precision for router computation

A small but often high-impact engineering trick is to compute router logits and softmax in float32 while keeping the rest of the model in lower precision. Switch Transformer discusses precision issues and advocates selective higher precision for router operations (Fedus et al., 2022).

### 4) Encourage early exploration

Shazeer et al. (2017) introduced noisy gating. The intuition is to avoid early deterministic routing that locks the system into a poor local optimum. Related work like Dense-to-Sparse Gate for Mixture-of-Experts (Nie et al., 2021) explores smoothing the transition from soft to hard routing.

A useful shared principle:

### 5) Router learning-rate and initialization care

The router is small, but it can destabilize the whole run if it moves too aggressively early. Common conservative choices include:

### 6) Fine-tuning protocols and expert dropout

Switch Transformer discusses fine-tuning protocols that increase dropout inside experts to regularize large expert capacity on smaller tasks (Fedus et al., 2022). This is different from dropping experts entirely. The point is that large expert capacity can overfit when fine-tuning on limited data, so experts often need stronger regularization.

***Key takeaways (Part B)***

***· SMoE training can fail via collapse, starving experts, and router numeric instability.***

***· The stabilization toolbox has converged to a fairly standard baseline (auxiliary balancing, router logit regularization, selective higher precision, and careful early‑training dynamics) but large‑scale MoE runs still fail in practice if these pieces are mis‑configured, and new routing/balancing ideas continue to appear.***

***· Fine-tuning often needs extra regularization inside experts.***

## Part C: The systems tax you pay for conditional compute

At this point, SMoE may sound like a modeling trick. But in practice, the performance story is mostly a systems story.

## All-to-all communication is the default pattern

In large SMoE models, experts are typically sharded across devices. Routing means tokens must move to the device that owns the chosen expert.

That dispatch is an **all-to-all** communication step:

GShard (Lepikhin et al., 2020) describes this at scale and pairs it with a partitioning strategy that makes the MoE layer efficient on Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) pods.

## Compute versus communication: a quick intuition check

Shazeer et al. (2017) highlights a useful ratio: for a simple FFN, the compute-to-input/output ratio is roughly the hidden size of the FFN. In practice, this often means larger experts can amortize communication better than tiny experts.

A counterintuitive lesson:

## Memory: more parameters still have to live somewhere

SMoE keeps FLOPs per token closer to a dense baseline, but the full expert parameter set must exist in memory across the training or serving fleet.

So we trade:

This is why SMoE is usually deployed in environments that can afford multi-device inference.

## Throughput versus latency: why the charts look different

The headline SMoE efficiency gains are usually **throughput** gains (tokens per second on large parallel hardware), not “one request gets faster.”

Why?

This is also why many systems batch requests, even if it adds a small amount of queuing delay.

One practical framing for autoregressive generation:

ST-MoE guidance emphasizes that in **latency**-bound settings, routing overhead and load imbalance can increase tail latency, which is why hybrid layouts are common (Zoph et al., 2022).

Beyond routing itself, KV‑cache bandwidth becomes a practical bottleneck during autoregressive decode. In expert‑parallel MoE, you often pay twice: first to move tokens to the right experts via all‑to‑all, and then to read sharded KV caches across devices. Even when the theoretical per‑token FLOPs look favorable, the combined communication and memory‑access pattern can push small‑batch decode into a bandwidth‑bound regime where dense models win on wall‑clock latency.

A final practical wrinkle is **low‑bit inference**. Aggressive quantization (for example, 4‑ or 8‑bit weights and KV caches) is now standard for dense LLM serving. MoE inherits all of those issues and adds a few of its own: per‑expert activation distributions can differ substantially, the router can create sharp activation outliers on specific experts, and shared versus routed experts may benefit from different quantization schemes. Getting a large MoE to behave well under tight latency and memory budgets usually requires more careful per‑expert calibration than an equivalently sized dense model.

Recent systems work, including vendor guidance on hybrid expert parallel and topology‑aware all‑to‑all, shows that practical MoE performance hinges on overlapping communication with expert compute and respecting the physical interconnect topology.

***Key takeaways (Part C)***

***· SMoE’s scaling story relies on expert sharding and all-to-all dispatch.***

***· Communication overhead is manageable when expert compute is large enough; tiny experts can be a trap.***

***· SMoE often improves throughput more than single-request latency, especially for autoregressive decode.***

## Part D: Where SMoE wins, where dense still wins (with evidence)

Now the natural question: does SMoE actually work in practice?

## Pretraining efficiency and scaling

Switch Transformer reports that, at large scale, top-1 routing can preserve quality while improving training efficiency. In their reported experiments, they describe reaching comparable quality with substantially higher pretraining speed (reported up to about 7 times faster in their setup) relative to dense Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer (T5) baselines, under comparable compute budgets (Fedus et al., 2022).

GLaM reports a similar headline story: strong downstream performance with lower training cost than dense baselines (reported at roughly one third of the training cost in their setup), and roughly half the inference FLOPs for comparable quality in their reported evaluations (Du et al., 2022).

One important nuance: these comparisons are typically iso‑compute (iso‑FLOPs or roughly iso training cost), not iso‑memory. Sparse MoE models like Switch and GLaM often use substantially more total parameters and require more aggregate device memory to host all experts, even when the per‑token FLOPs budget is comparable to dense baselines.

Public model reports also show MoE ideas spreading beyond a few labs. For example, Mixtral routes each token to two experts out of an expert set in the feed-forward block (Mistral AI, 2023). DeepSeekMoE proposes architectural tweaks aimed at stronger specialization, including isolating shared experts and using finer-grained expert segmentation (Dai et al., 2024). [DeepSeek‑V3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437) extends these ideas to a production‑scale MoE LLM with hundreds of billions of total parameters and on‑the‑order‑of‑tens of billions of active parameters per token, using hybrid shared+routed experts and topology‑aware, node‑limited routing to keep all‑to‑all communication efficient at cluster scale. These are not apples-to-apples benchmark comparisons with Switch or GLaM, but they are useful public reference points for modern MoE designs.

**“1 shared + k routed experts”** has become a common pattern in frontier models (DeepSeek‑V3, Qwen3, GLM‑4.5, some Llama variants). One shared expert always active plus several routed experts, for stability and transfer.

Shazeer et al. (2017) also reported that a sparsely-gated MoE layer improved language model perplexity while using only a small fraction of the compute of an equivalently large dense alternative (they report a large perplexity reduction at roughly 6 percent of the FLOPs of the dense baseline).

A consistent theme across these works:

## Why dense can still win

Dense models have structural advantages that matter in practical settings:

This does not mean SMoE is bad for multi-task learning. It means routing and expert count interact with your data distribution and your objectives.

## A compact decision framework: when SMoE versus dense

Use this as a starting checklist, not a law.

Lean toward SMoE if:

Lean toward dense if:

## Comparison table: SMoE versus dense (at a glance)

![]()

***Key takeaways (Part D)***

***· Evidence from Switch, GLaM, and GShard supports SMoE efficiency claims at large scale.***

***· Dense still has real advantages for simplicity, strict latency, and some transfer regimes.***

***· Decide with your constraints in mind: hardware, batchability, latency targets, and data distribution.***

## Part E: The practitioner playbook

This is the “what do we actually do on Monday morning?” section: configuration knobs, monitoring signals, pitfalls, and misconceptions.

## Configuration knobs that matter

### 1) Number of experts (N)

More experts increases capacity, but also increases:

A practical approach is to sweep N in powers of two (16, 32, 64, 128) and watch both quality and routing health metrics.

Recent MoE‑specific scaling law works, S Abnar (2025), J Ludziejewski (2025), and G Zhao (2025), go beyond heuristics and show that for fixed compute and memory budgets there is an optimal sparsity level and expert configuration; beyond that point, adding more experts or total parameters without more data/compute can hurt performance.

### 2) Top-k (k)

Top-1 is simpler and cheaper. Top-2 can be more robust, but more expensive.

If you are new to SMoE and want a stable baseline, top-1 routing inspired by Switch is often a reasonable starting point (Fedus et al., 2022).

### 3) Capacity factor

Capacity factor is both a systems knob and a modeling knob:

Start near commonly used defaults (often around 1.0 to 1.25 in many systems) and tune based on overflow rate and utilization.

### 4) Balancing loss weight

This prevents collapse, but can suppress useful specialization if overdone.

Treat it like a primary hyperparameter. Track how it affects:

### 5) Router regularization and precision

If you see instability or extremely peaky routing:

## Monitoring: the minimum “must-log” list

If you only monitor loss and perplexity, you are flying blind. Add router and expert telemetry.

A practical minimum set:

## Common pitfalls (and how to avoid them)

### Pitfall 1: treating overflow as a minor implementation detail

Overflow is both a quality and a stability issue. If many tokens are dropped or rerouted, you can silently degrade the model. Track overflow explicitly.

### Pitfall 2: assuming routing will “self-fix”

Routing does learn, but it can also lock into a bad pattern early. If you see collapse early, do not wait too long. Adjust balancing, exploration, and router regularization.

### Pitfall 3: underestimating communication and batching constraints

If you cannot batch enough tokens to keep experts busy, SMoE can underperform dense baselines in wall-clock terms. This affects both training throughput and serving.

## Clearing up misconceptions (quickly)

***Key takeaways (Part E)***

***· Start with a simple baseline and treat balancing and capacity as first-class hyperparameters.***

***· Instrument routing and expert health early; most failures are visible quickly if you log the right signals.***

***· Most SMoE wins require systems readiness, not just architecture changes.***

## Overview

* Neural networks have become the cornerstone of modern deep learning, providing a powerful mechanism for discovering complex patterns and extracting meaningful insights from massive datasets. However, the performance and expressiveness of such networks often scale with their parameter count — larger models tend to perform better but at the cost of exponentially increasing computational and memory demands.
* **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** offers an elegant and efficient solution to this scaling bottleneck. Rather than activating all parameters for every input, MoE adopts a **conditional computation** paradigm — selectively activating only a small subset of “experts” based on the data. This approach allows models to achieve near-linear parameter scaling without a proportional increase in compute cost, making it a cornerstone of today’s ultra-large architectures.
* The MoE concept was first introduced in [Mixture of Experts](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/jjnh91.pdf) by Jacobs et al. (1991), which established the foundational principles of “gating” and “experts.” The gating network, acting as a dynamic controller, decides which expert (or subset of experts) should handle a given input. Each expert, in turn, specializes in a particular region of the input space, enabling the ensemble to capture complex, heterogeneous data distributions more effectively than monolithic models. This early framework laid the groundwork for later developments in conditional computation and ensemble learning.
* As deep learning matured, these ideas were revisited and dramatically scaled:

  + **The Sparsely-Gated Revolution:**
    - [Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538) by Shazeer et al. (2017) introduced **top-\(k\) routing**, a breakthrough mechanism that routes each input token through only the top \(k\) most relevant experts based on gating scores. This innovation drastically reduced computation while maintaining performance, making it feasible to train neural networks with billions of parameters. Additionally, the authors introduced **load-balancing losses** to ensure even expert utilization, mitigating the instability caused by uneven routing.
  + **Scaling with Simplicity:**
    - The [Switch Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) by Fedus et al. (2021) simplified the MoE architecture by using *top-1 routing* — assigning each token to a single expert instead of multiple ones. Despite this simplification, the Switch Transformer achieved state-of-the-art performance across large-scale NLP benchmarks while dramatically reducing communication overhead. It became a key stepping stone in scaling models like Google’s T5 family and influenced architectures underlying large-scale systems such as GPT and PaLM.
  + **Structured Sparsity and Efficiency:**
    - Building upon these advances, [Dropless MoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.15841) by Gale et al. (2022) reformulated sparse MoE computation using **block-sparse matrix multiplication**, a paradigm implemented in the **MegaBlocks** system. This approach removed the need for token “dropping” and capacity constraints that limited earlier MoE implementations. As a result, MegaBlocks achieved both superior scaling efficiency and hardware utilization, representing one of the fastest industry-grade sparse MoE frameworks to date.
* Together, these works reflect the steady evolution of MoE architectures — from theoretical ensemble models in the early 1990s to the computational backbone of trillion-parameter systems in the 2020s. This three-decade journey demonstrates the field’s resilience and innovation, with each milestone bringing a new balance between scalability, efficiency, and specialization.
* The infographic below [(source)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sflender/) summarizes these milestones in the history of sparse MoE technology. It highlights how these innovations — from Jacobs’ early gating networks to Shazeer’s sparsely-gated layers and Fedus’s streamlined switch routing — have shaped the trajectory of scalable AI systems such as OpenAI’s GPT-4, Google’s Switch Transformer, and emerging multimodal MoEs. Together, they showcase a recurring theme: **efficient specialization at scale** — the central promise of the Mixture-of-Experts paradigm.

#### Modern Implementations: Hardware-Aware and Domain-Adaptive MoEs

* The following generation of research, exemplified by [Dropless MoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.15841) by Gale et al. (2022), shifted focus toward *hardware-aware sparsity*. By reformulating MoE computation as block-sparse matrix operations, Dropless MoE (via the **MegaBlocks** framework) removed routing constraints and improved FLOPs utilization — allowing modern accelerators to exploit MoE sparsity efficiently. This efficiency breakthrough laid the foundation for **industrial-scale distributed MoEs**, particularly those powering multimodal and multilingual systems.

#### Influence on Next-Generation Models

* Modern models such as **Mixtral-8×7B**, **DeepSeek-V2**, **Gemini 1.5**, and **Claude 3** continue this lineage by embedding MoE principles not only in feed-forward layers but also in attention and cross-modal fusion mechanisms. Specifics below:

  + **[Mixtral-8×7B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088)** by Mistral AI (2024) integrates expert routing across decoder blocks, combining the efficiency of sparse activation with the expressivity of dense transformers.
  + **[DeepSeek-V2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434)** extends MoE routing into multimodal alignment, using shared experts for vision-language fusion.
  + **[Gemini 1.5](https://blog.google/technology/ai/google-gemini-1-5/)** by Google DeepMind (2024) applies hierarchical expert routing to unify text, image, and code understanding — marking one of the first large-scale commercial systems to employ *joint MoE* across modalities.
* A recent frontier-scale example is [Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534) by Kimi Team et al. (2025), which advances sparse MoE design by scaling to 1.04T total parameters with 32B activated parameters, 384 experts, 8 activated experts per token, and sparsity 48; its design shows that modern MoE scaling is increasingly governed by empirical sparsity laws, routing stability, optimizer stability, and expert-parallel communication efficiency rather than parameter count alone.

#### The Continuing Trajectory

* Across these stages, the Mixture-of-Experts paradigm has evolved from an ensemble-learning curiosity into a **core architectural principle of scalable intelligence**. By selectively activating computation, MoEs align compute expenditure with information complexity — a concept increasingly central to the sustainability and interpretability of trillion-parameter AI systems.
* Future directions now explore **structural routing**, **expert specialization across modalities**, and **dynamic compute allocation**, heralding a new era of adaptable, efficient, and semantically aware expert networks.

### Taxonomy of Modern MoE Architectures

* As Mixture-of-Experts architectures have evolved, researchers have introduced a variety of formulations tailored for efficiency, specialization, and scalability across modalities and tasks. Modern MoE systems can be organized into several key categories—each representing a distinct approach to expert routing, activation, and integration within large-scale models.

#### Sparse MoE Architectures

* Sparse MoE models activate only a small subset of experts for each input, achieving massive parameter scaling while maintaining computational efficiency.

  + **[Switch Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961)** by Fedus et al. (2021) exemplifies this paradigm, using *top-1 routing* to send each token to a single expert.
  + **[GLaM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.06905)** by Du et al. (2021) extends this with balanced token-to-expert assignments and importance-weighted routing.
  + **[Mixtral-8×7B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088)** by Mistral AI (2024) improves upon Switch’s efficiency with optimized load balancing and routing parallelism.
* **Key property:** Sparse activation ensures that only a fraction of model parameters are active per token, making these architectures ideal for large-scale pretraining.

#### Dense–Hybrid MoE Architectures

* Dense–Hybrid models blend the efficiency of sparse MoE layers with the robustness of dense transformer blocks. They selectively introduce MoE layers into deeper or more specialized parts of the network.

  + **[T5-MoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.08906)** by Zoph et al. (2022) incorporates sparse experts within the feed-forward layers of T5, combining dense attention with sparse computation.
  + **[DeepSeek-V2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434)** introduces hybrid routing within both encoder and decoder stacks, adapting expert utilization based on modality and context complexity.
* **Key property:** Hybrid models retain the stability of dense layers while exploiting MoE sparsity for scaling efficiency.

#### Hierarchical and Structured MoE Architectures

* Hierarchical MoEs introduce multiple layers or levels of routing, enabling structured specialization. Experts can operate at different semantic or abstraction levels (e.g., local vs. global).

  + **[Hierarchical Mixture of Experts (HMoE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.05144)** by Zhou et al. (2022) models expert hierarchies explicitly, allowing high-level experts to coordinate low-level ones.
  + **[Sparse-Transformer++](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07260)** by Xu et al. (2025) implements multi-stage routing—first among global experts, then among local sub-experts—enhancing interpretability and specialization.
  + **[HC-SMoE](https://openreview.net/pdf/643366be110a2f570b95fab96c6edba91a84eaec.pdf)** by Chen et al. (2025) clusters experts post-training using hierarchical clustering, merging redundant experts without retraining.
* **Key property:** These models enable *multi-granular routing*, improving efficiency and interpretability across hierarchical representations.

#### Joint MoE and Multimodal Architectures

* In multimodal MoE systems, both attention and feed-forward components are expert-based, allowing cross-modal interaction and dynamic parameter sharing.

  + **[Uni-MoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11273)** by Li et al. (2024) jointly routes text and vision tokens through shared experts, unifying multimodal learning.
  + **[Union of Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.02495)** by Yang et al. (2025) employs hierarchical routing where global experts manage modality fusion, while local experts refine within-modality reasoning.
* **Key property:** Joint MoEs exploit shared structure across modalities, enabling scalable multimodal reasoning and cross-domain generalization.

#### Adaptive and Dynamic MoE Architectures

* These architectures dynamically adjust the number of active experts or routing intensity based on input complexity or importance.

  + **[AdaMoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13233)** by Zeng et al. (2024) introduces token-adaptive routing with *null experts*, which skip computation for trivial tokens.
  + **[Expert Choice Routing (EC-MoE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09368)** by Zhou et al. (2022) reverses the routing direction—allowing experts to choose tokens—achieving better load balancing and conceptual clustering.
* **Key property:** Adaptive MoEs align compute allocation with token complexity, improving efficiency and semantic coherence.

#### Modern MoE Landscape

| **Type** | **Representative Models** | **Routing Mechanism** | **Key Advantage** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sparse | Switch Transformer, GLaM, Mixtral | Top-k token routing | Extreme scalability |
| Dense–Hybrid | T5-MoE, DeepSeek-V2 | Partial MoE integration | Stability + efficiency |
| Hierarchical | HMoE, Sparse-Transformer++, HC-SMoE | Multi-level expert routing | Interpretability, multi-scale reasoning |
| Joint / Multimodal | Uni-MoE, Union of Experts | Cross-modal routing | Unified multimodal processing |
| Adaptive / Dynamic | AdaMoE, EC-MoE | Token- or expert-adaptive | Compute proportional to complexity |

* In essence, modern MoE systems are evolving from simple token-wise routers into **hierarchically organized, multimodal, and adaptive ecosystems** of experts. This taxonomy captures the expanding design space of MoEs — from sparse parameter efficiency to cross-modal intelligence — underscoring their central role in next-generation AI architectures.

## Motivation: Why Mixture-of-Experts?

### The scaling bottleneck of dense neural networks

* Modern deep learning has been driven by a clear empirical trend: increasing model capacity improves performance when sufficient data and optimization stability are available. This pattern underlies the success of large Transformer-based models such as [BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805) by Devlin et al. (2018), [GPT-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165) by Brown et al. (2020), and [PaLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.02311) by Chowdhery et al. (2022). However, dense scaling suffers from a fundamental inefficiency: all parameters are activated for every token.
* As model size grows, this dense activation regime causes training and inference costs to rise sharply, not only due to increased FLOPs but also because of memory bandwidth pressure, inter-device communication, and synchronization overheads. Shazeer et al. explicitly describe this issue as a “quadratic blow-up” when both model size and dataset size increase in dense architectures ([Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538) by Shazeer et al. (2017)). This dense-activation regime quickly becomes economically and physically infeasible at trillion-parameter scale.
* The core challenge is therefore not a lack of representational power, but the inability of dense architectures to scale computation efficiently with model capacity.

### Conditional computation as a principled solution

* Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures address this challenge by introducing conditional computation. Rather than executing the full network for every token, an MoE model activates only a small subset of specialized sub-networks (experts), selected dynamically by a learned routing function.
* This idea traces back to early modular and ensemble methods such as [Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/jj.pdf) by Jacobs et al. (1991) and was later formalized in deep learning contexts through conditional computation frameworks like [Conditional Computation in Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.3432) by Bengio et al. (2013).
* Formally, given a token representation \(x\), a router produces a sparse gating vector \(g(x) \in \mathbb{R}^N\) over \(N\) experts, and only the top-\(k\) experts are evaluated:

  \[y(x) = \sum\_{i \in \text{Top-}k(g(x))} g\_i(x), f\_i(x)\]
  + where \(f\_i\) denotes the \(i^{th}\) expert network.
* This mechanism decouples model capacity from per-token compute, enabling models to grow in parameter count without incurring a proportional increase in computational cost.

### Scaling training with sparse activation

* The primary training advantage of MoE lies in compute-efficient scaling. By activating only a small fraction of parameters per token, MoE models can dramatically increase total parameter count while keeping training FLOPs nearly constant relative to a dense baseline.
* The sparsely-gated MoE layer introduced by Shazeer et al. (2017) demonstrated that it is possible to train models with orders-of-magnitude more parameters than dense Transformers, while maintaining similar training throughput. This insight was extended to large-scale distributed systems by [GShard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668) by Lepikhin et al. (2020), which showed that expert parameters could be sharded across thousands of accelerators and trained jointly using sparse routing.
* Further simplification came from [Switch Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) by Fedus et al. (2021), which demonstrated that routing each token to a single expert is sufficient to retain model quality while substantially reducing communication overhead. These results established sparse MoE as a practical path to training trillion-parameter models.
* In effect, MoE allows training compute to scale with the number of active experts per token rather than the total number of parameters, fundamentally altering the economics of large-scale pretraining.

### Training efficiency and expert specialization

* From a learning perspective, MoE enables specialization without explicit supervision. Empirical evidence suggests that experts self-organize around latent structures in the data, such as syntax, domain, or modality ([Towards Understanding Mixture of Experts in Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02868) by Chen et al. (2022)). Because each expert processes a narrower distribution of inputs, gradients are less noisy and convergence can be faster than in dense counterparts of comparable quality.
* This specialization effect becomes especially important in multilingual, multimodal, and instruction-tuned models, as demonstrated in [GLaM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.06905) by Du et al. (2021), [Mixtral of Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088) by Jiang et al. (2024), and [MoE-LLaVA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08017) by Xu et al. (2024).
* In large-scale pretraining regimes, this implicit specialization improves representational efficiency by reducing interference between unrelated patterns, allowing different experts to focus on distinct subspaces of the data distribution while sharing a common embedding and attention backbone.

### Efficient inference through conditional routing

* At inference time, MoE architectures provide a compelling quality–cost trade-off. Although the total parameter count may be extremely large, inference cost per token depends only on the number of activated experts, not on the full model size.
* This enables MoE models to achieve performance comparable to very large dense models while maintaining inference latency closer to that of much smaller networks. As a result, MoE is particularly attractive for deployment scenarios where throughput and cost efficiency are critical.
* Moreover, conditional routing allows computation to adapt to input complexity. Simple or redundant tokens can be handled by a small subset of experts, while more complex tokens may engage more specialized computation paths. This form of adaptive inference is fundamentally unavailable in fully dense architectures.

### Why MoE enables scalable neural networks

* Taken together, Mixture-of-Experts architectures provide a structural solution to the scaling limits of dense neural networks. By introducing sparsity at the level of parameter activation, MoE enables:

  + massive increases in model capacity without proportional training cost,
  + improved representational efficiency through expert specialization,
  + inference costs that scale with active computation rather than total parameters,
  + adaptive computation aligned with input complexity.
* As summarized in [A Comprehensive Survey of Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14393) by Jiang et al. (2025), MoE has evolved from an ensemble-learning technique into a central architectural principle for large-scale neural networks. Its success reflects a broader shift away from uniform computation toward models that allocate resources dynamically—making MoE a cornerstone of scalable training and inference in next-generation AI systems.

## Mixture-of-Experts: The Classic Approach

* The MoE concept is a type of ensemble learning technique initially developed within the field of artificial neural networks. It introduces the idea of training experts on specific subtasks of a complex predictive modeling problem.
* In a typical ensemble scenario, all models are trained on the same dataset, and their outputs are combined through simple averaging, weighted mean, or majority voting. However, in an MoE architecture, each “expert” model within the ensemble is only trained on a subset of data where it can achieve optimal performance, thus narrowing the model’s focus. Put simply, MoE is an architecture that divides input data into multiple sub-tasks and trains a group of experts to specialize in each sub-task. These experts can be thought of as smaller, specialized models that are better at solving their respective sub-tasks.
* The popularity of MoE only rose recently as the appearance of Large Language Models (LLMs) and transformer-based models in general swept through the machine learning field. Consequently, this is because of modern datasets’ increased complexity and size. Each dataset contains different regimes with vastly different relationships between the features and the labels.
* To appreciate the essence of MoE, it is crucial to understand its architectural elements:
  1. **Division of dataset into local subsets:** First, the predictive modeling problem is divided into subtasks. This division often requires domain knowledge or employs an unsupervised clustering algorithm. It’s important to clarify that clustering is not based on the feature vectors’ similarities. Instead, it’s executed based on the correlation among the relationships that the features share with the labels.
  2. **Expert Models:** These are the specialized neural network layers or experts that are trained to excel at specific sub-tasks. Each expert receives the same input pattern and processes it according to its specialization. Put simply, an expert is trained for each subset of the data. Typically, the experts themselves can be any model, from Support Vector Machines (SVM) to neural networks. Each expert model receives the same input pattern and makes a prediction.
  3. **Gating Network (Router):** The gating network, also called the router, is responsible for selecting which experts to use for each input data. It works by estimating the compatibility between the input data and each expert, and then outputs a softmax distribution over the experts. This distribution is used as the weights to combine the outputs of the expert layers. Put simply, this model helps interpret predictions made by each expert and decide which expert to trust for a given input.
  4. **Pooling Method:** Finally, an aggregation mechanism is needed to make a prediction based on the output from the gating network and the experts.
* The gating network and expert layers are jointly trained to minimize the overall loss function of the MoE model. The gating network learns to route each input to the most relevant expert layer(s), while the expert layers specialize in their assigned sub-tasks.
* This divide-and-conquer approach effectively delegates complex tasks to experts, enabling efficient processing and improved accuracy. Together, these components ensure that the right expert handles the right task. The gating network effectively routes each input to the most appropriate expert(s), while the experts focus on their specific areas of strength. This collaborative approach leads to a more versatile and capable overall model.
* In summary, MoEs improve efficiency by dynamically selecting a subset of model parameters (experts) for each input. This architecture allows for larger models while keeping computational costs manageable by activating only a few experts per input.

> Put simply, MoE is how an ensemble of AI models decides as one. It is basically multiple “experts”, i.e., individual models, in a “trend coat”.

### Top-level Intuition

* MoE leverages multiple specialized models (experts) to solve complex tasks by dividing the problem space. Each expert becomes proficient in a specific subset of the data, leading to more efficient learning and problem-solving.
  + Specifically, in the feed-forward parts of the model (not the attention blocks) the router selects an expert layer for every token. In the architecture proposed in the seminal paper [Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538), within the feed-forward components of the model (excluding the attention blocks), the router assigns an expert layer for each token. The figures below (source: [Nathan Lambert’s tweet](https://twitter.com/natolambert/status/1734326629521035588), the [Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) and [Switch Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) paper) illustrates this feed-forward-based MoE architecture.
  + Conversely, recent publications such as [JetMoE: Reaching Llama2 Performance with 0.1M Dollars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07413) have expanded this approach, modeling both feed-forward and attention blocks as MoEs.
* A gating network determines which expert(s) to activate for a given input, ensuring the most relevant expertise is applied. The gate learns to assign inputs to experts dynamically, optimizing performance based on the task’s needs.
* MoE architectures reduce computational cost by only activating a subset of experts for each input, rather than the entire model. This approach allows for scalability and adaptability, making MoE suitable for large-scale and diverse datasets.

#### Gate Functionality

* This section seeks to answer how the gating network (also called gate, router, or switch) in MoE models works under the hood.
* Let’s explore two distinct but interconnected functions of the gate in a MoE model:
  1. **Clustering the Data**: In the context of an MoE model, clustering the data means that the gate is learning to identify and group together similar data points. This is not clustering in the traditional unsupervised learning sense, where the algorithm discovers clusters without any external labels. Instead, the gate is using the training process to recognize patterns or features in the data that suggest which data points are similar to each other and should be treated similarly. This is a crucial step because it determines how the data is organized and interpreted by the model.
  2. **Mapping Experts to Clusters**: Once the gate has identified clusters within the data, its next role is to assign or map each cluster to the most appropriate expert within the MoE model. Each expert in the model is specialized to handle different types of data or different aspects of the problem. The gate’s function here is to direct each data point (or each group of similar data points) to the expert that is best suited to process it. This mapping is dynamic and is based on the strengths and specialties of each expert as they evolve during the training process.
* In summary, the gate in an MoE model is responsible for organizing the incoming data into meaningful groups (clustering) and then efficiently allocating these groups to the most relevant expert models within the MoE system for further processing. This dual role of the gate is critical for the overall performance and efficiency of the MoE model, enabling it to handle complex tasks by leveraging the specialized skills of its various expert components.

## Hands-On Exercise: How does an MoE model work?

* Credits to [Tom Yeh](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tom-yeh?miniProfileUrn=urn%3Ali%3Afsd_profile%3AACoAAAD1V7ABSoHPrWi3L_G0ivIOw29nEBQ1uKQ&lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Ad_flagship3_detail_base%3Bip616P99S4%2B9S%2Fi%2F3dqcQw%3D%3D) for this exercise.
* Let’s calculate an MoE model by hand, with the following config: (i) number of experts: 2, (ii) tokens: 2, (iii) sparse.
* Step-by-step walkthrough:
  1. The MoE block receives two tokens (blue, orange).
  2. Gate Network processes \(X\_1\) (blue) and determined \(\text{Expert}\_2\) should be activated.
  3. \(\text{Expert}\_2\) processes \(X\_1\) (blue).
  4. Gate Network processes \(X\_2\) (orange) and determined \(\text{Expert}\_1\) should be activated.
  5. \(\text{Expert}\_1\) processes \(X\_2\) (orange).
  6. ReLU activation function processes the outputs of the experts and produces the final output.

#### Key Benefits

* **Size:** The model can get really large (while still being efficient, as highlighted in the next point) simply by adding more experts. In this example, adding one more expert means adding 16 more weight parameters.
* **Efficiency:** The gate network will select a subset of experts to actually compute, in the above exercise: one expert. In other words, only 50% of the parameters are involved in processing a token.

## The Deep Learning Way: Sparsely-Gated MoE

* In 2017, an extension of the MoE paradigm suited for deep learning was proposed by Shazeer et al. in [Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538).
* In most deep learning models, increasing model capacity generally translates to improved performance when datasets are sufficiently large. Generally, when the entire model is activated by every example, it can lead to “a roughly quadratic blow-up in training costs, as both the model size and the number of training examples increase”, stated by [Shazeer et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538).
* Although the disadvantages of dense models are clear, there have been various challenges for an effective conditional computation method targeted toward modern deep learning models, mainly for the following reasons:
  1. Modern computing devices like GPUs and TPUs perform better in arithmetic operations than in network branching.
  2. Larger batch sizes benefit performance but are reduced by conditional computation.
  3. Network bandwidth can limit computational efficiency, notably affecting embedding layers.
  4. Some schemes might need loss terms to attain required sparsity levels, impacting model quality and load balance.
  5. Model capacity is vital for handling vast data sets, a challenge that current conditional computation literature doesn’t adequately address.
* The MoE technique presented by Shazeer et al. aims to achieve conditional computation while addressing the abovementioned issues. They could increase model capacity by more than a thousandfold while only sustaining minor computational efficiency losses.
* The authors introduced a new type of network layer called the “Sparsely-Gated MoE Layer.” They are built on previous iterations of MoE and aim to provide a general-purpose neural network component that can be adapted to different types of tasks.
* The Sparsely-Gated MoE architecture (henceforth, referred to as the MoE architecture), consists of numerous expert networks, each being a simple feed-forward neural network and a trainable gating network. The gating network is responsible for selecting a sparse combination of these experts to process each input.

* The fascinating feature here is the use of sparsity in the gating function. This means that for every input instance, the gating network only selects a few experts for processing, keeping the rest inactive. This sparsity and expert selection is achieved dynamically for each input, making the entire process highly flexible and adaptive. Notably, the computational efficiency is preserved since inactive parts of the network are not processed.
* The MoE layer can be stacked hierarchically, where the primary MoE selects a sparsely weighted combination of “experts.” Each combination utilizes a MoE layer.
* Moreover, the authors also introduced an innovative technique called Noisy Top-\(K\) Gating. This mechanism adds a tunable Gaussian noise to the gating function, retains only the top \(k\) values, and assigns the rest to negative infinity, translating to a zero gating value. Such an approach ensures the sparsity of the gating network while maintaining robustness against potential discontinuities in the gating function output. Interestingly, it also aids in load balancing across the expert networks.
* In their framework, both the gating network and the experts are trained jointly via back-propagation, the standard training mechanism for neural networks. The output from the gating network is a sparse, n-dimensional vector, which serves as the gate values for the n-expert networks. The output from each expert is then weighted by the corresponding gating value to produce the final model output.
* The Sparse MoE architecture has been a game-changer in LLMs, allowing us to scale up modeling capacity with almost constant computational complexity, resulting breakthroughs such as the Switch Transformer, GPT-4, Mixtral-8x7b, and more.

## The “How” Behind MoE

* Although the success of MoE is clear in the deep learning field, as with most things in deep learning, our understanding of how it can perform so well is rather unclear.
* Notably, each expert model is initialized and trained in the same manner, and the gating network is typically configured to dispatch data equally to each expert. Unlike traditional MoE methods, all experts are trained jointly with the MoE layer on the same dataset. It is fascinating how each expert can become “specialized” in their own task, and experts in MoE do not collapse into a single model.

# Mixture of Experts (MoE) — Comprehensive Overview

## Overview and Motivation
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is an architectural paradigm that enables massive scaling of neural networks through **conditional computation** — selectively activating only a small subset of "experts" per input rather than all parameters. This decouples model capacity from per-token compute, allowing near-linear parameter scaling without proportional compute cost increases. The concept originated with Jacobs et al. (1991) and was revolutionized by Shazeer et al. (2017) with **Sparsely-Gated MoE** and top-k routing, followed by the **Switch Transformer** (Fedus et al., 2021) with top-1 routing, and **MegaBlocks/Dropless MoE** (Gale et al., 2022) with block-sparse matrix multiplication.

## Key Milestones
- **1991**: Jacobs et al. introduce MoE with gating networks and expert specialization
- **2017**: Shazeer et al. introduce Sparsely-Gated MoE with top-k routing and load-balancing losses
- **2020**: GShard (Lepikhin et al.) scales MoE to distributed systems
- **2021**: Switch Transformer simplifies to top-1 routing, reducing communication overhead
- **2022**: MegaBlocks introduces block-sparse computation, removing token dropping
- **2024-2025**: Modern models like Mixtral-8×7B, DeepSeek-V2, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3, and Kimi K2 (1.04T parameters, 384 experts, sparsity 48) embed MoE principles broadly

## Taxonomy of Modern MoE Architectures
1. **Sparse MoE**: Switch Transformer, GLaM, Mixtral — top-k token routing, extreme scalability
2. **Dense–Hybrid MoE**: T5-MoE, DeepSeek-V2 — partial MoE integration for stability + efficiency
3. **Hierarchical/Structured MoE**: HMoE, Sparse-Transformer++, HC-SMoE — multi-level expert routing for interpretability
4. **Joint/Multimodal MoE**: Uni-MoE, Union of Experts — cross-modal routing for unified multimodal processing
5. **Adaptive/Dynamic MoE**: AdaMoE, Expert Choice Routing — compute proportional to input complexity

## Core Technical Concepts

### Expert Capacity and Capacity Factor
The capacity factor determines how many tokens each expert can process, defined as: capacity = (tokens per batch / number of experts) × capacity factor. Key implications include token overflow/dropping, load-balancing trade-offs, and computational efficiency.

### Load Balancing
Auxiliary loss functions encourage even token distribution across experts, preventing routing collapse where all tokens go to a few experts.

### Expert Specialization
Experts self-organize around latent data structures (syntax, domain, modality) without explicit supervision. Models like Mixtral-8×7B and MoE-LLaVA demonstrate this specialization empirically.

### Shared Experts
Separate common knowledge from specialized knowledge by having always-active "shared experts" alongside routed experts, improving specialization and reducing routing dependence.

### Expert Choice Routing
Reverses routing direction — experts choose which tokens to process — achieving better load balancing and conceptual clustering.

### Expert Parallelism
Distributes expert parameters across devices, routing tokens to the appropriate device for processing, with hybrid parallel strategies combining data, model, and expert parallelism.

## Key Benefits
- **Massive capacity scaling** without proportional training cost
- **Training compute scales with active experts per token**, not total parameters
- **Inference cost depends on activated experts**, enabling quality-cost trade-offs
- **Adaptive computation** aligned with input complexity
- **Expert specialization** improves representational efficiency

## Limitations
- **Inference-time memory**: All expert parameters must reside in VRAM despite sparse activation
- **Training instability and load imbalance**
- **Communication overhead** in distributed settings
- **Routing complexity and gradient fragmentation**
- **Underutilization of model capacity** and inference latency variability

## Modern Frontier Example: Kimi K2 (2025)
Demonstrates MoE scaling governed by sparsity laws, routing stability, and optimizer stability: 1.04T total parameters, 32B activated, 384 experts, 8 activated per token, sparsity 48.

## Popular MoE Models
- **GPT-4** (rumored MoE architecture)
- **Mixtral 8x7B** (Mistral AI, 2024)
- **OpenMoE**
- **DeepSeek-V2**, **Gemini 1.5**, **Claude 3**

## Future Directions
Structural routing, cross-modal expert specialization, dynamic compute allocation, and semantically aware expert networks.

[Fedus et al., 2022] 9 Expert Count: Fine-Grained Experts (Strategy 2) Strategy 2: keep total parameters ﬁxed, make experts smaller and more numerous [DeepSeek, 2024]: Split each expert’s hidden dimension by n, create n× more experts: Baseline Fine-grained Experts/layer 8 (dim d) 16 (dim d/2) Activated 2 4 Combinations �8 2  = 28 �16 4  = 1,820 Same total parameters and FLOPs, but vastly more routing ﬂexibility.
10 Fine-Grained Expert Segmentation Diminishing returns after a certain granularity. More communication costs if not managed well.
[DeepSeek, 2024] 11 Shared Experts Idea: keep a ﬁxed set of experts always active, route to the rest.
Example: 1 shared expert + 3 routed experts selected from 31 total.
Intuition: shared expert learns common info, reducing redundancy.
12 Shared Experts: Mixed Results • DeepSeek-MoE: 2 shared experts — reports improvement • OLMoE: no shared expert — comparable performance [AI2, 2025] • Reduces modeling ﬂexibility (fewer parameters available for routing) 13 Routing: Basic Idea Step 1: compute a score for each (token, expert) pair.
Surprisingly simple: introduce a weight vector ei for each expert, take dot products: st,i = softmaxi  ˜ hT t ei  Step 2: select experts according to some strategy: Token choice Each token chooses its top-k experts (most common) Expert choice Each expert chooses its top-k tokens Global choice Globally optimize the assignment 14 Top-k Token-Choice Routing The dominant approach in all major MoE LLMs: Gating weights: gi,t =    si,t if si,t ∈Top-k({sj,t}N j=1, K) 0 otherwise Output: h′ t = N X i=1 gi,t FFNi(˜ ht) + ˜ ht Pros: simple, ensures every token gets processed.
Cons: load balancing is tricky (all tokens may pick the same expert), top-k selection is not diﬀerentiable.
15 Routing: Worked Example 16 Top-k Routing Diagram [Fedus et al., 2022] 17 Class Poll If you remove the load balancing loss during MoE training, what happens?
(A) All experts get used equally (B) A few experts get all the tokens (C) Training gets slower but still works (D) No diﬀerence 17 Load Balancing and Token Dropping Solution: add an auxiliary load balancing loss.
18 Token Dropping and Capacity [Fedus et al., 2022] 19 Alternative: Expert Choice Routing Each expert chooses a ﬁxed number of tokens (instead of vice versa).
Pros: • Solves load balancing by construction • Model can allocate more capacity to certain tokens (selected by multiple experts) Cons: • At generation time, only one token at a time — need a diﬀerent selection mechanism • Some tokens may not be selected by any expert (token dropping) Other alternatives: hashing [Roller et al., 2021], RL-based routing [Clark et al., 2022], linear assignment, optimal transport — but top-k token choice dominates in practice.
20 Expert Choice vs. Token Choice Both models: 8-expert MoE, 2 experts active. Same active parameters. [AI2, 2025] Comparable performance — token choice slightly better on downstream tasks and simpler at inference time.
21 Expert Balancing Loss Penalize experts that receive too many tokens or too much probability mass: Lbalance = α N X i=1 fi · Pi • fi: fraction of tokens in the batch routed to expert i • Pi: fraction of routing probability assigned to expert i • α: loss weight (typically 0.001–0.01) Heuristic, but surprisingly eﬀective and widely used. [Zoph et al., 2022] Without this loss, training quickly collapses — one expert gets all tokens.
22 Eﬀect of Load Balancing 23 Poll Answer: (B) A Few Experts Get All the Tokens Without load balancing, the router collapses: it learns to send everything to 1–2 “popular” experts.
Why? Self-reinforcing loop: 1. Expert i gets slightly more tokens by chance 2. Expert i gets more gradient updates ⇒becomes better 3. Router sends even more tokens to expert i 4. Other experts starve and never improve This is why the balancing loss and z-loss are essential — they break this feedback loop.
24 Stability: Router Z-Loss Large router logits cause instability. Explicitly penalize them: LZ(x) = 1 B B X i=1  log N X j=1 exi,j   2 where x ∈RB×N are the router logits.
• Makes the softmax denominator smaller ⇒more uniform routing • Prevents numerical overﬂow in mixed-precision training • Typical weight: 0.001 Full training loss: L = LLM + α Lbalance + β LZ 25 Per-Expert vs. Per-Device Balancing In practice, two levels of balancing are used together: Per-expert The loss we just saw: balance tokens across individual experts. Ensures all experts are utilized.
Per-device Group experts by GPU. Apply a separate loss to balance across groups.
Ensures no GPU is idle while others are overloaded.
Why both? Per-expert balancing can still leave devices unbalanced if all the “popular” experts happen to live on the same GPU. Per-device balancing directly optimizes for hardware utilization.
Used in DeepSeek-MoE (expert + device-level balance loss) and standard in most production MoE training.
26 Hashing vs. Learned Routers Learned router (standard): a weight vector per expert, trained end-to-end.
st,i = softmaxi(˜ hT t ei) Hash router [Roller et al., 2021]: no learned parameters at all.
• Assign each token to an expert via a ﬁxed hash function • Perfectly balanced by construction (if hash is uniform) • No training instability, no auxiliary losses needed Surprising result: hash routing performs reasonably well — suggesting that much of the MoE beneﬁt comes from having more parameters, not from smart routing.
But learned routing still wins, especially at scale. All production MoE LLMs use learned routers.
27 Expert Parallelism Experts can reside on diﬀerent accelerators. Data is dynamically dispatched.
Parallelism type What’s split Data parallelism Same model on each device, diﬀerent data Model parallelism Model layers split across devices Expert parallelism Diﬀerent experts on diﬀerent devices In practice, combine expert parallelism with data and model parallelism.
Key challenge: all-to-all communication — each token must be sent to its assigned expert’s device and results sent back. Load imbalance ⇒some devices idle.
28 Parallelism Strategies 29 Sparse Upcycling Idea: convert a pretrained dense model into a MoE model.
1. Clone the dense MLP N times to create N experts 2. Introduce fresh router parameters 3. Continue pretraining as MoE Claim: dense pretraining + sparse upcycle > sparse pretraining from scratch (at ﬁxed total FLOPs).
But: mixed results — OLMoE found sparse pretraining from scratch catches up quickly (25% of dense model’s budget). [AI2, 2025] Can also bias optimization: if the pretrained model is well-trained, hard for experts to diverge from each other.
30 DeepSeek-MoE Architecture • 16B total, 2.8B active • 66 experts, 8 activated • 512 hidden dim per expert • 2 shared experts • All FFN layers →MoE Training • Per-token routing • Pipeline parallelism (no EP) • No token dropping • Balance loss weight: 0.001 • Device-level balance loss Result: with 40% of pretraining compute, matches dense DeepSeek 7B.
31 OLMoE Architecture • 6.9B total, 1.3B active • 64 small experts, 8 activated • 1,024 FFN dim (“small expert”) • No shared expert Training • Per-token, dropless routing • Balance loss weight: 0.01 • Router z-loss weight: 0.001 Eﬃciency: 23,600 tok/sec/GPU (MoE) vs. 37,500 (dense). Reaches dense model performance 2× faster in wall-clock time.
Fully open-source: weights, data, code, training logs. [AI2, 2025] 32 Domain Specialization Some experts in some layers activate more frequently for particular domains: • Certain experts specialize in code (GitHub data) • Others specialize in scientiﬁc text (arXiv) • Specialization is more pronounced in later layers This emerges naturally from training — experts are not explicitly assigned to domains.
33 Summary MoE Replace FFN with N experts + router. Only k experts active per token.
Scaling More total parameters at ﬁxed FLOPs. New scaling dimension.
Routing Top-k token choice dominates. Score = dot product with expert weight vectors.
Training Need auxiliary losses: expert balancing + z-loss for stability.
Systems Expert parallelism + all-to-all communication. Sparse upcycling from dense models.
In practice Used by Gemini, GPT-oss, DeepSeek V3, Qwen 3, Mixtral.
34

args.summary:
This webpage provides a comprehensive overview of Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures in large language models. The key idea is replacing the Transformer FFN layer with a sparse layer containing N experts (FFNs) and a router that selects which experts to use per token. MoE decouples total parameters from compute per token (e.g., a 47B total parameter MoE model may only have 13B active parameters and ~13B FLOPs/token). This enables better inference-cost vs. performance and more efficient training. MoE is used in top LLMs including Gemini, GPT-4, Qwen 3, DeepSeek V3, and Mixtral.

**Key Design Decisions:**
- Experts are placed in FFN layers (attention layer possible but less stable)
- More experts generally improve performance with diminishing returns
- Fine-grained experts: split hidden dimension to create more, smaller experts for greater routing flexibility
- Shared experts: some always active, others routed; mixed results

**Routing:** Top-k token-choice routing dominates in practice. Each token selects its top-k experts via dot product with expert weight vectors. Alternative: expert-choice routing (each expert picks tokens), which solves load balancing but has generation-time issues.

**Training Challenges & Solutions:**
- Load balancing is critical; without it, 1-2 experts get all tokens (self-reinforcing collapse loop)
- Auxiliary load balancing loss: L_balance = α * Σ(f_i * P_i) — penalizes experts receiving too many tokens or probability mass
- Router z-loss prevents large logits and numerical overflow: L_Z = (1/B) Σ(log Σ e^x_i,j)²
- Full loss: L = LLM + α L_balance + β L_Z
- Per-device balancing also used to prevent GPU load imbalance

**Downsides:** System complexity, new losses/hyperparameters, high memory requirements (all parameters must be hosted), training instability.

**Case Studies:**
- DeepSeek-MoE: 16B total/2.8B active, 66 experts (8 activated), 2 shared experts, matches dense 7B with 40% of pretraining compute
- OLMoE: 6.9B total/1.3B active, 64 small experts (8 activated), no shared expert, reaches dense performance 2× faster in wall-clock time

**Additional Notes:** Domain specialization emerges naturally (some experts specialize in code, scientific text, etc.). Sparse upcycling (converting dense to MoE) vs. training from scratch is debated. Expert parallelism with all-to-all communication is the standard systems approach.
