## What is a Mixture of Experts (MoE)?

The scale of a model is one of the most important axes for better model quality. Given a fixed computing budget, training a larger model for fewer steps is better than training a smaller model for more steps.

Mixture of Experts enable models to be pretrained with far less compute, which means you can dramatically scale up the model or dataset size with the same compute budget as a dense model. In particular, a MoE model should achieve the same quality as its dense counterpart much faster during pretraining.

So, what exactly is a MoE? In the context of transformer models, a MoE consists of two main elements:

![Switch Layer](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/00_switch_transformer.png)

So, to recap, in MoEs we replace every FFN layer of the transformer model with an MoE layer, which is composed of a gate network and a certain number of experts.

Although MoEs provide benefits like efficient pretraining and faster inference compared to dense models, they also come with challenges:

Now that we have a rough idea of what a MoE is, let’s take a look at the research developments that led to their invention.

## A Brief History of MoEs

The roots of MoEs come from the 1991 paper [Adaptive Mixture of Local Experts](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/jjnh91.pdf). The idea, akin to ensemble methods, was to have a supervised procedure for a system composed of separate networks, each handling a different subset of the training cases. Each separate network, or expert, specializes in a different region of the input space. How is the expert chosen? A gating network determines the weights for each expert. During training, both the expert and the gating are trained.

Between 2010-2015, two different research areas contributed to later MoE advancement:

These works led to exploring a mixture of experts in the context of NLP. Concretely, [Shazeer et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538) (2017, with “et al.” including Geoffrey Hinton and Jeff Dean, [Google’s Chuck Norris](https://www.informatika.bg/jeffdean)) scaled this idea to a 137B LSTM (the de-facto NLP architecture back then, created by Schmidhuber) by introducing sparsity, allowing to keep very fast inference even at high scale. This work focused on translation but faced many challenges, such as high communication costs and training instabilities.

![MoE layer in LSTM](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/01_moe_layer.png)

MoEs have allowed training multi-trillion parameter models, such as the open-sourced 1.6T parameters Switch Transformers, among others. MoEs have also been explored in Computer Vision, but this blog post will focus on the NLP domain.

## What is Sparsity?

Sparsity uses the idea of conditional computation. While in dense models all the parameters are used for all the inputs, sparsity allows us to only run some parts of the whole system.

Let’s dive deeper into Shazeer's exploration of MoEs for translation. The idea of conditional computation (parts of the network are active on a per-example basis) allows one to scale the size of the model without increasing the computation, and hence, this led to thousands of experts being used in each MoE layer.

This setup introduces some challenges. For example, although large batch sizes are usually better for performance, batch sizes in MOEs are effectively reduced as data flows through the active experts. For example, if our batched input consists of 10 tokens, **five tokens might end in one expert, and the other five tokens might end in five different experts, leading to uneven batch sizes and underutilization**. The [Making MoEs go brrr](#making-moes-go-brrr) section below will discuss other challenges and solutions.

How can we solve this? A learned gating network (G) decides which experts (E) to send a part of the input:

y=∑i=1nG(x)iEi(x)
y = \sum\_{i=1}^{n} G(x)\_i E\_i(x)
y=i=1∑n​G(x)i​Ei​(x)

In this setup, all experts are run for all inputs - it’s a weighted multiplication. But, what happens if G is 0? If that’s the case, there’s no need to compute the respective expert operations and hence we save compute. What’s a typical gating function? In the most traditional setup, we just use a simple network with a softmax function. The network will learn which expert to send the input.

Gσ(x)=Softmax(x⋅Wg)
G\_\sigma(x) = \text{Softmax}(x \cdot W\_g)
Gσ​(x)=Softmax(x⋅Wg​)

Shazeer’s work also explored other gating mechanisms, such as Noisy Top-k Gating. This gating approach introduces some (tunable) noise and then keeps the top k values. That is:

H(x)i=(x⋅Wg)i+StandardNormal()⋅Softplus((x⋅Wnoise)i)
H(x)\_i = (x \cdot W\_{\text{g}})\_i + \text{StandardNormal()} \cdot \text{Softplus}((x \cdot W\_{\text{noise}})\_i)
H(x)i​=(x⋅Wg​)i​+StandardNormal()⋅Softplus((x⋅Wnoise​)i​)

KeepTopK(v,k)i={viif vi is in the top k elements of v,−∞otherwise.
\text{KeepTopK}(v, k)\_i = \begin{cases}
v\_i & \text{if } v\_i \text{ is in the top } k \text{ elements of } v, \\
-\infty & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
KeepTopK(v,k)i​={vi​−∞​if vi​ is in the top k elements of v,otherwise.​

G(x)=Softmax(KeepTopK(H(x),k))
G(x) = \text{Softmax}(\text{KeepTopK}(H(x), k))
G(x)=Softmax(KeepTopK(H(x),k))

This sparsity introduces some interesting properties. By using a low enough k (e.g. one or two), we can train and run inference much faster than if many experts were activated. Why not just select the top expert? The initial conjecture was that routing to more than one expert was needed to have the gate learn how to route to different experts, so at least two experts had to be picked. The [Switch Transformers](#switch-transformers) section revisits this decision.

Why do we add noise? That’s for load balancing!

## Load balancing tokens for MoEs

As discussed before, if all our tokens are sent to just a few popular experts, that will make training inefficient. In a normal MoE training, the gating network converges to mostly activate the same few experts. This self-reinforces as favored experts are trained quicker and hence selected more. To mitigate this, an **auxiliary loss** is added to encourage giving all experts equal importance. This loss ensures that all experts receive a roughly equal number of training examples. The following sections will also explore the concept of expert capacity, which introduces a threshold of how many tokens can be processed by an expert. In `transformers`, the auxiliary loss is exposed via the `aux_loss` parameter.

`transformers`
`aux_loss`

## MoEs and Transformers

Transformers are a very clear case that scaling up the number of parameters improves the performance, so it’s not surprising that Google explored this with [GShard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668), which explores scaling up transformers beyond 600 billion parameters.

GShard replaces every other FFN layer with an MoE layer using top-2 gating in both the encoder and the decoder. The next image shows how this looks like for the encoder part. This setup is quite beneficial for large-scale computing: when we scale to multiple devices, the MoE layer is shared across devices while all the other layers are replicated. This is further discussed in the [“Making MoEs go brrr”](#making-moes-go-brrr) section.

![MoE Transformer Encoder](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/02_moe_block.png)

To maintain a balanced load and efficiency at scale, the GShard authors introduced a couple of changes in addition to an auxiliary loss similar to the one discussed in the previous section:

The GShard paper has contributions by expressing parallel computation patterns that work well for MoEs, but discussing that is outside the scope of this blog post.

**Note:** when we run inference, only some experts will be triggered. At the same time, there are shared computations, such as self-attention, which is applied for all tokens. That’s why when we talk of a 47B model of 8 experts, we can run with the compute of a 12B dense model. If we use top-2, 14B parameters would be used. But given that the attention operations are shared (among others), the actual number of used parameters is 12B.

## Switch Transformers

Although MoEs showed a lot of promise, they struggle with training and fine-tuning instabilities. [Switch Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) is a very exciting work that deep dives into these topics. The authors even released a [1.6 trillion parameters MoE on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/google/switch-c-2048) with 2048 experts, which you can run with transformers. Switch Transformers achieved a 4x pre-train speed-up over T5-XXL.

![Switch Transformer Layer](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/03_switch_layer.png)

Just as in GShard, the authors replaced the FFN layers with a MoE layer. The Switch Transformers paper proposes a Switch Transformer layer that receives two inputs (two different tokens) and has four experts.

Contrary to the initial idea of using at least two experts, Switch Transformers uses a simplified single-expert strategy. The effects of this approach are:

Switch Transformers also explores the concept of expert capacity.

Expert Capacity=(tokens per batchnumber of experts)×capacity factor
\text{Expert Capacity} = \left(\frac{\text{tokens per batch}}{\text{number of experts}}\right) \times \text{capacity factor}
Expert Capacity=(number of expertstokens per batch​)×capacity factor

The capacity suggested above evenly divides the number of tokens in the batch across the number of experts. If we use a capacity factor greater than 1, we provide a buffer for when tokens are not perfectly balanced. Increasing the capacity will lead to more expensive inter-device communication, so it’s a trade-off to keep in mind. In particular, Switch Transformers perform well at low capacity factors (1-1.25)

Switch Transformer authors also revisit and simplify the load balancing loss mentioned in the sections. For each Switch layer, the auxiliary loss is added to the total model loss during training. This loss encourages uniform routing and can be weighted using a hyperparameter.

The authors also experiment with selective precision, such as training the experts with `bfloat16` while using full precision for the rest of the computations. Lower precision reduces communication costs between processors, computation costs, and memory for storing tensors. The initial experiments, in which both the experts and the gate networks were trained in `bfloat16`, yielded more unstable training. This was, in particular, due to the router computation: as the router has an exponentiation function, having higher precision is important. To mitigate the instabilities, full precision was used for the routing as well.

`bfloat16`
`bfloat16`
![Table shows that selective precision does not degrade quality.](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/04_switch_table.png)

This [notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1aGGVHZmtKmcNBbAwa9hbu58DDpIuB5O4?usp=sharing) showcases fine-tuning Switch Transformers for summarization, but we suggest first reviewing the [fine-tuning section](#fine-tuning-moes).

Switch Transformers uses an encoder-decoder setup in which they did a MoE counterpart of T5. The [GLaM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.06905) paper explores pushing up the scale of these models by training a model matching GPT-3 quality using 1/3 of the energy (yes, thanks to the lower amount of computing needed to train a MoE, they can reduce the carbon footprint by up to an order of magnitude). The authors focused on decoder-only models and few-shot and one-shot evaluation rather than fine-tuning. They used Top-2 routing and much larger capacity factors. In addition, they explored the capacity factor as a metric one can change during training and evaluation depending on how much computing one wants to use.

## Stabilizing training with router Z-loss

The balancing loss previously discussed can lead to instability issues. We can use many methods to stabilize sparse models at the expense of quality. For example, introducing dropout improves stability but leads to loss of model quality. On the other hand, adding more multiplicative components improves quality but decreases stability.

Router z-loss, introduced in [ST-MoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.08906), significantly improves training stability without quality degradation by penalizing large logits entering the gating network. Since this loss encourages absolute magnitude of values to be smaller, roundoff errors are reduced, which can be quite impactful for exponential functions such as the gating. We recommend reviewing the paper for details.

## What does an expert learn?

The ST-MoE authors observed that encoder experts specialize in a group of tokens or shallow concepts. For example, we might end with a punctuation expert, a proper noun expert, etc. On the other hand, the decoder experts have less specialization. The authors also trained in a multilingual setup. Although one could imagine each expert specializing in a language, the opposite happens: due to token routing and load balancing, there is no single expert specialized in any given language.

![Experts specialize in some token groups](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/05_experts_learning.png)

## How does scaling the number of experts impact pretraining?

More experts lead to improved sample efficiency and faster speedup, but these are diminishing gains (especially after 256 or 512), and more VRAM will be needed for inference. The properties studied in Switch Transformers at large scale were consistent at small scale, even with 2, 4, or 8 experts per layer.

## Fine-tuning MoEs

Mixtral is supported with version 4.36.0 of transformers. You can install it with `pip install transformers==4.36.0 --upgrade`

`pip install transformers==4.36.0 --upgrade`

The overfitting dynamics are very different between dense and sparse models. Sparse models are more prone to overfitting, so we can explore higher regularization (e.g. dropout) within the experts themselves (e.g. we can have one dropout rate for the dense layers and another, higher, dropout for the sparse layers).

One question is whether to use the auxiliary loss for fine-tuning. The ST-MoE authors experimented with turning off the auxiliary loss, and the quality was not significantly impacted, even when up to 11% of the tokens were dropped. Token dropping might be a form of regularization that helps prevent overfitting.

Switch Transformers observed that at a fixed pretrain perplexity, the sparse model does worse than the dense counterpart in downstream tasks, especially on reasoning-heavy tasks such as SuperGLUE. On the other hand, for knowledge-heavy tasks such as TriviaQA, the sparse model performs disproportionately well. The authors also observed that a fewer number of experts helped at fine-tuning. Another observation that confirmed the generalization issue is that the model did worse in smaller tasks but did well in larger tasks.

![Fine-tuning learning curves](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/06_superglue_curves.png)

One could experiment with freezing all non-expert weights. That is, we'll only update the MoE layers. This leads to a huge performance drop. We could try the opposite: freezing only the parameters in MoE layers, which worked almost as well as updating all parameters. This can help speed up and reduce memory for fine-tuning. This can be somewhat counter-intuitive as 80% of the parameters are in the MoE layers (in the ST-MoE project). Their hypothesis for that architecture is that, as expert layers only occur every 1/4 layers, and each token sees at most two experts per layer, updating the MoE parameters affects much fewer layers than updating other parameters.

![Only updating the non MoE layers works well in fine-tuning](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/07_superglue_bars.png)

One last part to consider when fine-tuning sparse MoEs is that they have different fine-tuning hyperparameter setups - e.g., sparse models tend to benefit more from smaller batch sizes and higher learning rates.

![Table comparing fine-tuning batch size and learning rate between dense and sparse models.](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/08_superglue_dense_vs_sparse.png)

At this point, you might be a bit sad that people have struggled to fine-tune MoEs. Excitingly, a recent paper, [MoEs Meets Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.14705.pdf) (July 2023), performs experiments doing:

When the authors fine-tuned the MoE and the T5 equivalent, the T5 equivalent was better. When the authors fine-tuned the Flan T5 (T5 instruct equivalent) MoE, the MoE performed significantly better. Not only this, the improvement of the Flan-MoE over the MoE was larger than Flan T5 over T5, indicating that MoEs might benefit much more from instruction tuning than dense models. MoEs benefit more from a higher number of tasks. Unlike the previous discussion suggesting to turn off the auxiliary loss function, the loss actually prevents overfitting.

![MoEs benefit even more from instruct tuning than dense models](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/09_fine_tune_evals.png)

## When to use sparse MoEs vs dense models?

Experts are useful for high throughput scenarios with many machines. Given a fixed compute budget for pretraining, a sparse model will be more optimal. For low throughput scenarios with little VRAM, a dense model will be better.

**Note:** one cannot directly compare the number of parameters between sparse and dense models, as both represent significantly different things.

## Making MoEs go brrr

The initial MoE work presented MoE layers as a branching setup, leading to slow computation as GPUs are not designed for it and leading to network bandwidth becoming a bottleneck as the devices need to send info to others. This section will discuss some existing work to make pretraining and inference with these models more practical. MoEs go brrrrr.

### Parallelism

Let’s do a brief review of parallelism:

With expert parallelism, experts are placed on different workers, and each worker takes a different batch of training samples. For non-MoE layers, expert parallelism behaves the same as data parallelism. For MoE layers, tokens in the sequence are sent to workers where the desired experts reside.

![Image illustrating model, expert, and data prallelism](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/10_parallelism.png)

### Capacity Factor and communication costs

Increasing the capacity factor (CF) increases the quality but increases communication costs and memory of activations. If all-to-all communications are slow, using a smaller capacity factor is better. A good starting point is using top-2 routing with 1.25 capacity factor and having one expert per core. During evaluation, the capacity factor can be changed to reduce compute.

### Serving techniques

You can deploy [mistralai/Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1](https://ui.endpoints.huggingface.co/new?repository=mistralai%2FMixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1&vendor=aws&region=us-east-1&accelerator=gpu&instance_size=2xlarge&task=text-generation&no_suggested_compute=true&tgi=true&tgi_max_batch_total_tokens=1024000&tgi_max_total_tokens=32000) to Inference Endpoints.

A big downside of MoEs is the large number of parameters. For local use cases, one might want to use a smaller model. Let's quickly discuss a few techniques that can help with serving:

### More on efficient training

FasterMoE (March 2022) analyzes the performance of MoEs in highly efficient distributed systems and analyzes the theoretical limit of different parallelism strategies, as well as techniques to skew expert popularity, fine-grained schedules of communication that reduce latency, and an adjusted topology-aware gate that picks experts based on the lowest latency, leading to a 17x speedup.

Megablocks (Nov 2022) explores efficient sparse pretraining by providing new GPU kernels that can handle the dynamism present in MoEs. Their proposal never drops tokens and maps efficiently to modern hardware, leading to significant speedups. What’s the trick? Traditional MoEs use batched matrix multiplication, which assumes all experts have the same shape and the same number of tokens. In contrast, Megablocks expresses MoE layers as block-sparse operations that can accommodate imbalanced assignment.

![Matrix multiplication optimized for block-sparse operations.](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/moe/11_expert_matmuls.png)

## Exciting directions of work

Further experiments on **distilling** a sparse MoE back to a dense model with fewer parameters but similar quality.

Another area will be quantization of MoEs. [QMoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16795) (Oct. 2023) is a good step in this direction by quantizing the MoEs to less than 1 bit per parameter, hence compressing the 1.6T Switch Transformer which uses 3.2TB accelerator to just 160GB.

args.summary:
This Hugging Face blog post (published 2023) provides a comprehensive overview of Mixture of Experts (MoE) in transformer models, with a focus on the Mixtral 8x7B release. Key points:

**What is MoE?** MoE replaces every Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layer in transformers with an MoE layer consisting of a gate network and multiple "experts." Only a subset of experts is activated per input (sparsity), enabling models to be pretrained with far less compute while achieving similar quality to dense counterparts.

**Key Concepts:**
- **Sparsity**: Uses conditional computation - only parts of the network activate per example. Top-K gating (e.g., top-2) selects which experts to use.
- **Load Balancing**: An auxiliary loss encourages equal use of all experts, preventing tokens from being routed to just a few popular experts.
- **Expert Capacity**: (tokens per batch / number of experts) × capacity factor. A buffer for imbalanced token distribution.

**History & Research:**
- Originated from 1991 paper "Adaptive Mixture of Local Experts"
- Shazeer et al. (2017) scaled to 137B LSTM with sparsity
- GShard scaled transformers beyond 600B parameters, replacing every other FFN with MoE
- Switch Transformers (2021) achieved 4x pre-train speedup over T5-XXL, using simplified single-expert strategy
- ST-MoE introduced router Z-loss for training stability

**Practical Considerations:**
- MoE models are more prone to overfitting during fine-tuning; higher regularization (dropout) is recommended
- Fine-tuning MoE parameters alone doesn't work well; freezing MoE layers while updating others works almost as well as full fine-tuning
- MoEs benefit more from instruction tuning than dense models
- MoE inference: a 47B model with 8 experts runs with compute of a ~12B dense model (top-2)
- More experts improve sample efficiency but with diminishing returns (especially after 256-512), and require more VRAM for inference

**Serving & Efficiency:**
- Expert parallelism places experts on different workers
- Capacity factor affects quality vs. communication costs tradeoff
- Techniques like FasterMoE, Megablocks, and quantization (QMoE) improve efficiency
- Open source MoEs include Mixtral 8x7B, Switch Transformers, and NLLB-MoE

## Abstract

A sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model with 7 billion parameters achieves superior performance by using only 1 billion parameters per input token and outperforms larger models in various experiments.

We introduce OLMoE, a fully open, state-of-the-art language model leveraging
[sparse Mixture-of-Experts](/papers?q=sparse%20Mixture-of-Experts) (MoE). [OLMoE-1B-7B](/papers?q=OLMoE-1B-7B) has 7 billion (B) parameters but
uses only 1B per input token. We pretrain it on 5 trillion tokens and further
adapt it to create [OLMoE-1B-7B-Instruct](/papers?q=OLMoE-1B-7B-Instruct). Our models outperform all available
models with similar active parameters, even surpassing larger ones like
[Llama2-13B-Chat](/papers?q=Llama2-13B-Chat) and [DeepSeekMoE-16B](/papers?q=DeepSeekMoE-16B). We present various experiments on MoE
training, analyze routing in our model showing high specialization, and
open-source all aspects of our work: model weights, training data, code, and
logs.

Related models include allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924, allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-Instruct, allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct, and allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0125. The code is available at https://github.com/allenai/OLMoE.

# OLMoE: An open, small, and state-of-the-art mixture-of-experts model

September 4, 2024

Niklas Muennighoff - Ai2

---

We're introducing OLMoE, jointly developed with [Contextual AI](https://contextual.ai/olmoe-mixture-of-experts/), which is the first mixture-of-experts model to join the OLMo family. OLMoE brings two important aspects to the space of truly open models - it is the first model to be on the Pareto frontier of performance and size, while also being released with open data, code, evaluations, logs, and intermediate training checkpoints. Over the last few years, mixture-of-experts architectures have become a core technology used by closed AI labs to more efficiently serve and train leading language models (LMs). We've seen similar gains in our training stack, where this MoE model trained 2x faster than equivalent dense models.

OLMoE is a sparse MoE model with 1 billion active and 7 billion total parameters. It was trained on 5 trillion tokens built on a new data mix incorporating lessons from Ai2's Dolma and building heavily on [DataComp-Baseline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794). We performed extensive experimentation on many crucial MoE details, including the routing algorithm, auxiliary loss functions, and sparse upcycling. A comparison of the model to other Ai2 OLMo models and models of similar size categories is below.

The release of this model is also accompanied by a preview version of our new Tulu 3 post-training pipeline. This version includes additional instruction data from HuggingFace's No Robots human data, math, and code data, and a subset of Nvidia's Daring Anteater synthetic data. This mix gives noticeable improvements across math, code, and instruction following evaluations, which is then passed into the standard UltraFeedback preference tuning with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). A comparison of the gains from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and DPO is shown below.

## Variants and details

We are releasing many variants and checkpoints of this model to enable multiple directions of LM research.

* 244 checkpoints for the pretrained model, one every 5000 steps.
* The annealed and unannealed checkpoints.
* Fine-tuned versions on both the annealed and unannealed base models.
* Fine-tuned versions with and without load balancing through the experts.

# OLMoE: Open Mixture-of-Experts Language Models

Fully open, state-of-the-art Mixture of Expert model with 1.3 billion active and 6.9 billion total parameters. All data, code, and logs released.

  

This repository provides an overview of all resources for the paper ["OLMoE: Open Mixture-of-Experts Language Models"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02060).

* [Artifacts](#artifacts)
* [Inference](#inference)
* [Pretraining](#pretraining)
* [Adaptation](#adaptation)
* [Evaluation](#evaluation)
  + [During pretraining](#during-pretraining)
  + [After pretraining](#after-pretraining)
  + [After adaptation](#after-adaptation)
* [Visuals](#visuals)
* [Citation](#citation)

### Artifacts

* **Paper**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02060>
* **Pretraining** [Checkpoints](https://hf.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924), [Final Checkpoint GGUF](https://hf.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-GGUF), [Code](https://github.com/allenai/OLMo/tree/Muennighoff/MoE), [Data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/OLMoE-mix-0924) and [Logs](https://wandb.ai/ai2-llm/olmoe/reports/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924--Vmlldzo4OTcyMjU3).
* **SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning)** [Checkpoints](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-SFT), [Code](https://github.com/allenai/open-instruct/), [Data](https://hf.co/datasets/allenai/tulu-v3.1-mix-preview-4096-OLMoE) and [Logs](https://github.com/allenai/OLMoE/blob/main/logs/olmoe-sft-logs.txt).
* **DPO/KTO (Direct Preference Optimization/Kahneman-Tversky Optimization)**, [Checkpoints](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-Instruct), [Final Checkpoint GGUF](https://hf.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-Instruct-GGUF), [Preference Data](https://hf.co/datasets/allenai/ultrafeedback_binarized_cleaned), [DPO code](https://github.com/allenai/open-instruct/), [KTO code](https://github.com/Muennighoff/kto/blob/master/kto.py) and [Logs](https://github.com/allenai/OLMoE/blob/main/logs/olmoe-dpo-logs.txt).

### Inference

OLMoE has been integrated into [vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm), [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang), [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp), and [transformers](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers). The transformers implementation is slow, thus we recommend using the others, e.g. vLLM, where possible. Below are examples for using it with vLLM and transformers.

#### vLLM

Install the `vllm` library and run:

```
from vllm import LLM SamplingParams model = LLM"allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924" out = model generate "Bitcoin is" SamplingParams temperature =0.0 print "Bitcoin is" + out 0 outputs 0 text# Bitcoin is a digital currency that is not controlled by any central authority. It is a peer
```

#### llama.cpp

Install `llama.cpp`, download a quantized GGUF of the final checkpoint (e.g. [`olmoe-1b-7b-0924-q4_0.gguf`](https://hf.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-GGUF/resolve/main/olmoe-1b-7b-0924-q4_0.gguf)) and run in a shell:

```
"Bitcoin is" " "
```

#### transformers

Install the `transformers` & `torch` libraries and run:

```
from transformers import OlmoeForCausalLM AutoTokenizer import torch DEVICE = "cuda" if torch cuda is_available else "cpu"# Load different ckpts via passing e.g. `revision=step10000-tokens41B`# also check allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-SFT & allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-Instruct model = OlmoeForCausalLM from_pretrained"allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924" to DEVICE tokenizer = AutoTokenizer from_pretrained"allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924" inputs = tokenizer "Bitcoin is" return_tensors = "pt" inputs = k v to DEVICE for k v in inputs items out = model generate** inputs max_length = 64 print tokenizer decode out 0# Bitcoin is a digital currency that is created and held electronically. No one controls it. Bitcoins aren’t printed, like dollars or euros – they’re produced by people and businesses running computers all around the world, using software that solves mathematical
```

You can list all revisions/branches by installing `huggingface-hub` & running:

```
from huggingface_hub import list_repo_refs out = list_repo_refs"allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924" branches = b name for b in out branches
```

### Pretraining

1. Clone this [OLMo branch](https://github.com/allenai/OLMo/tree/Muennighoff/MoE) & create an environment with its dependencies via `cd OLMo; pip install -e .`. If you want to use new features in OLMo clone from the `main` branch instead.
2. Run `pip install git+https://github.com/Muennighoff/megablocks.git@olmoe`
3. Setup a config file. `configs/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924.yml` was used for the pretraining of `OLMoE-1B-7B-0924`. You can find configs from various ablations in `configs/ablations`.
4. Download the data from <https://hf.co/datasets/allenai/OLMoE-mix-0924>, tokenize it via the command below and adapt the `paths` in your training config to point to it.

```
${PATH_TO_DOWNLOADED_DATA}${PATH_WHERE_TO_SAVE_TOKENIZED_DATA}'allenai/gpt-neox-olmo-dolma-v1_5' ' ' '2_147_483_648' ' '${NUMBER_OF_CPU_CORES_TO_USE}
```

1. Submit your job. We used `bash scripts/olmoe-gantry.sh` which invokes <https://github.com/allenai/OLMo/blob/Muennighoff/MoE/scripts/train.py> and uses [beaker gantry](https://github.com/allenai/beaker-gantry) but you will likely need to change the script to work with your setup.
2. To run annealing after the main pretraining we use [this config](https://github.com/allenai/OLMoE/blob/main/configs/ablations/olmoe-8x1b-newhp-newds-final-anneal.yml) - the only changes from the pretraining config are the `optimizer` and `scheduler` fields as well as `max_duration` and `stop_at`.
3. To convert you pretraining checkpoint to Hugging Face transformers after training, you can use the script & instructions [here](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/8f8af0fb38baa851f3fd69f564fbf91b5af78332/src/transformers/models/olmoe/convert_olmoe_weights_to_hf.py#L14).

#### Other design choices

For most of our experiments on other design choices, you can simply set them in the config file (e.g. change the respective hyperparam), except for:

1. **Sparse upcycling:** To sparse upcycle your model, train it dense first using e.g. [this config](https://github.com/allenai/OLMoE/blob/main/configs/ablations/olmo-1b-newhp-newds-cx5.yml), then convert any of its checkpoints into an MoE using [this script](https://github.com/allenai/OLMoE/blob/main/scripts/sparsify_ckpt_unsharded.py) & its instructions at the top while making sure to modify the hardcoded values (num experts etc) as you'd like your model to be, then place the newly created model (`model_sparse.safetensors`) into a new folder with a name that ends in `-unsharded` and place the model file inside of it with the name `model.safetensors`, then launch a job that loads this model similar to [our sparse upcycling job](https://wandb.ai/ai2-llm/olmoe/runs/1w3srbb3/overview) (note the settings `--load_path=path_to_upcycled_ckpt --reset_optimizer_state=True --reset_trainer_state=True` and `--fast_forward_batches=XXX` if you also want to continue on the same dataset with the same order). Also make sure to have the changes from this PR in your code: [allenai/OLMo#573](https://github.com/allenai/OLMo/pull/573). Finally, if you want to reproduce upcycling from OLMo-1B (0724) as in the paper, the OLMo 1B checkpoint turned into an MoE with 8 experts to start from is here: <https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMo-1B-0724-954000steps-unsharded>; download the files inside of it (e.g. `wget https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMo-1B-0724-954000steps-unsharded/resolve/main/model.safetensors`), then use a config similar to [this one](https://wandb.ai/ai2-llm/olmoe/runs/1w3srbb3/overview) to train the upcycled MoE from it.
2. **Expert choice:** To run experiments with our expert choice implementation, you need to instead use the olmo branch `Muennighoff/OLMoSE` or simply copy over the small config changes that enable expert choice (i.e. [here](https://github.com/allenai/OLMo/blob/b7b312aa2d9ee0ec0816a042955f34e27f9f4628/olmo/config.py#L524)) to the `Muennighoff/MoE` branch. You can then run expert choice by activating it in your config (it will use this code: <https://github.com/Muennighoff/megablocks/blob/4a25bc7b5665bcb9da93d72d5ad0c14d41e1a351/megablocks/layers/moe.py#L462> or <https://github.com/Muennighoff/megablocks/blob/4a25bc7b5665bcb9da93d72d5ad0c14d41e1a351/megablocks/layers/moe.py#L477> depending on your selection; both should be ~equivalent implementations of expert choice; neither was better than dropless token choice in our experiments)
3. **Shared MoE layers (Appendix):** For these experiments you need to use the olmo branch `Muennighoff/OLMoSE` and create your own config e.g. like the one used in [this run](https://wandb.ai/ai2-llm/olmoe/reports/Plot-Shared-vs-Dense--Vmlldzo4NDI0MTc5).

### Adaptation

1. Clone Open Instruct [here](https://github.com/allenai/open-instruct/) & follow its setup instructions. If you run into any problems, try upgrading your transformers version with `pip install --upgrade transformers` first.
2. SFT: After adapting as needed, run:

```
accelerate launch \ --mixed_precision bf16 \ --num_machines 1 \ --num_processes 8 \ --use_deepspeed \ --deepspeed_config_file configs/ds_configs/stage3_no_offloading_accelerate.conf \ open_instruct/finetune.py \ --model_name_or_path allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924 \ --tokenizer_name allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924 \ --use_flash_attn \ --max_seq_length 4096 \ --preprocessing_num_workers 128 \ --per_device_train_batch_size 2 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps 8 \ --learning_rate 2e-05 \ --lr_scheduler_type linear \ --warmup_ratio 0.03 \ --weight_decay 0.0 \ --num_train_epochs 2 \ --output_dir output/ \ --with_tracking \ --report_to wandb \ --logging_steps 1 \ --reduce_loss sum \ --model_revision main \ --dataset_mixer_list allenai/tulu-v3-mix-preview-4096-OLMoE 1.0 ai2-adapt-dev/daring-anteater-specialized 1.0 \ --checkpointing_steps epoch \ --add_bos 
```

1. DPO: Run

```
accelerate launch \ --mixed_precision bf16 \ --num_machines 1 \ --num_processes 8 \ --use_deepspeed \ --deepspeed_config_file configs/ds_configs/stage3_no_offloading_accelerate.conf \ open_instruct/dpo_tune.py \ --model_name_or_path allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-SFT \ --tokenizer_name allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-SFT \ --use_flash_attn \ --gradient_checkpointing \ --dataset_name argilla/ultrafeedback-binarized-preferences-cleaned \ --max_seq_length 4096 \ --preprocessing_num_workers 16 \ --per_device_train_batch_size 1 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \ --learning_rate 5e-7 \ --lr_scheduler_type linear \ --warmup_ratio 0.1 \ --weight_decay 0. \ --num_train_epochs 3 \ --output_dir output/ \ --report_to tensorboard \ --logging_steps 1 \ --reduce_loss sum \ --add_bos \ --checkpointing_steps epoch \ --dpo_beta 0.1 
```

1. KTO: Install `trl` and run <https://github.com/Muennighoff/kto/blob/master/kto.py> via `WANDB_PROJECT=olmoe accelerate launch --config_file=config_8gpusdsz2_m7.yml kto.py --model_name_or_path allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-SFT --output_dir OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-SFT-KTO-3EP --report_to "wandb" --per_device_train_batch_size 4 --gradient_accumulation_steps 1 --optim rmsprop --learning_rate 5e-07 --beta 0.1 --logging_steps 1 --bf16 --sanity_check False --num_train_epochs 3` (if you want to run the Adam optimizer change to `--optim adamw_torch`). We used `trl==0.9.6`.

### Evaluation

#### During pretraining

Evaluation during pretraining is done automatically and configured in the config file. It uses the code here: <https://github.com/allenai/OLMo/tree/Muennighoff/MoE/olmo/eval>.

#### After pretraining

OLMES Evals: Follow the instructions at <https://github.com/allenai/OLMo-Eval/blob/51c5ba579e75ef4ce7e9b29936eaa72c1a0e99eb/olmo_eval/tasks/olmes_v0_1/README.md>

DCLM Evals: Run `scripts/run_dclm_evals*` and refer to instructions from <https://github.com/mlfoundations/dclm>

#### After adaptation

* Setup <https://github.com/allenai/open-instruct/>
* Run `sbatch scripts/adapteval.sh` after changing it as necessary / extract the commands from the script and run them one by one.

### Visuals

* Figure 1, `visuals/figures/overview.pdf`: Run "Main plot" in `scripts/olmoe_visuals.ipynb` equivalent to [this colab](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15PTwmoxcbrwWKG6ErY44hlJlLLKAj7Hx?usp=sharing) and add the result into this drawing to edit it further: <https://docs.google.com/drawings/d/1Of9-IgvKH54zhKI_M4x5HOYEF4XUp6qaXluT3Zmv1vk/edit?usp=sharing> (the drawing used for [this tweet](https://x.com/Muennighoff/status/1831159130230587486) is [here](https://docs.google.com/drawings/d/133skqIfE8f7iOO9hMidV5tBZ7MAle28VxEm9U8Q8ioU/edit?usp=sharing))
* Figure 2, `visuals/figures/olmoe.pdf`: <https://www.figma.com/design/Es8UpNHKgugMAncPWnSDuK/olmoe?node-id=0-1&t=SeuQKPlaoB12TXqe-1> (also contains some other figures used on Twitter)
* Figure 3 & 25, `visuals/figures/trainingeval*pdf`: Run "During training" in `scripts/olmoe_visuals.ipynb` equivalent to [this colab](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15PTwmoxcbrwWKG6ErY44hlJlLLKAj7Hx?usp=sharing)
* Figure 4 - 19, 24, 26-29, `visuals/figures/...pdf`: Run respective parts in `scripts/olmoe_visuals.ipynb` equivalent to [this colab](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15PTwmoxcbrwWKG6ErY44hlJlLLKAj7Hx?usp=sharing)
* Figure 20, 21, 23, 30, 31, Table 8, `visuals/figures/...pdf`: `scripts/run_moe_analysis.py` (If you do not want to rerun inference on the model generate the routing statistics you can download them from <https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/analysis_olmoe> & <https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/analysis_mixtral>)
* Figure 22, 33-36 `visuals/figures/...pdf`: Run `scripts/run_routing_analysis.py` & then `scripts/plot_routing_analysis_v2.ipynb` / `scripts/plot_routing_analysis_v2_top1.ipynb` / `scripts/plot_routing_analysis_v2_cross_layer.ipynb`
* Figure 32, `visuals/figures/...pdf`: Run `scripts/run_routing_analysis.py` & then `scripts/plot_routing_analysis.ipynb`
* Table 13: `scripts/make_table.py`

<summary>
# Dynamic Model Routing and Cascading for Efficient LLM Inference: A Survey

This paper provides a systematic survey of state-of-the-art approaches for routing between multiple independently trained large language models (LLMs) at inference time. The core problem addressed is that static model deployment fails to account for varying query complexity, leading to suboptimal performance and cost. Dynamic routing systems adaptively select models based on query characteristics, matching computational resources to requirements.

## Key Routing Paradigms

The survey organizes methods into six main paradigms:

1. **Difficulty-aware Routing** (Section 2): Routes based on estimated query complexity using methods like heuristic-based approaches, learned classifiers, or LLM-as-judge. Methods include BEST-Route (uses DeBERTa-v3-small for multi-head routing), vLLM Semantic Router (ModernBERT classifier), RouteLMT (LoRA adaptation), EmbedLLM (matrix factorization for model embeddings), ICL-Router (in-context vectors), GraphRouter (GNN-based heterogeneous graph), and IRT-Router (Item Response Theory inspired).

2. **Human Preference-aligned Routing** (Section 3): Leverages human preference data to train routers. Key methods include RouteLLM (win prediction model trained on Chatbot Arena data), Arch-Router (allows user-defined domain-action pairs with a 1.5B parameter model), P2L (prompt-specific Bradley-Terry coefficients), Eagle (training-free ELO-based routing), and Zooter (reward-guided supervised learning).

3. **Clustering-based Routing** (Section 4): Groups similar queries via unsupervised learning. UniRoute applies K-means clustering and assigns clusters to optimal LLMs; Avengers-Pro uses similar clustering for cost-performance optimization.

4. **Reinforcement Learning Routing** (Section 5): Includes policy optimization methods (Router-R1 using PPO, R2-Reasoner using GRPO, SCOPE for performance estimation) and bandit-based methods (MetaLLM as multi-armed bandit, MixLLM with contextual bandit and policy gradient, PILOT with LinUCB, GreenServ for energy efficiency, Dueling Feedback with Thompson sampling, TI-UCB for time-varying performance).

5. **Uncertainty-based Routing** (Section 6): Routes based on model confidence. Covers probe-based methods (trained classifiers on hidden states), probability-based methods (conformal prediction via CP-Router), and LLM-as-judge approaches.

6. **Cascading** (Section 7): Sequential multi-model approaches where smaller models are queried first, escalating to larger models when needed. Methods include FrugalGPT (routing + quality estimation + stop judge), Cascade Routing (unified framework), AutoMix (self-verification with POMDP), Self-REF (fine-tuned confidence tokens), and LM-Blender (ensemble with pairwise ranking and fusion).

## Conceptual Framework

The paper introduces a three-dimensional framework for characterizing routing systems:
- **When decisions are made**: Pre-generation, post-generation, or multi-stage
- **What information is used**: Query features, model metadata, response signals, or external feedback
- **How decisions are computed**: Heuristic rules, supervised classifiers, bandit algorithms, or RL policy optimization

## Evaluation and Multimodal Extensions

The survey covers RouterBench (405k+ precomputed outputs across 11 LLMs and 7 tasks) and discusses multimodal routing, including Model-Spider, ReLope (for multimodal LLMs), and MMR-Bench. Key challenges remain in developing routing mechanisms that generalize across diverse architectures, modalities, and applications.
</summary>

RouteLLM introduces a training framework for learning efficient router models that dynamically select between a stronger (expensive) and weaker (cheaper) LLM during inference to balance performance and cost. # Awesome-Routing-LLMs

This is a curated GitHub repository (MilkThink-Lab/Awesome-Routing-LLMs) that catalogs research papers on the paradigm of **Routing LLMs** — dynamically selecting which language model to use for a given query to optimize quality, cost, latency, and other constraints.

## Structure

The repository organizes papers into the following major categories:

### 1. Pre‑judgment Routing
Routing decisions made before generation begins, based only on the initial query and static model information. Three sub‑categories:

- **Constrained Optimization** (30+ papers): Casts routing as constrained utility maximization (e.g., budget, latency) using RL, multi‑objective optimization, or adaptive policies. Key papers include RADAR (NeurIPS 2025 Workshop), CARROT (ICLR 2025 Workshop), IRT-Router (ACL 2025), OmniRouter (KDD 2025), and xRouter (ArXiv 2025).
- **Feature Matching** (15+ papers): Aligns query and model capability representations in a shared space. Includes EmbedLLM (ICLR 2025), RouterDC (NeurIPS 2024), RadialRouter (EMNLP 2025), and The Avengers (AAAI 2025).
- **Predictive Scoring** (30+ papers): Learns parametric estimators to predict model utility per query. Includes RouteLLM (ICLR 2024), BEST-Route (ICML 2025), Zooter (NAACL 2024), and ICL-Router (AAAI 2025).

### 2. Verification Routing
Routing decisions that consider intermediate generation states (partial outputs, confidence scores). Two sub‑categories:

- **Collaborative Generation** (16 papers): Multiple models collaborate step‑wise or token‑wise. Includes Mixture of Thoughts (ICLR 2026), Router-R1 (NeurIPS 2025), FusionRoute (ICML 2026), and STEER (AAAI 2026).
- **Self‑Assessment** (14 papers): Models use confidence/uncertainty signals to decide whether to escalate to a stronger model. Includes AutoMix (NeurIPS 2024), Self-REF (ICML 2025), SATER (EMNLP 2025), and X-Router (Findings of ACL 2026).

### 3. Memory‑based Routing
Routing decisions conditioned on persistent historical memory (past queries, outcomes). Two sub‑categories:

- **Retrieval** (10 papers): Uses kNN or proximity weighting from historical samples. Includes Eagle (NeurIPS 2024 Workshop), PORT (NeurIPS 2025 Workshop), and SCOPE (ICML 2026).
- **Structured** (2 papers): Graph‑based routing using GNNs. Includes GraphRouter (ICLR 2025) and GMTRouter (ArXiv 2025).

### 4. System Analysis
Theoretical modeling, benchmarks, and safety analysis:

- **Theoretical Modeling** (4 papers): Pricing theory, queueing analysis, game theory.
- **Benchmark and Evaluation** (19 papers): RouterBench, RouterEval, RouterArena, MMR-Bench, VL-RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, AgentSelect, and others.
- **Safety Analysis** (4 papers): Adversarial risks, security, privacy. Includes Rerouting LLM Routers (COLM 2025) and R2A Attack (ACL 2026).

The repository has 169 stars, 14 forks, and is actively maintained with contributions welcome.

<summary>
This is an extended survey paper titled "Doing More with Less – Implementing Routing Strategies in Large Language Model-Based Systems" by Clovis Varangot-Reille et al. It explores routing mechanisms in LLM-based systems, where a router directs user queries to the most suitable components (e.g., smaller LLMs, domain experts) to optimize the performance-cost trade-off.

**Key Background:**
- Traditional LLM-based systems (e.g., conversational agents, RAG architectures) are monolithic, using a single generalist LLM for all queries, which wastes resources on simple tasks.
- Routing aims to select the best model/pipeline element for each query, minimizing cost while maximizing performance (accuracy, quality).
- The routing problem is formalized as: given a set of models M, maximize scoring function s(q,M) subject to cost constraint C_M(q) ≤ B.

**When Routing Occurs:**
1. **Pre-generation routing** – Assesses LLM ability to answer a query before generation (based on domain knowledge or complexity inference). Minimizes latency.
2. **Post-generation routing (cascade routing)** – Generates responses sequentially, moving to larger models if response quality is deemed inadequate. More resource-intensive but can be hybridized with pre-generation.

**Routing Strategies (classified by resource requirements):**

**High-Resource Strategies (Section 4.1):**
- *Supervised Routing*: Includes answer confidence inference (e.g., FrugalGPT using DistilBERT to assess response alignment, saving 59-98% costs) and decoder-only encoding (e.g., Routoo Orchestrator using Mistral-7B, achieving 75.9% on MMLU vs 69.9% for Llama2-70B at similar/lower cost).
- *Generative-based Routing*: Prompt-based routing (function calling, verbalized confidence), sequence probability, LLM fine-tuning for classification/regression, and repeated calls (e.g., Automix using POMDP, outperforming FrugalGPT and HybridLLM).
- *Code Execution*: EcoAssistant iteratively executes code, routing to larger LLMs only when code fails.

**Low-Resource Strategies (Section 4.2):**
- *Similarity-based Routing*: Query similarity (1NN, Semantic-Router, contrastive learning like OrchestraLLM and RouterDC), clustering previous interactions (k-means with TF-IDF or dense embeddings), and preference similarity (RouteLLM with Bradley-Terry algorithm, Eagle with ELO-based ranking).
- *Supervised Routing*: Recommendation system approaches like matrix factorization (RouteLLM's BT approach) showing better cost-quality trade-offs than classification-based methods.

**Key Findings:**
- FrugalGPT saved 59-98% costs while maintaining accuracy similar to GPT-4.
- Routoo achieved 75.9% on MMLU with open-source models vs 69.9% for Llama2-70B at lower cost.
- Self-Route reduced token usage by 61% on average for GPT-4o while maintaining comparable performance.
- RouterDC outperformed standalone LLMs and other routing methods across out-of-distribution datasets.
- Preference-based methods (RouteLLM, Eagle) matched or surpassed BERT-based classifiers and fine-tuned LLMs.
- Critical challenges include ensuring complementary LLMs for routing, avoiding over-reliance on the largest model, and the need for diverse training data for clustering approaches.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# LLM Model Routing in 2026: Cost-Quality Optimization

This guide covers model routing—sending each LLM request to the cheapest capable model rather than using frontier models for every call. Published June 14, 2026.

## Key Findings

**Economic Case:** The price spread between cheapest and most capable models is ~100× (DeepSeek V4 at ~$0.44/M input tokens to GPT-5.5-pro at $30/$180 per M). Teams report bill reductions of 40-85% with tuned routing layers.

**RouteLLM Proof:** Peer-reviewed at ICLR 2025, RouteLLM achieved 85% cost savings on MT Bench at 95% of GPT-4 quality, needing the frontier model on only 14% of queries. Results are benchmark-specific.

**Savings Matrix:** Savings compound when cheap-model traffic share crosses 50%. Example splits:
- 70% Haiku / 30% Opus → ~67% input-token reduction
- 80% DeepSeek V4 / 20% Opus → ~79% reduction

**Router Overhead:** Negligible vs. inference time. Rule-based <1ms, embeddings ~5ms, ML classifiers 50-100ms—against LLM responses of 500-2,000ms.

## Router Decision Framework

Three axes: **when** (pre-request, during inference, post-response), **what** information (query features, model metadata, past performance), **how** computed (rules, classifiers, reinforcement learning, cascades).

## Six Production Tools

1. **Vercel AI Gateway** — Zero-markup, cost/ttft/tps sort, 40+ providers, <20ms overhead. Best for Next.js/AI SDK teams.
2. **OpenRouter** — Inverse-square price weighting, Auto Router with cost-quality dial, 5% markup (waived with own keys). Fast multi-provider access.
3. **LiteLLM** — Open source, 5 strategies, 100+ providers, self-hosted. Best for Kubernetes/self-hosted.
4. **NotDiamond** — ML quality-aware routing, enterprise clients (Hugging Face, Dropbox, IBM). Accuracy-led.
5. **Portkey** — Apache 2.0 open source, 250+ providers, 40+ guardrails, conditional routing. Governance at scale.
6. **Azure AI Foundry Model Router** — Balanced/Cost/Quality modes, 27+ models, single endpoint. Azure-native.

## Critical Warning: Silent Quality Regression

The hidden risk: routing to cheaper models can degrade answer quality (missed nuances, hallucinations, tool-call failures) that surfaces days later via customer tickets, not dashboards. **Mitigation:** A pre-merge CI eval gate running 50-500 representative cases (groundedness, context adherence, LLM-as-judge) that blocks routing changes dropping quality below threshold.

## Conclusion

Routing is the largest cost lever most teams haven't pulled. The playbook: start with conservative splits, instrument an eval gate before widening, increase cheap-model share incrementally while watching quality metrics. The savings are immediate and visible; the quality cost is invisible and delayed—the eval gate is what lets teams claim savings safely.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review paper published in the International Journal of Scientific Research and Technology (IJSRT) on July 30, 2026, authored by Mahiba Jeyaraj and Sujata Deshmukh from Fr. Conceicao Rodrigues College of Engineering, Mumbai University. The paper surveys Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques for lightweight Large Language Models (LLMs), covering literature from 2021 to 2026.

**Key Contributions:**
- The review organizes PEFT methods into six families: additive, reparameterization, quantization-aware, selective/sparse, gradient-projection, and mixture-of-experts approaches.
- A comparative table summarizes trainable-parameter and inference overhead across representative methods (e.g., LoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, VeRA, QLoRA, BitFit, IA3, GaLore, LoRAMoE).

**Methodology:** Structured literature search across arXiv, ACL Anthology, IEEE Xplore, and Springer/Nature using terms like "parameter-efficient fine-tuning", "low-rank adaptation", "LoRA", "QLoRA", etc., limited to papers from 2021 to July 2026.

**Key PEFT Methods Discussed:**
- **Additive Methods:** Adapter tuning (~1-4% params), Prefix/Prompt tuning (<0.1% params)
- **Reparameterization (LoRA variants):** LoRA (0.1-1%), DoRA (magnitude-direction decomposition), AdaLoRA (adaptive rank allocation), VeRA (<0.1% with shared frozen matrices)
- **Quantization-aware:** QLoRA (4-bit NormalFloat backbone + double quantization), IR-QLoRA, QR-Adaptor, LoTA-QAF
- **Selective/Sparse:** BitFit (<0.1%, bias-only), IA3 (<0.05%, rescaling vectors)
- **Gradient-projection:** GaLore and Q-GaLore (low-rank gradient projection, full-rank weights trainable)
- **Mixture-of-Experts:** LoRAMoE, MOELoRA, HydraLoRA, MixLoRA (routing among LoRA experts)

**Applications:** On-device inference (MobileFineTuner), federated personalization (Heterogeneous LoRA), healthcare/clinical decision support, multimodal instruction tuning (PALO for multilingual vision-language), and low-resource language adaptation.

**Challenges Identified:**
1. Residual accuracy gap vs. full fine-tuning
2. Multi-adapter serving and composition efficiency
3. Hallucination, forgetting, and task interference
4. Heterogeneity in federated/edge settings
5. Lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks

**Future Directions:** Automatic configuration search, hardware-software co-design for on-device training, unifying PEFT with MoE while preserving mergeability, federated PEFT with rank-heterogeneous protocols, and hybrid gradient-projection + adapter methods.
</summary>

This paper presents a case study on adapting a small LLM (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) to Icelandic using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods with unstructured text data. - **LoRA in feed-forward (FF) layers** performed best overall, followed by bottleneck adapters. LoRA in attention layers required more parameters for comparable performance and was less robust to longer contexts.

- **Training on the curated Icelandic Gigaword Corpus (IGC)** did not outperform the web-crawled CCNet-filtered data, contrary to expectations.
- **In-context learning (1-shot without adaptation) was competitive** with many adapted setups, suggesting it can serve as an alternative to language adaptation when possible.

The study concludes that feed-forward modules are the most promising target for language adaptation, sufficient learning capacity is crucial, and careful placement of adapters matters more than simply adding more parameters.

--- SOURCE 1: RouterBench Benchmark ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/routerbench-dataset-f5365873-d6af-48a1-a3b8-206a8c80d9fd

SUMMARY:
<summary>
RouterBench is a benchmark and dataset designed to systematically assess multi-LLM routing systems, providing over 405k precomputed inference records, standardized evaluation metrics, and a formal evaluation framework. Published by Hu et al. at ICML 2024, it is hosted on GitHub under Apache 2.0 license.

**Scope & Design:** RouterBench addresses the need for a unified benchmark for routing strategies that dispatch user prompts to optimal LLMs. It covers diverse application domains including commonsense reasoning, knowledge QA, conversation, math, coding, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

**Data Collection:** The dataset comprises 405,467 inference records from 11 LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude-v1/v2, Llama-70B-chat, Mixtral-8x7B, Yi-34B-chat, Code-Llama-34B, Mistral-7B, WizardLM-13B, You.com API, sonar-small/medium-online). Domains include HellaSwag, Winogrande, ARC-Challenge, MMLU, MT-Bench, GSM8K, MBPP, and an in-house RAG set. Each record includes sample_id, model name, prompt, response, true label, performance score, and cost estimate, stored in JSON Lines format.

**Evaluation Framework:** Uses cost–quality analysis, non-decreasing convex hull (NDCH) for Pareto envelope, and the Average Improvement in Quality (AIQ) metric for comparing routing policies without real-time compute costs.

**Key Statistics:** Per-model accuracy ranges from ~38% (Claude-instant) to ~83% (GPT-4); per-model mean cost from $0.08 (Mistral-7B) to $4.09 (GPT-4); oracle router achieves ~0.96 mean performance at ~$0.30 mean cost. Cost–quality correlation is ρ≈0.7.

**Limitations:** No latency or throughput metrics; only 11 LLMs covered; limited to general benchmarks (no niche domains); RAG set only 800 queries; GPT-4 judging may introduce bias.

**Applications:** Training predictive routers (KNN, MLP, transformers), evaluating non-predictive strategies (cascades, rule-based), and benchmarking novel routing methodologies against theoretical bounds.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
RouterBench is a benchmark and dataset designed to systematically assess multi-LLM routing systems by providing a large pool of precomputed inference outcomes, model metadata, and a formal evaluation framework, RouterBench constitutes the first rigorously constructed dataset and benchmark specifically targeting the multi-LLM routing problem with cost–quality analysis, unified task coverage, and standardized access protocols, The dataset comprises 405,467 inference records, sampled from eight standard NLP/math/programming datasets plus an in-house RAG set, covering 11 representative LLMs, RouterBench formalizes router evaluation using the cost–quality plane and the Average Improvement in Quality (AIQ) metric, Key limitations: No latency or throughput metrics are included; the dataset quantifies only cost and accuracy; tasks are drawn from general benchmarks; quality signals on some tasks derive from automated GPT-4 judging, which may introduce systematic bias
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Towards Fair and Comprehensive Evaluation of Routers in Collaborative LLM Systems ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.11877v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents RouterXBench, a systematic evaluation framework for routers in collaborative LLM systems, along with a novel router called ProbeDirichlet. The framework evaluates routers across three dimensions: (1) Router Ability (measured by AUROC), (2) Scenario Alignment (using LPM, MPM, and HCR metrics for low-cost, balanced, and high-accuracy deployment regimes), and (3) Cross-Domain Robustness (across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks).

The authors propose ProbeDirichlet, which uses internal hidden states from the small model (rather than output probabilities or external embeddings) to capture model uncertainty before answer generation. It aggregates cross-layer representations via a Dirichlet distribution with learned concentration parameters, enabling probabilistic training with deterministic inference. The router is trained on multi-domain data (Alpaca, MMLU, Big Math) and generalizes robustly.

Key results: ProbeDirichlet achieves 16.68% relative improvement in router ability (AUROC) and 18.86% relative improvement in high-accuracy scenarios (HCR) over baselines. It consistently outperforms methods using verbose-based, logit-based, or embedding-based signals across model families (Llama-3.1, Qwen2.5), model scales, heterogeneous tasks, and agentic workflows. The analysis shows that (1) internal hidden states matter more than architecture complexity, (2) data diversity yields additive gains without interference, (3) lightweight linear probes suffice, and (4) the approach generalizes to agent-based inference scenarios.

The paper also identifies limitations: when both small and large models fail on the same query, routing becomes ineffective, suggesting the need for uncertainty-aware mechanisms and more capable model pools.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
We propose RouterXBench, a principled evaluation framework with three dimensions: router ability, scenario alignment, and cross-domain robustness., Our results show ProbeDirichlet achieves 16.68% and 18.86% relative improvements over the best baselines in router ability and high-accuracy scenarios, with consistent performance across model families, model scales, heterogeneous tasks, and agentic workflows., Internal hidden states directly capture model uncertainty before answer generation, proving more reliable than output probabilities that suffer from softmax overconfidence., Data diversity is additive, not competitive; diverse training improves robustness while preserving specialist capabilities., Our analysis shows that robustness is driven by training data diversity rather than architectural complexity.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Awesome-Routing-LLMs - GitHub ---
URL: https://github.com/MilkThink-Lab/Awesome-Routing-LLMs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Awesome-Routing-LLMs

This is a curated GitHub repository (MilkThink-Lab/Awesome-Routing-LLMs) that catalogs research papers on the paradigm of **Routing LLMs** — dynamically selecting which language model to use for a given query to optimize quality, cost, latency, and other constraints.

## Structure

The repository organizes papers into the following major categories:

### 1. Pre‑judgment Routing
Routing decisions made before generation begins, based only on the initial query and static model information. Three sub‑categories:

- **Constrained Optimization** (30+ papers): Casts routing as constrained utility maximization (e.g., budget, latency) using RL, multi‑objective optimization, or adaptive policies. Key papers include RADAR (NeurIPS 2025 Workshop), CARROT (ICLR 2025 Workshop), IRT-Router (ACL 2025), OmniRouter (KDD 2025), and xRouter (ArXiv 2025).
- **Feature Matching** (15+ papers): Aligns query and model capability representations in a shared space. Includes EmbedLLM (ICLR 2025), RouterDC (NeurIPS 2024), RadialRouter (EMNLP 2025), and The Avengers (AAAI 2025).
- **Predictive Scoring** (30+ papers): Learns parametric estimators to predict model utility per query. Includes RouteLLM (ICLR 2024), BEST-Route (ICML 2025), Zooter (NAACL 2024), and ICL-Router (AAAI 2025).

### 2. Verification Routing
Routing decisions that consider intermediate generation states (partial outputs, confidence scores). Two sub‑categories:

- **Collaborative Generation** (16 papers): Multiple models collaborate step‑wise or token‑wise. Includes Mixture of Thoughts (ICLR 2026), Router-R1 (NeurIPS 2025), FusionRoute (ICML 2026), and STEER (AAAI 2026).
- **Self‑Assessment** (14 papers): Models use confidence/uncertainty signals to decide whether to escalate to a stronger model. Includes AutoMix (NeurIPS 2024), Self-REF (ICML 2025), SATER (EMNLP 2025), and X-Router (Findings of ACL 2026).

### 3. Memory‑based Routing
Routing decisions conditioned on persistent historical memory (past queries, outcomes). Two sub‑categories:

- **Retrieval** (10 papers): Uses kNN or proximity weighting from historical samples. Includes Eagle (NeurIPS 2024 Workshop), PORT (NeurIPS 2025 Workshop), and SCOPE (ICML 2026).
- **Structured** (2 papers): Graph‑based routing using GNNs. Includes GraphRouter (ICLR 2025) and GMTRouter (ArXiv 2025).

### 4. System Analysis
Theoretical modeling, benchmarks, and safety analysis:

- **Theoretical Modeling** (4 papers): Pricing theory, queueing analysis, game theory.
- **Benchmark and Evaluation** (19 papers): RouterBench, RouterEval, RouterArena, MMR-Bench, VL-RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, AgentSelect, and others.
- **Safety Analysis** (4 papers): Adversarial risks, security, privacy. Includes Rerouting LLM Routers (COLM 2025) and R2A Attack (ACL 2026).

The repository has 169 stars, 14 forks, and is actively maintained with contributions welcome.
</summary>

It relies only on the initial query and static model information, making it suitable for fast, one‑shot allocation., Verification routing expands the decision space to intermediate generation states (partial outputs, confidence scores, or reasoning steps). It can revise routing decisions during inference, making the process more adaptive., Memory‑based routing conditions decisions not only on the current query but also on persistent historical memory – past queries, outcomes, or user interactions., Analytical work studies system‑level behavior: theoretical bounds, benchmark evaluation, and safety risks.

--- SOURCE 6: [PDF] Intention Chain-of-Thought Prompting with Dynamic Routing for Code ... ---
URL: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/37030/40992

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces RoutingGen, a difficulty-aware dynamic routing framework for code generation using large language models (LLMs). It addresses two key limitations of existing chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting methods: (1) overthinking on simple tasks due to uniform application of structured prompting, and (2) lack of intention abstraction (e.g., core algorithmic logic and time complexity modeling) in code generation.

Inspired by dual-process theory of human cognition (System 1 for intuitive responses, System 2 for deliberate reasoning), RoutingGen uses a difficulty classifier (Qwen3-8B) to estimate problem complexity. For simple tasks, it employs direct few-shot prompting; for complex tasks, it invokes a novel structured reasoning strategy called Intention Chain-of-Thought (ICoT), which comprises two stages: Specification (defining input-output constraints) and Idea (capturing core algorithmic logic and time complexity).

**Key Results:**
- RoutingGen achieves state-of-the-art Pass@1 performance across three models (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3-671B) and six benchmarks (HumanEval, HumanEval-ET, MBPP-sanitized, MBPP-ET, OpenEval, McEval).
- RoutingGen reduces total token usage by 46.37% on average across all settings.
- ICoT consistently outperforms six prompting baselines (Zero-shot, Few-shot, Self-CoT, ZS-CoT, Self-Planning, SCoT) on challenging benchmarks.
- On DeepSeek-V3-671B, RoutingGen achieves 91.83% on HumanEval and 90.21% on MBPP-sanitized.
- On MBPP-sanitized (64.40% classified as Simple), RoutingGen achieves a 59.22% token reduction and 4.60 percentage point accuracy improvement over SCoT.
- Ablation studies confirm both Specification and Idea stages contribute to ICoT's effectiveness, and RoutingGen is robust to variations in difficulty classifier models (Qwen3-8B vs. GPT-4o).

**Methodology:** The framework consists of two components: (1) a Difficulty-Aware Routing module that classifies problems as Simple or Complex with rationale, and (2) ICoT-Guided Generation for complex tasks, which first generates structured intention (Specification + Idea) and then generates code conditioned on that intention.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Harnessing Chain-of-Thought Metadata for Task Routing and Adversarial Prompt Detection ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2503.21464v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces the "Number of Thoughts (NofT)" metric, a measure derived from Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning steps generated by Large Language Models (LLMs), to estimate task complexity, detect adversarial prompts, and optimize model routing.

**Key Contributions:**

1. **Task Complexity Metric (NofT):** The authors propose using the number of intermediate reasoning steps in CoT processes as a proxy for task difficulty. They derive this metric by prompting DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and parsing the number of steps (using explicit numbering or keyword-based fallback).

2. **Random Forest Classifier:** A Random Forest classifier is trained on the MathInstruct dataset (using TF-IDF vectorization) to predict the NofT score for unseen prompts. Statistical analysis (t-tests, power analysis, Bayesian MCMC) shows the RF classifier can reliably distinguish between easy, medium, and hard prompts.

3. **Adversarial Prompt Detection:** The NofT metric is used to detect prompt injection attacks. On the DIA-Bench dataset, with a 90% probability threshold, the classifier achieves **95% accuracy** in distinguishing adversarial from non-adversarial prompts. On the deepset dataset, it achieves 74% accuracy.

4. **Routing Optimization Framework:** Prompts are routed to appropriately sized models (1.5B, 7B, 14B parameter quantized DeepSeek models) based on predicted NofT thresholds. Key results:
   - **Configuration 1 (1.5B ↔ 14B only):** 24.91% reduction in latency (from 8.72s to 6.53s) with minimal accuracy change.
   - **Configuration 2 (all three models):** 14.96% reduction in latency with 0.97% improvement in ROUGE-L score.

**Methodology:** The NofT is derived by prompting the model to number each step, then parsing the response. For the RF classifier, TF-IDF vectorization converts prompts to numeric features. Statistical tests (t-tests, power analysis, Bayesian MCMC) validate the metric's discriminative power.

**Datasets Used:** MathInstruct (for training), DIA-Bench (Dynamic Intelligence Assessment Benchmark), and deepset prompt injection dataset.

**Limitations:** Small sample size (100 MathInstruct samples), use of distilled/quantized models only, potential generalizability issues with different model families (e.g., TinyR1 showed poor performance).

URL: https://www.leewayhertz.com/parameter-efficient-fine-tuning

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article provides a comprehensive overview of Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT), a technique used in NLP to improve pre-trained language models on specific downstream tasks by fine-tuning only a small subset of parameters rather than the entire model.

**Key Concepts:** PEFT involves freezing most layers of a pre-trained model and fine-tuning only task-specific layers, significantly reducing computational and storage costs while achieving comparable performance to full fine-tuning. It addresses the impracticality of fine-tuning trillion-parameter LLMs by modifying hidden representations through small incremental changes (Δh) rather than full retraining.

**Benefits:** Decreased computational/storage costs, overcoming catastrophic forgetting, better performance in low-data regimes, portability (tiny checkpoints), comparable performance with fewer parameters, sustainability (lower carbon footprint), faster training cycles, and lower storage requirements.

**PEFT Techniques Covered:**
1. **Adapter** - Small submodules inserted after attention and feed-forward layers
2. **LoRA** - Low-Rank Adaptation using rank decomposition matrices, reducing trainable parameters by up to 10,000x
3. **Prefix Tuning** - Optimizes continuous task-specific "prefix" vectors (0.1% of parameters)
4. **Prompt Tuning** - Learns soft prompts through backpropagation at the input layer
5. **P-tuning** - Uses trainable continuous prompt embeddings for NLU tasks
6. **IA3** - Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations, rescales inner activations with learned vectors

**Comparison with Standard Fine-tuning:** PEFT uses smaller datasets, faster training, fewer resources, modifies only a subset of parameters, is less prone to overfitting, and is ideal for low-resource settings, though full fine-tuning may achieve slightly better performance with ample data.

**PEFT vs. Few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL):** PEFT outperforms ICL in accuracy while using 1,000x fewer FLOPs during inference and requiring only 30 minutes to train on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. PEFT's (IA)^3 scaling method and additional loss terms contribute to its superior performance.

**Use Cases:** NLP (text classification, sentiment analysis, NER, machine translation), conversational AI, computer vision, speech recognition, recommendation systems, healthcare (medical diagnostics, drug discovery), and finance (fraud detection).

**Common Pitfalls:** Overfitting, incorrect adapter sizing (recommended ~10% of model dimensions), suboptimal learning rates, and poor pre-trained model selection.

**Pre-trained models commonly used with PEFT:** BERT, GPT-3, T5, RoBERTa, XLNet, ELECTRA, and ALBERT.

The article also includes a code example demonstrating LoRA-based fine-tuning using Hugging Face's PEFT library for a Twitter complaint classification task with a sequence-to-sequence model.
</summary>

# Awesome-RAG-Reasoning GitHub Repository Summary

This is a curated collection of resources, papers, tools, and implementations that bridge the gap between **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** and **Reasoning** in Large Language Models and Agents. The repository is maintained by DavidZWZ and is based on the taxonomy from the survey paper "Towards Agentic RAG with Deep Reasoning: A Survey of RAG-Reasoning Systems in LLMs" (arXiv 2507.09477), which was featured in Hugging Face Daily Papers.

## Key Concepts

- **RAG** combines LLMs with external knowledge retrieval for accurate, factual responses, but has limitations in retrieving irrelevant information and being constrained by knowledge base quality.
- **Reasoning** enhances LLMs' logical processing and multi-step inference capabilities, but struggles with hallucination and accessing up-to-date information.
- These two domains have traditionally been developed independently, but the repository argues they should be combined for real-world applications requiring both knowledge access and sophisticated reasoning.

## Taxonomy Structure

The repository organizes papers into three main categories:

1. **Reasoning-Enhanced RAG** (one-way enhancement): Subcategories include Retrieval Optimization, Integration Enhancement, and Generation Enhancement.
2. **RAG-Enhanced Reasoning** (one-way enhancement): Subcategories include External Knowledge Retrieval (Knowledge Base, Web Retrieval, Tool Using) and In-context Retrieval (Prior Experience, Example/Training Data).
3. **Synergized RAG-Reasoning Systems** (iterative mutual enhancement): Subcategories include Reasoning Workflow (Chain-based, Tree-based, Graph-based) and Agentic Orchestration (Single-Agent with Prompting/SFT/RL, Multi-Agent).

## Papers Listed (Partial Selection)

The repository contains extensive paper listings spanning 2024-2026 venues including ACL, EMNLP, NeurIPS, AAAI, ICLR, SIGIR, CVPR, WWW, and arXiv. Notable papers include:
- R3: Optimizing Retrieval for RAG via Reinforcement Learning (NeurIPS 2025)
- Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented LLMs through Question Complexity (NAACL 2024)
- Open-RAG: Enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning with Open-Source LLMs (EMNLP 2024)
- KBLaM: Knowledge Base augmented Language Model (ICLR 2025)
- RAG-Critic: Leveraging Automated Critic-Guided Agentic Workflow (ACL 2025)
- Various papers on Deep Research, GraphRAG, and multi-agent systems

## Benchmarks & Datasets

The repository covers benchmarks across: Single-hop QA, Multi-hop QA, Multi-choice QA, Multi-step QA, Multimodal QA, Long-form QA, Graph QA, Code, Dialog, Fact Checking, Text Summarization, Deep Research, and Retrieval Evaluation.

## Related Resource

A companion repository, **Awesome-Deep-Research** (https://github.com/DavidZWZ/Awesome-Deep-Research), covers cutting-edge deep research papers and products.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This position paper from NeurIPS critically examines the current state of Multi-Agent Systems of Large Language Models (MAS LLMs). The authors argue that despite growing interest in using multiple LLMs to tackle complex tasks, many implementations misuse MAS terminology without engaging with the field's foundational principles. The paper identifies four key areas of discrepancy between traditional MAS theory and current MAS LLMs implementations: (1) the social aspect of agency, (2) environment design, (3) coordination and communication protocols, and (4) measuring emergent behaviors. The authors contend that many MAS LLMs lack essential multi-agent characteristics such as autonomy, social interaction, and structured environments, often relying on oversimplified, LLM-centric architectures. They warn that the field risks slowing down and losing traction by revisiting problems already addressed in MAS literature. The paper advocates for better integration of established MAS concepts and more precise terminology to avoid mischaracterization and missed research opportunities.
