## 1. Model Selection / Routing Between Different Model Sizes or Families

### 1.1 FrugalGPT

**Full Title:** FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance  
**Authors:** Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou  
**Venue & Year:** Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), May 2023  
**Link:** [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/FrugalGPT%3A-How-to-Use-Large-Language-Models-While-Chen-Zaharia/585f8b9725f5f5e5495c3508d39f70d1c053e190](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/FrugalGPT%3A-How-to-Use-Large-Language-Models-While-Chen-Zaharia/585f8b9725f5f5e5495c3508d39f70d1c053e190)

**Findings:**
FrugalGPT proposes a simple yet flexible instantiation of an LLM cascade which learns which combinations of LLMs to use for different queries in order to reduce cost and improve accuracy, laying a foundation for using LLMs sustainably and efficiently [1][2]. FrugalGPT revolves around three key techniques:
1. **Prompt Adaptation:** Using concise, optimized prompts to minimize token costs (e.g., selecting top k similar examples instead of all examples reduced costs by 70%, and combining similar requests reduced costs by 50%).
2. **LLM Approximation:** Utilizing caches and model fine-tuning to avoid repeated expensive queries (simple caching yields ~8% cache hits with 99% cost savings, semantic caching yields ~21% cache hits with 95% cost reduction, and fine-tuning smaller models can achieve up to 94% cost reduction).
3. **LLM Cascade:** Dynamically selecting the optimal sequence of LLMs to query based on confidence scoring, which can match GPT-4 performance with up to 98% cost reduction.

Key results: "FrugalGPT can match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction or improve the accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% with the same cost." [1] Additional techniques include converting zero-shot prompts for larger models into few-shot prompts for smaller models (up to 98.5% cost reduction with 78% speed improvement) and prompt compression using LLMLingua (2.5x-5x compression ratios). The paper has 874 citations and 57 references [2]. It has spawned significant follow-up work including MetaLLM, OptLLM, ThriftLLM, and other frameworks focused on cost-effective LLM routing, selection, and query allocation [2].

### 1.2 RouteLLM

**Full Title:** RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data  
**Authors:** Isaac Ong, Amjad Almahairi, et al. (UC Berkeley)  
**Venue & Year:** ICLR 2025 (peer-reviewed at ICLR 2025; also listed as ICLR 2024 in some sources)  
**Link:** [https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm) (Open-source framework page; paper on alphaxiv: [https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2406.18665](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2406.18665))

**Findings:**
RouteLLM introduces a training framework for learning efficient router models that dynamically select between a stronger (expensive) and weaker (cheaper) LLM during inference to balance performance and cost [3][4]. The framework leverages human preference data from Chatbot Arena (80k battles) and employs data augmentation techniques (golden-labeled data from MMLU and LLM-judge-labeled data from GPT-4). The authors evaluate several router architectures: Similarity-weighted (SW) ranking, Matrix Factorization, BERT classifier, and Causal LLM classifier (Llama 3 8B).

Key results show that routers can reduce costs by over 2x (up to 3.66x) without sacrificing response quality [3]. On MT Bench, the best routers (trained on augmented data) achieve APGR improvements of 50-60% over random baselines. The matrix factorization router required half the GPT-4 calls of random to achieve 50% performance gap recovery. Routers also demonstrate strong generalization to unseen model pairs (Claude 3 Opus/Sonnet and Llama 3.1 70B/8B) without retraining [3]. The paper finds that data augmentation is critical—routers trained solely on Arena data perform poorly on out-of-distribution benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K, but augmentation with as little as 1500 in-domain samples significantly improves performance [3][4].

Specific cost savings: "cost reductions of over 85% on MT Bench, 45% on MMLU, and 35% on GSM8K as compared to using only GPT-4, while still achieving 95% of GPT-4's performance." [4] "matrix factorization is able to achieve 95% of GPT-4 performance using 26% GPT-4 calls, which is approximately 48% cheaper as compared to the random baseline." [4] RouteLLM outperforms commercial offerings (Martian and Unify AI) by achieving the same performance while being over 40% cheaper [4].

The key innovation lies in "framing LLM routing as a preference learning problem. Rather than relying on synthetic metrics or fixed routing rules, ROUTELLM learns from human preference data to predict when a strong model will outperform a weak model for a given query." [3]

### 1.3 A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs (Cascade Routing)

**Full Title:** A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs  
**Authors:** Jasper Dekoninck, Maximilian Baader, Martin Vechev  
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2025  
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46183](https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46183)

**Findings:**
This research addresses model selection strategies for large language models. It identifies three key limitations in existing approaches (routing and cascading): lack of formal optimality proofs, failure to identify conditions for effectiveness, and inability to combine both paradigms [5]. The authors derive a novel optimal strategy for cascading and prove the optimality of an existing routing strategy. They propose "cascade routing," a unified framework that integrates routing and cascading into a theoretically optimal strategy [5]. The work identifies good quality estimators as critical for model selection success. Experiments show cascade routing consistently outperforms individual approaches by a large margin (up to 14% improvement). "Instead of always running models in a fixed sequence or sticking to just one, cascade routing iteratively picks the best model, and thus can skip models, reorder them, or running only as few as needed." [5]

**Findings:**
SELECT-THEN-ROUTE (StR) is a two-stage framework that first selects a small, task-appropriate pool of LLMs and then routes each query within that pool through an adaptive cascade [9]. **Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46753](https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46753)

**Findings:**
L2R introduces a strategy for continual learning (CL) in pre-trained language models (PLMs) using parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques [10]. Tradicional PEFT-based CL methods face two issues: interference with previously trained modules and suboptimal module composition [10]. L2R addresses these by isolating the training of new PEFT modules to ensure task-specific specialization, and then learning to combine these modules by training a router network that leverages a small memory of prior task examples [10]. The approach was evaluated in two CL setups across various benchmarks, and results show that L2R effectively composes PEFT modules, leading to improved generalization and performance compared to other methods [10].

The framework covers various design dimensions including functional and composition strategies [11]. **Authors:** Researchers from The Ohio State University, Imperial College London, University of Michigan, Amazon AWS AI, Google Research, and Microsoft Research Asia

**Findings:**
This comprehensive survey provides a systematic review of efficiency techniques for LLMs, organized into three main categories: (1) Model-Centric Methods, covering model compression (quantization, pruning, low-rank approximation, knowledge distillation, parameter sharing), efficient pre-training, fine-tuning, inference (parallel/speculative decoding, KV-cache optimization), and efficient architecture (attention mechanisms, Mixture of Experts, long-context LLMs, transformer alternatives like State Space Models); (2) Data-Centric Methods, covering data selection and prompt engineering (few-shot prompting, prompt compression/generation); and (3) System-Level Efficiency Optimization and LLM Frameworks [14]. ## 3. Routing to Different Retrieval Depths for RAG (Adaptive Retrieval, Multi-hop Retrieval Routing)

### 3.1 Adaptve-RAG

**Full Title:** Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
**Authors:** Soyeong Jeon, Jinheon Baek, Sukmin Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Jong C. Park (KAIST)
**Venue & Year:** NAACL 2024
**Link:** [https://aclanthologyorg/2024.naacl-long.389.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.389.pdf) | [https://pure.kaist.ac.kr/en/publications/adaptive-rag-learning-to-adapt-retrieval-augmented-large-language](https://pure.kaist.ac.kr/en/publications/adaptive-rag-learning-to-adapt-retrieval-augmented-large-language)

**Findings:**
Adaptive-RAG proposes a novel adaptive QA framework that can dynamically select the most suitable retrieval-augmented strategy for LLMs from the simplest to the most sophisticated ones based on query complexity [15][16]. The framework uses a trained classifier (a smaller LM) to categorize queries into three complexity levels: 'A' (straightforward, answerable by LLM alone), 'B' (moderate complexity, requiring single-step retrieval), and 'C' (complex, requiring multi-step iterative retrieval) [15]. The classifier is trained on automatically labeled data derived from model prediction outcomes and inductive biases from existing datasets (single-hop vs multi-hop QA datasets) [15].

The framework is validated on open-domain QA datasets including single-hop (SQuAD, Natural Questions, TriviaQA) and multi-hop (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) queries, using FLAN-T5 (3B and 11B) and GPT-3.5 models [15]. Results show Adaptive-RAG improves both accuracy and efficiency compared to baselines including Adaptive Retrieval and Self-RAG. For example, with FLAN-T5-XL (3B), Adaptive-RAG achieves 46.94 F1 and 2.17 steps per query, compared to the multi-step approach's 48.85 F1 but 4.69 steps, and no retrieval's 21.12 F1 and 0 steps [15]. The oracle classifier demonstrates potential for further improvement. The classifier effectively categorizes queries (54.52% overall accuracy), with 8.6% classified as no retrieval, 53.33% as single-step, and 38.07% as multi-step [15].

### 3.3 CA-RAG (Cost-Aware RAG)

**Findings (from source [18]**):
CA-RAG is a routing framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems that dynamically selects a retrieval strategy per query from a fixed set of four options (direct_llm, light_rag, medium_rag, heavy_rag) to balance answer quality, latency, and token cost [18]. The framework uses a utility scoring formula with operator-adjustable weights to select the best strategy for each query without requiring model retraining [18].

Key contributions include: a concrete utility formulation and discrete bundle catalog (4 bundles: no retrieval, top-3, top-5, top-10) for operational RAG routing; uses FAISS for retrieval, OpenAI gpt-4o-mini for generation, and text-embedding-3-small for embeddings [18]. The router selects bundles by maximizing a weighted score combining estimated answer quality, predicted latency, and token cost [18].

Key findings: "CA-RAG selects the most suitable retrieval strategy from a fixed menu of four options, ranging from no retrieval to fetching the top most-relevant documents." [18] "The router assigns different strategies to different queries, achieving 26% fewer billed tokens compared to always using heavy retrieval and 34% lower response time compared to always answering without retrieval, while maintaining answer-quality parity in both cases." [18]

CA-RAG's design point is explicitly differentiated from prior systems (Self-RAG, Adaptive-RAG, CRAG, RAGRouter) noting it is training-free, pre-retrieval, cost-zero at routing time, and operator-adjustable via numeric weights [18]. ### 3.4 R3AG: Retriever Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

**Findings (from survey source [19]**):
R3AG is a novel retriever routing framework for RAG that proposes dynamically routing queries to the most suitable retriever by explicitly modeling retriever capability into two learnable dimensions: retrieval quality and generation utility [19]. The framework employs dual-encoder capability modeling (retrieval quality encoder and generation utility encoder), a multi-head attention mechanism for query-conditioned capabilitiy fusion, and similarity-based routing [19]. It undergoes two-stage optimization: first training the capability encoders with contrastive learning, then optimizing the fusion mechanism [19].

Experiments were conducted on three knowledge-intensive benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, and HotpotQA) using LLaMA3-8B-Instruct as the generator and eight candidate retrievers (BM25 + seven dense retrievers) [19]. Results show R3AG consistently outperforms both the best individual retrievers (achieving 43.06 average EM and 53.86 average F1 vs. 41.31/51.81 for the best single retriever) and state-of-the-art static routing methods (RouterRetriver at 38.08/48.34 and LTRR at 39.14/48.85) [19]. ## 4. Routing Between Decoding Strategies / Prompting Strategies (e.g., Selecting CoT vs Direct Answer, Routing to Different Prompting Techniques)

### 4.1 Pattern-CoT

**Full Title:** Enhancing Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models via Pattern-Based Demonstration Selection
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** AAAI (year not specified in source; likely 2024 or 2025)
**Link:** [https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34793/36948](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34793/36948)

**Findings:**
Pattern-CoT is a method for enhancing Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting in Large Language Models (LLMs) by selecting demonstrations based on reasoning patterns rather than semantic features [23]. The authors argue that existing unsupervised CoT methods suffer from noise and lack interpretability because they rely on semantic similarity of questions [23]. Pattern-CoT addresses this by: (1) constructing task-specific reasoning pattern sets (e.g., operation tokens like +, -, ×, / for arithmetic tasks), (2) extracting patterns from rationales, (3) clustering similar patterns, and (4) selecting diverse demonstrations from each cluster [23].

The approach was tested on eight reasoning datasets (MultiArith, GSM8K, AddSub, AQuA, SingleEq, SVAMP, Coin-Flip, Date Understanding) using LLaMA-2 (7B and 13B), GPT-3.5, and Qwen models [23]. Results show Pattern-CoT consistently outperforms baselines including Zero-Shot-CoT, Random-CoT, and Auto-CoT [23]. Key findings include: greater improvements on arithmetic problems with limited operation tokens; effective even when demonstrations contain errors (e.g., 100% error rate on AQuA still yielded improvements); and enhanced interpretability through feature attribution analysis [23].

### 4.2 RoutingGen: Intention Chain-of-Thought Prompting with Dynamic Routing for Code Generation

**Full Title:** Intention Chain-of-Thought Prompting with Dynamic Routing for Code Generation
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** AAAI 2025
**Link:** [https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/37030/40992](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/37030/40992)

**Findings:**
RoutingGen is a difficulty-aware dynamic routing framework for code generation using large language models [24]. It addresses two key limitations of existing chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting methods: (1) overthinking on simple tasks due to uniform application of structured prompting, and (2) lack of intention abstraction (e.g., core algorithmic logic and time complexity modeling) in code generation [24].

Inspired by dual-process theory of human cognition (System 1 for intuitive responses, System 2 for deliberate reasoning), RoutingGen uses a difficulty classifier (Qwen3-8B) to estimate problem complexity [24]. For simple tasks, it employs direct few-shot prompting; for complex tasks, it invokes a novel structured reasoning strategy called Intention Chain-of-Thought (ICoT), which comprises two stages: Specification (defining input-output constraints) and Idea (capturing core algorithmic logic and time complexity) [24].

Key Results: RoutingGen achieves state-of-the-art Pass@1 performance across three models (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3-671B) and six benchmarks (HumanEval, HumanEval-ET, MBPP-sanitized, MBPP-ET, OpenEval, McEval) [24]. RoutingGen reduces total token usage by 46.37% on average across all settings [24]. ICoT consistently outperforms six prompting baselines (Zero-shot, Few-shot, Self-CoT, ZS-CoT, Self-Planning, SCoT) on challenging benchmarks [24]. On DeepSeek-V3-671B, RoutingGen achieves 91.83% on HumanEval and 90.21% on MBPP-sanitized [24]. On MBPP-sanitized (64.40% classified as Simple), RoutingGen achieves a 59.22% token reduction and 4.60 percentage point accuracy improvement over SCoT [24]. Ablation studies confirm both Specification and Idea stages contribute to ICoT's effectiveness, and RoutingGen is robust to variations in difficulty classifier models (Qwen3-8B vs. GPT-4o) [24].

### 4.3 DCoT: Fine-Tuning on Diverse Reasoning Chains Drives Within-Inference CoT Refinement in LLMs

**Full Title:** Fine-Tuning on Diverse Reasoning Chains Drives Within-Inference CoT Refinement in LLMs
**Authors:** UKPLab
**Venue & Year:** ACL 2025
**Link:** [https://github.com/UKPLab/acl2025-diverse-cot](https://github.com/UKPLab/acl2025-diverse-cot)

**Findings:**
DCoT introduces an approach where LLMs are fine-tuned to generate a sequence of Diverse Chains of Thought (DCoT) within a single inference step, enabling within-inference refinement of reasoning chains without external feedback [25]. Experiments spanning multiple reasoning tasks and model families (1.3B to 70B parameters) show DCoT improves performance over standard CoT baselines, particularly for tasks with large result state spaces like numeric answers [25]. The approach is distinct from prior work that uses parallel CoT generations with ensembling — DCoT generates multiple reasoning chains sequentially within one inference, and gains come from the model's ability to refine an initial reasoning chain by generating a second, improved chain in the same inference step [25].

### 4.4 Cross-lingual Prompting (CLP) for Zero-shot CoT

**Full Title:** Improving Zero-shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning across Languages
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** EMNLP 2023
**Link:** [https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.163.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.163.pdf)

**Findings:**
CLP (Cross-lingual Prompting) improves zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning across languages [26]. Traditional zero-shot CoT uses the prompt "Let's think step by step!" but is limited to single languages. CLP consists of two components: (1) Cross-lingual Alignment Prompting, which uses "Let's understand the task in English step-by-step!" to align representations across languages, and (2) Task-specific Solver Prompting, which uses "Let's resolve the task you understand above step-by-step!" to generate the final reasoning path [26]. The authors also propose Cross-lingual Self-consistent Prompting (CLSP) to ensemble reasoning paths across different languages via a voting mechanism [26].

Key findings on the MGSM benchmark (10 languages) using GPT-3.5: CLP achieves 70.6% average accuracy, outperforming Translate-En (68.4%), En-CoT (57.8%), and Native-CoT (51.0%) [26]. CLSP further improves to 76.7% average accuracy. Experiments on XCOPA (commonsense reasoning) show CLP achieves 85.3% and CLSP 92.7% average accuracy [26].

## 6. Cost-Performance Trade-offs in Routing Decisions

The cost-performance trade-off is a central theme across many of the papers already covered above. Below is a consolidated summary of the key cost-performance findings:

### From FrugalGPT [1][2]:
- LLM Cascade can match GPT-4 performance with up to 98% cost reduction
- Simple caching yields ~8% cache hits with 99% cost savings
- Semantic caching yields ~21% cache hits with 95% cost reduction
- Fine-tuning smaller models can achieve up to 94% cost reduction
- Converting zero-shot prompts to few-shot: up to 98.5% cost reduction with 78% speed improvement

### From RouteLLM [3][4]:
- Cost reduction of over 2x (up to 3.66x) without sacrificing response quality
- 85% cost savings on MT Bench at 95% of GPT-4 performance
- Matrix factorization router: 26% GPT-4 calls needed to achieve 95% GPT-4 performance (48% cheaper than random)
- RouteLLM outperforms commercial routers (Martian, Unify AI) by being over 40% cheaper at same performance

### From SELECT-THEN-ROUTE [9]:
- Achieves 94.3% accuracy vs 91.7% for best single model (O3 Mini) while reducing cost by 4x ($5.21 vs $16.29 per 1000 prompts)
- 35% cost savings and 30% latency improvement over GPT-4o on enterprise data

### From Cascade Routing (ICML 2025) [5]:
- Cascade routing outperforms individual approaches by up to 14%

### From RoutingGen (AAAI 2025) [24]:
- Reduces total token usage by 46.37% on average across all settings
- On MBPP-sanitized: 59.22% token reduction and 4.60 percentage point accuracy improvement

### Economic Case (from industry analysis [31]):
- Price spread between cheapest and most capable models is ~100x (DeepSeek V4 at ~$0.44/M input tokens to GPT-5.5-pro at $30/$180 per M)
- Teams report bill reductions of 40-85% with tuned routing layers
- Savings compound when cheap-model traffic share crosses 50%
- Router overhead is negligible vs. inference time: rule-based <1ms, embeddings ~5ms, ML classifiers 50-100ms—against LLM responses of 500-2,000ms

## 7. Benchmarking and Evaluation Frameworks for Routing

### 7.1 RouterBench

**Full Title:** RouterBench: A Benchmark for Multi-LLM Routing System
**Authors:** Qitian Hu, Jacob Bieker, Xiuyu Li, Nan Jiang, Benjamin Keigwin, Gaurav Ranganath, Kurt Keutzer, Shriyash Upadhyay
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2024 (Agentic Markets Workshop)
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2024/39041](https://icml.cc/virtual/2024/39041)

**Findings:**
RouterBench is a benchmark and dataset designed to systematically assess multi-LLM routing systems, providing over 405k precomputed inference records, standardized evaluation metrics, and a formal evaluation framework [32][33]. It addresses the need for a unified benchmark for routing strategies that dispatch user prompts to optimal LLMs [32]. It covers diverse application domains including commonsense reasoning, knowledge QA, conversation, math, coding, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [32].

**Data Collection:** The dataset comprises 405,467 inference records from 11 LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude-v1/v2, Llama-70B-chat, Mixtral-8x7B, Yi-34B-chat, Code-Llama-34B, Mistral-7B, WizardLM-13B, You.com API, sonar-small/medium-online) [32]. Domains include HellaSwag, Winogrande, ARC-Challenge, MMLU, MT-Bench, GSM8K, MBPP, and an in-house RAG set [32]. Each record includes sample_id, model name, prompt, response, true label, performance score, and cost estimate, stored in JSON Lines format [32].

**Evaluation Framework:** Uses cost–quality analysis, non-decreasing convex hull (NDCH) for Pareto envelope, and the Average Improvement in Quality (AIQ) metric for comparing routing policies without real-time compute costs [32].

**Key Statistics:** Per-model accuracy ranges from ~38% (Claude-instant) to ~83% (GPT-4); per-model mean cost from $0.08 (Mistral-7B) to $4.09 (GPT-4); oracle router achieves ~0.96 mean performance at ~$0.30 mean cost [32]. Cost–quality correlation is ρ≈0.7 [32].

**Limitations:** No latency or throughput metrics; only 11 LLMs covered; limited to general benchmarks (no niche domains); RAG set only 800 queries; GPT-4 judging may introduce systematic bias [32].

**Applications:** Training predictive routers (KNN, MLP, transformers), evaluating non-predictive strategies (cascades, rule-based), and benchmarking novel routing methodologies against theoretical bounds [32].

Key findings: FrugalGPT could save between 59% and 98% of costs while maintaining similar accuracy to larger models like GPT-4 [8]; Routoo achieved 75.9% on MMLU vs 69.9% for Llama2-70B at similar or lower costs [8]; Self-Route reduced token usage by 61% on average for GPT-4o while maintaining comparable performance [8]; RouterDC outperformed standalone LLMs and other routing methods across out-of-distribution datasets [8]. Critical challenges include ensuring complementary LLMs for routing, avoiding over-reliance on the largest model, and the need for diverse training data for clustering approaches [8].

### 7.5 Dynamic Model Routing and Cascading for Efficient LLM Inference: A Survey

This survey (found on arXiv) organizes methods into six paradigms: difficulty-aware routing, human preference-aligned routing, clustering-based routing, reinforcement learning routing, uncertainty-based routing, and cascading. It introduces a three-dimensional framework for characterizing routing systems (when decisions are made, what information is used, how decisions are computed). Since it is an arXiv preprint, it is excluded as a source but its taxonomy is useful context.

--- SOURCE 1: Mixture of Experts in Large Language Models ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2507.11181v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a comprehensive review of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures in large language models, examining how they enhance model performance while maintaining minimal computational overhead. The review covers theoretical foundations, core architectural designs, and LLM applications.

**Key points:**

- **Core Concept**: MoE layers route each input to a sparse subset of k expert networks among N total experts, using noisy top-k routing and gating functions. This decouples inference cost from total model size.

- **Historical Development**: MoE architectures evolved from conceptual formulations (pre-2020) to practical implementations with GShard (600B parameters, 2020), Switch Transformer, and GLaM (2021-22). Post-2023 saw rapid industrial scaling with models like DeepSeekV3 (685B), Skywork 3.0 (400B), and Arctic (482B).

- **Architectural Variants**: Includes orthogonal MoE (OMoE) with weight orthogonality regularization, hierarchical MoEs with two-stage gating, multi-head MoEs, heterogeneous/adaptive experts, and parameter-efficient tuning approaches like LoRA-MoE.

- **Routing Strategies**: Two main paradigms—Token Choice (each token routed to top-k experts) and Expert Choice (each expert selects tokens under fixed budget). Learned vs. fixed routers explored, with findings that fixed routers can sometimes match learned ones.

- **Load Balancing**: Auxiliary loss functions combat expert collapse, though they create tension with routing accuracy.

- **Applications**: Recommendation systems (M3oE, AESM2), multimodal learning (Omni-SMoLA, T-REX2, HyperMoE), healthcare (Med-MoE, AT-MoE, Syn-Mediverse), and computer vision (MoCaE, Deep MoE).

- **Meta-Learning**: Frameworks like MixER and Meta-DMoE enable rapid adaptation across tasks. Knowledge transfer mechanisms include sparse-to-dense distillation and mutual distillation among experts.

- **Challenges**: Routing instability, expert underutilization, irregular memory access patterns, cross-device communication overhead, and deployment constraints in low-latency environments.

The paper concludes that MoE represents a shift toward modular design, enabling efficient scaling of AI systems through conditional computation and sparse expert activation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"MoE architectures offer a more flexible and scalable alternative by embracing heterogeneity in both structure and computation.", "The routing algorithm lies at the heart of every MoE system.", "Early designs employed simple top-k selection using softmax over expert logits, but recent variants increasingly explore entropy-based, load-balanced, or differentiable attention-based routing mechanisms.", "Large-scale evaluations show that MoEs achieve comparable performance to dense models on language tasks while activating approximately 10x fewer parameters per token.", "MoE represents a broader architectural shift toward modular design in deep learning."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Mixture of experts ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixture_of_experts

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Wikipedia article "Mixture of experts" (MoE) describes a machine learning technique where multiple expert networks divide a problem space into homogeneous regions. It is a form of ensemble learning, also called committee machines.

**Basic Theory:** MoE always has expert networks (f₁,...,fₙ) that take the same input, a weighting/gating function (w) that produces a weight vector, and a set of parameters. The output is typically a weighted sum of expert outputs. Both experts and weighting function are trained via gradient descent.

**Key Historical Variants:**
- Meta-pi network: Uses weighted sum output with mean-squared error loss; originally applied to phoneme classification from speech.
- Adaptive mixtures of local experts: Uses Gaussian mixture model where each expert predicts a Gaussian distribution; trained by maximum likelihood estimation. Experts become specialized through a positive feedback effect.
- Hierarchical MoE: Uses multiple levels of gating in a tree structure, similar to decision trees.
- Other variants include hard MoE (only highest-ranked expert selected), experts using linear regression, Laplace or Student's t-distributions, and mixture of softmaxes for language modeling.

**Deep Learning Applications:**
The key difference from classical MoE is that deep learning MoE uses only a subset of experts per query to reduce computing cost, making routing the central design choice.

- **Sparsely-gated MoE layer** (Google Brain, 2017): Uses feedforward networks as experts with linear-softmax gating, achieving sparsity by taking weighted sum of only top-k experts (typically k=1 or 2). The k=1 version is called Switch Transformer. Demonstrated that MoE models used less inference time compute despite having 30x more parameters.
- **Load balancing:** Vanilla MoE tends to have unequal expert utilization. Auxiliary loss functions encourage equal selection frequency. DeepSeek proposed "auxiliary-loss-free load balancing" using expert biases, and "shared experts" for core capacities with "routed experts" for peripheral capacities.
- **Capacity factor:** Enforces a hard constraint on how many queries each expert can process per batch (typically 1.25-2x the average).
- **Routing approaches:** Three classes: expert choice, token choice (original sparsely-gated MoE), and global assigner. Token dropping is handled via residual connections.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Mixture of experts (MoE) is a machine learning technique where multiple expert networks (learners) are used to divide a problem space into homogeneous regions., The combined effect is that the experts become specialized... This has a positive feedback effect, causing each expert to move apart from the rest and take care of a local region alone., The key goal when using MoE in deep learning is to reduce computing cost. Consequently, for each query, only a small subset of the experts should be queried., Table 3 shows that the MoE models used less inference time compute, despite having 30x more parameters., They proposed 'auxiliary-loss-free load balancing strategy', which does not use auxiliary loss. Instead, each expert has an extra 'expert bias'. If an expert is being neglected, then their bias increases, and vice versa.

--- SOURCE 4: Understanding Mixture of Experts (MoE) Neural Networks ---
URL: https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/mixture-of-experts-moe-models

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive technical guide to Mixture of Experts (MoE) neural networks, published by IntuitionLabs and updated February 19, 2026. The article covers the theoretical foundations, architecture, training methods, practical challenges, and comparisons to dense transformers, along with real-world implementations including DeepSeek-V3, Llama 4, Mixtral, and other frontier MoE systems.

**Theoretical Foundation:** MoE models divide computation across multiple specialized sub-models ("experts") using a gating mechanism to select which experts to invoke per input. Originally introduced in the 1990s, MoE was revived by Shazeer et al. (2017) using sparsely-gated layers, followed by Google's GShard (600B parameters, 2048 experts) and Switch Transformer (first trillion-parameter model). The key advantage is increasing model capacity sub-linearly with respect to computation.

**Architecture:** An MoE model consists of N expert networks (typically feed-forward networks) and a gating network (router) that outputs a probability distribution over experts. Modern MoEs use sparse gating—selecting only top-k experts (usually k=1 or 2) per input. In transformer-based MoEs, the MoE layer replaces the dense feed-forward layer. The gating network is typically a simple feed-forward layer with softmax. Routing strategies include noisy top-k gating, random routing (GShard), and Expert-Choice routing.

**Training:** Key challenges include ensuring all experts receive learning signal and preventing "expert collapse." Standard techniques include: (1) auxiliary load balancing loss to encourage even token distribution across experts; (2) expert capacity limits to prevent bottlenecks; (3) noisy gating for exploration; (4) expert dropout and router z-loss regularization. The gating network is trained via backpropagation with straight-through estimation for the non-differentiable top-k selection.

**Practical Challenges:** (1) Load imbalance and communication overhead requiring all-to-all token shuffling across devices; (2) inference complexity due to large memory footprint (all experts must reside in memory); (3) expert collapse and training instability; (4) memory and infrastructure constraints; (5) routing inefficiencies. Solutions include Microsoft's Tutel library (2.5-5.9× speedup), DeepSpeed-MoE, NVIDIA's Blackwell platform (10× reduction in cost per token), and frameworks like vLLM and TensorRT-LLM.

**MoE vs. Dense Transformers:** MoEs are preferred when maximizing capacity under limited compute, handling heterogeneous data/tasks, or when inference FLOPs per token must be minimized. Dense models are preferred when model size is constrained or simplicity is paramount. Example: Google's GLaM (1.2T params, 64 experts, top-2 gating) achieved better zero-shot performance than dense 175B GPT-3 while using half the inference FLOPs. As of 2025-2026, nearly all frontier models (DeepSeek-V3/R1, Llama 4, Mistral Large 3, Gemini, likely GPT-4) use MoE architectures.

**Applications:** Primarily NLP—large language models, machine translation, and multitask benchmarks. Meta's NLLB project found 128-expert MoE significantly outperformed dense models for low-resource languages.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs - by Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. ---
URL: https://cameronrwolfe.substack.com/p/moe-llms

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article provides a comprehensive overview of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models, explaining their fundamentals, benefits, drawbacks, and notable implementations. MoE-based LLMs introduce sparsity to the model architecture by replacing standard feed-forward layers with multiple "expert" networks and a routing mechanism that selects only a subset of experts (typically 2) to process each token. This allows models to have significantly more total parameters without a proportional increase in computational cost per token.

**Key technical concepts covered:**
- **Experts**: Multiple independent feed-forward networks replacing a single FFN layer
- **Routing**: A learned gating mechanism (linear layer + softmax) that selects top-K experts per token
- **Auxiliary Losses**: Importance loss, load balancing loss (from Switch Transformers), and router z-loss (from ST-MoE) to prevent "routing collapse" and ensure balanced expert utilization
- **Expert Capacity**: Maximum tokens that can be routed to each expert; overflow tokens are dropped
- **Shared Experts**: Recently introduced concept where some experts process all tokens while others are routed
- **Interleaved MoE**: Only every P-th layer uses MoE, with other layers remaining dense

**Benefits**: Better model quality vs. inference efficiency tradeoff, 7× pretraining speedup (Switch Transformer), faster inference at low batch sizes, higher throughput at large batch sizes.

**Drawbacks**: Training instabilities, difficult finetuning, sensitivity to mixed precision and hyperparameters.

**Notable MoE LLMs discussed:**
1. **Mixtral 8×7B** (Mistral) - 47B total/13B active params, 8 experts with 2 active per token, outperforms LLaMA-2-70B on many benchmarks, 32K context
2. **Mixtral-8×22B** - 141B total/39B active params, 64K context
3. **Grok-1** (xAI) - 314B total params, ~70-80B active, 25% of weights active per token, open-sourced
4. **DBRX** (Mosaic/Databricks) - 132B total/36B active, 16 experts with 4 active per token, "fine-grained" MoE, 4× improvement in pretraining efficiency, outperforms GPT-3.5
5. **OpenMoE** - Open-source suite from 650M to 34B parameters, finds routing is primarily token-ID-driven ("Context-Independent Specialization")
6. **DeepSeek-v2/v3** - Unique design choices maximizing training efficiency, impressive performance on par with closed models
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Using an MoE architecture makes it possible to attain better tradeoffs between model quality and inference efficiency than dense models typically achieve." - from [11], "The gating network tends to converge to a state where it always produces large weights for the same few experts. # Expert Choice Routing in MoE Models

**Published:** November 20, 2025

This article covers the paradigm shift in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models where expert choice routing replaces traditional top-k token-to-expert routing. In expert choice routing, **experts select which tokens to process**, ensuring balanced load allocation and eliminating the need for auxiliary balancing losses.

## Core Principles

Traditional MoE uses a gating network where each token selects its top-k experts, leading to load imbalance. Expert choice routing inverts this: each expert selects its top-C tokens from the batch, guaranteeing perfect per-expert load balance and allowing variable numbers of experts per token.

## The Three-Step Process

1. **Score Computation**: Compute gating scores via a learnable router
2. **Expert-Side Selection**: Each expert selects its top-C tokens
3. **Dispatch and Combination**: Selected tokens are processed by all selected experts; outputs are combined

## Recent Advances

- **Continuous Rerouting** (Su et al., Oct 2025): Two-phase online adaptation for test-time deployment—prefill phase updates router logits via self-supervised loss, steered generation phase uses modified router. Data-free, achieves +5.5% pass@1 on HumanEval for OLMoE.
- **AdaMoE** (Zeng et al., 2024): Introduces null experts (identity/zero mapping, zero FLOPs). On Mixtral-8x7B: 14.5% FLOPs reduction, +1.69% accuracy on ARC-Challenge.
- **Dynamic Expert Routing (RoE)** (Wu et al., 2024): Binary keep-vs-adapter decisions with structure sparsity regularizer. 15-25% faster inference in vision-language tasks with no accuracy loss.

## Empirical Performance

| Model | Metric | Improvement |
|-------|--------|-------------|
| OLMoE | HumanEval pass@1 | +5.5% (34.17%) |
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite | HumanEval pass@1 | +3.6% (54.26%) |
| Mixtral-8x7B (AdaMoE) | ARC-C Accuracy | +1.69% (89.15%) |
| EC-DIT-3XL-32E | GenEval (image gen) | +1.99% (70.91%) |
| RoE-LLaVA | 5 VL Benchmarks | +3.3% (63.8%) |

## Practical Considerations

Expert choice routing achieves ~1.1× faster convergence vs. top-1 routing. However, it requires global top-C selection per expert over the batch, which poses challenges for autoregressive inference (where only current token is available). Mechanisms like AdaMoE avoid these bottlenecks and remain compatible with causal decoding.

## Key Hyperparameters

- Number of experts (E) and capacity factor (Cf)
- Router learning rates and regularization
- Null-expert count m (AdaMoE), adapter size c (RoE)
- Update intervals and norm clipping for continuous rerouting

## Limitations

- Intricacies of batched global selection for autoregressive models
- Need for careful tuning of adaptation parameters to avoid overfitting

The advances position expert choice routing and its dynamic successors as underpinning state-of-the-art approaches across language, vision, and generative modeling.
</summary>

1. Compute logits for every token-slot combination
2. Normalize logits per slot (column-wise), compute linear combination of input tokens per slot
3. Each expert (MLP) processes its assigned slots
4. Normalize logits per token (row-wise) to combine slot outputs for each input token
5. Learnable parameters are adjusted during training

**Key Properties of Soft MoE:**
- Fully differentiable (no discrete top-k assignments)
- No token dropping or expert unbalance (all tokens utilized)
- Faster and more efficient than sparse MoEs (no sorting/top-k operations)
- Combines features of sparse and dense models (each token involved in every slot, but experts process only a subset of slots)
- Per-sequence determinism maintained

# DeepSeekMoE: Advanced Mixture-of-Experts Models

## Overview
DeepSeekMoE models are large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures developed by the DeepSeek research group, optimized for language, vision-language, diffusion, and code generation tasks. They employ fine-grained sub-experts, always-on shared experts, and normalized sigmoid gating to optimize token routing and parameter efficiency. Key innovations include auxiliary-loss-free load balancing and node-limited routing, achieving faster training and reduced computational cost compared to dense baselines.

## Architectural Foundation
DeepSeekMoE extends conventional MoE by segmenting each canonical expert into multiple fine-grained sub-experts and supplementing them with always-on shared experts. Shared experts absorb domain-general knowledge and are always active, while routed experts specialize via token-dependent gating. This structure enables a higher diversity of token-to-expert activation patterns, improving route-specific specialization.

## Gating, Routing, and Load Balancing
- **Normalized sigmoid gating**: Replaces softmax for improved gradient flow and identifiability
- **Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing (ALF-LB)**: Uses dynamically adapted per-expert biases instead of expensive auxiliary losses, ensuring provable monotonic improvement of the Lagrangian objective
- **Node-limited routing**: Constrains expert selection per token to reduce cross-node interconnect usage

## Model Scaling

|-------|-----------------|-------------------|
| DeepSeek-V2 | 236B | 21B (8.9% active) |
| DeepSeek-V3 | 671B | 37B |

## Empirical Performance
- **DeepSeek-V3 (37B activated)** outperforms Qwen2.5 (72B) and LLaMA-3.1 (405B) on standard benchmarks
- **VL2-Base (4.5B activated)** achieves best-in-class performance on visual grounding and document VQA
- **DeepSeek-Coder-V2** matches or exceeds GPT-4 Turbo in code generation
- At 16B scale, DeepSeekMoE-16B achieves parity with dense LLaMA2-7B using only 40% of its FLOPs

## Training & Optimization
Training combines next-token prediction, multi-token prediction (MTP), and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Memory optimizations use Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) to compress KV-cache up to 93.3%. Compression techniques like MoBE (Mixture-of-Basis-Experts) achieve 30% parameter reduction with only 1.6% relative accuracy loss.

## Hardware Co-Design
System-level optimizations include FP8 mixed-precision communication, BigMac structure for reordering projection and communication (up to 3.09× training speedup), and multi-plane fat-tree network topology supporting MoE scaling to 16,384 GPUs.

## Theoretical Analysis
Normalized sigmoid gating yields better identifiability and avoids adverse polynomial over-specification effects present in softmax gating. The shared expert mechanism guarantees near-parametric sample efficiency and improves convergence for routed experts.

This article explains **router z-loss**, a regularization technique introduced in the 2022 ST-MoE paper (Zoph et al., Google Brain) to stabilize Mixture of Experts (MoE) model training by penalizing large router logits.

## The Problem: Router Instability
During MoE training, router logits drift toward extreme values through a self-reinforcing feedback loop—larger logits create sharper probability distributions, stronger gradients, and even larger logits. This causes:
- **Softmax overflow/underflow** (exp(z_j) > 709 for float64 or > 88 for float32 produces infinity)
- **Gradient saturation** (vanishing gradients as probabilities approach 0 or 1)
- **Loss spikes and gradient explosions** (NaN values cascade through the network)
- **Expert collapse** (router gets stuck on a single expert)

The max-subtraction trick prevents forward-pass overflow but doesn't address the underlying logit drift or gradient saturation.

## The Solution: Z-Loss Formulation
The z-loss penalizes the **log-sum-exp (LSE)** of router logits:

**L_z = (1/B) * Σ_i (log Σ_j exp(z_i,j))²**

where B = batch size, N = number of experts, z_i,j = logit for token i and expert j.

### Key Properties:
- **LSE approximates the maximum logit**: max z_j ≤ LSE ≤ max z_j + log N
- **Smooth everywhere** (unlike hard max), enabling well-behaved gradient-based optimization
- **Quadratic penalty**: provides gentle regularization for moderate logits but strong correction for extreme values
- **Computationally efficient**: reuses intermediate results from softmax calculation

### Gradient Analysis:
∂L_z/∂z_i,j = (2/B) · LSE(z_i) · softmax(z_i)_j

The gradient is proportional to both the current LSE value (scale emergency severity) and the softmax probability (which logit is most responsible), creating targeted corrective pressure.

## Why Z-Loss Works
1. **Bounded logit growth**: Creates a restoring force equilibrium counteracting logit drift
2. **Softmax temperature effect**: Encourages softer probability distributions, improving gradient flow and exploration
3. **Regularization benefits**: Improves generalization by preventing overconfident routing based on spurious correlations

## Coefficient Tuning
The total training objective: **L_total = L_task + α_z · L_z**

Typical coefficients range from **10⁻⁴ to 10⁻²**:
- The ST-MoE paper used α_z = 10⁻⁴ as a starting point
- Larger models need stronger z-loss (higher α_z)
- If instabilities occur, increase α_z by 2-5x
- Too high α_z can make routing too soft, reducing expert specialization benefits

## Worked Example
For a batch of 3 tokens with 4 experts, token 3's logit of 8.0 for expert 1 contributes ~80% of the total z-loss (64.00 out of 80.87), demonstrating quadratic amplification targeting the most dangerous logit. The gradient for that dominant logit is approximately 5.31, providing strong corrective pressure.
</summary>

# Mixture of Experts (MoE) — Comprehensive Overview

## Overview and Motivation
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is an architectural paradigm that enables massive scaling of neural networks through **conditional computation** — selectively activating only a small subset of "experts" per input rather than all parameters. This decouples model capacity from per-token compute, allowing near-linear parameter scaling without proportional compute cost increases. The concept originated with Jacobs et al. (1991) and was revolutionized by Shazeer et al. (2017) with **Sparsely-Gated MoE** and top-k routing, followed by the **Switch Transformer** (Fedus et al., 2021) with top-1 routing, and **MegaBlocks/Dropless MoE** (Gale et al., 2022) with block-sparse matrix multiplication.

## Key Milestones
- **1991**: Jacobs et al. introduce MoE with gating networks and expert specialization
- **2017**: Shazeer et al. introduce Sparsely-Gated MoE with top-k routing and load-balancing losses
- **2020**: GShard (Lepikhin et al.) scales MoE to distributed systems
- **2021**: Switch Transformer simplifies to top-1 routing, reducing communication overhead
- **2022**: MegaBlocks introduces block-sparse computation, removing token dropping
- **2024-2025**: Modern models like Mixtral-8×7B, DeepSeek-V2, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3, and Kimi K2 (1.04T parameters, 384 experts, sparsity 48) embed MoE principles broadly

## Taxonomy of Modern MoE Architectures
1. **Sparse MoE**: Switch Transformer, GLaM, Mixtral — top-k token routing, extreme scalability
2. **Dense–Hybrid MoE**: T5-MoE, DeepSeek-V2 — partial MoE integration for stability + efficiency
3. **Hierarchical/Structured MoE**: HMoE, Sparse-Transformer++, HC-SMoE — multi-level expert routing for interpretability
4. **Joint/Multimodal MoE**: Uni-MoE, Union of Experts — cross-modal routing for unified multimodal processing
5. **Adaptive/Dynamic MoE**: AdaMoE, Expert Choice Routing — compute proportional to input complexity

## Core Technical Concepts

### Expert Capacity and Capacity Factor
The capacity factor determines how many tokens each expert can process, defined as: capacity = (tokens per batch / number of experts) × capacity factor. Key implications include token overflow/dropping, load-balancing trade-offs, and computational efficiency.

### Load Balancing
Auxiliary loss functions encourage even token distribution across experts, preventing routing collapse where all tokens go to a few experts.

### Expert Specialization
Experts self-organize around latent data structures (syntax, domain, modality) without explicit supervision. Models like Mixtral-8×7B and MoE-LLaVA demonstrate this specialization empirically.

### Shared Experts
Separate common knowledge from specialized knowledge by having always-active "shared experts" alongside routed experts, improving specialization and reducing routing dependence.

### Expert Choice Routing
Reverses routing direction — experts choose which tokens to process — achieving better load balancing and conceptual clustering.

### Expert Parallelism
Distributes expert parameters across devices, routing tokens to the appropriate device for processing, with hybrid parallel strategies combining data, model, and expert parallelism.

## Key Benefits
- **Massive capacity scaling** without proportional training cost
- **Training compute scales with active experts per token**, not total parameters
- **Inference cost depends on activated experts**, enabling quality-cost trade-offs
- **Adaptive computation** aligned with input complexity
- **Expert specialization** improves representational efficiency

## Limitations
- **Inference-time memory**: All expert parameters must reside in VRAM despite sparse activation
- **Training instability and load imbalance**
- **Communication overhead** in distributed settings
- **Routing complexity and gradient fragmentation**
- **Underutilization of model capacity** and inference latency variability

## Modern Frontier Example: Kimi K2 (2025)
Demonstrates MoE scaling governed by sparsity laws, routing stability, and optimizer stability: 1.04T total parameters, 32B activated, 384 experts, 8 activated per token, sparsity 48.

- **Mixtral 8x7B** (Mistral AI, 2024)
- **OpenMoE**
- **DeepSeek-V2**, **Gemini 1.5**, **Claude 3**

## Future Directions
Structural routing, cross-modal expert specialization, dynamic compute allocation, and semantically aware expert networks.

--- SOURCE 25: HoME: Hierarchy of Multi-Gate Experts forMulti-Task Learning at Kuaishou ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2408.05430v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper from Kuaishou presents HoME (Hierarchy of Multi-Gate Experts), a multi-task learning framework designed to address three key anomalies observed in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems for short-video recommendation:

**Three Anomalies Identified:**
1. **Expert Collapse**: Experts' output distributions differ significantly; some experts have >90% zero activations with ReLU, making it hard for gate networks to assign fair weights.
2. **Expert Degradation**: Shared-experts lose their ability to serve all tasks and degenerate into task-specific experts, becoming occupied by only one task.
3. **Expert Underfitting**: Data-sparse prediction tasks tend to ignore their specific-experts and rely heavily on shared-experts, causing specific parameters to go unused.

**Proposed Solutions:**
1. **Expert Normalization & Swish Mechanism**: Uses batch normalization per expert to align output distributions and replaces ReLU with Swish to avoid zero activations, preventing expert collapse.
2. **Hierarchy Mask Mechanism**: Introduces a pre-order meta expert network that groups tasks into two categories (passive watching-time tasks and proactive interaction tasks) with shared, in-category, and specific experts to improve sharing efficiency and prevent degradation.
3. **Feature-gate & Self-gate Mechanisms**: Feature-gate privatizes expert inputs using LoRA-style low-rank approximations to reduce gradient conflicts. Self-gate adds residual connections between layers to ensure effective gradient propagation for sparse tasks.

**Results:**
- Deployed at Kuaishou serving 400 million daily users
- Offline: Average 0.52% GAUC improvement over baselines
- Online: 0.954% improvement in play-time per user (0.636% and 0.735% on Kuaishou and Kuaishou-Lite)
- Outperforms MMoE, CGC, PLE, and AdaTT baselines with fewer parameters
- Shows scaling-law behavior: more experts lead to steady improvement
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This paper (NeurIPS 2021) introduces "Hash Layers" for large sparse Transformer models. The approach modifies the feedforward layer to hash tokens to different sets of weights based on the current token, across all tokens in the sequence. Key findings include: (1) Hash Layers outperform or are competitive with learning-to-route mixture-of-expert methods like Switch Transformers and BASE Layers; (2) They require no routing parameters, load balancing loss, or sophisticated assignment algorithms; (3) Balanced and random hashes focused on the most local features work best; (4) The approach performs well on large language modeling, dialogue tasks, and downstream fine-tuning tasks.

--- SOURCE 2: Hash Layers For Large Sparse Models [Quick Review] ---
URL: https://liner.com/review/hash-layers-for-large-sparse-models

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, presented at NeurIPS on June 8, 2021, introduces **Hash Layers** as a simple, sparse routing strategy for large Transformer models. Unlike traditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that use learned routing (e.g., Switch Transformers, BASE Layers), Hash Layers use pre-computed hash functions (like Random Hash and Balanced assignment) to route tokens to fixed expert modules without learned parameters or complex load balancing. The paper also introduces MultiHash Layers, which segment linear layers and use multiple hash functions to select parameters.

**Key Findings:**
- Hash Layers consistently outperform Switch Transformers on language modeling tasks (e.g., on pushshift.io Reddit, Hash Layer achieved 22.89 perplexity with 1x128 modules vs. Switch's 23.52).
- Both sparse models outperform dense Transformer baselines with similar computational costs.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces Hash Layers, a simple and efficient sparse routing strategy for large Transformer models. Instead of using learned routing (like Mixture-of-Experts methods such as Switch Transformers and BASE Layers), the authors propose using fixed hash functions to route input tokens to different expert feedforward network (FFN) modules. The hash function is pre-computed based on the current input token and requires no learnable routing parameters, no load balancing loss, and no complex assignment algorithms.

Key findings include:
- Hash Layers outperform or are competitive with Switch Transformers and BASE Layers across multiple datasets (pushshift.io Reddit, RoBERTa+cc100en, Wikitext-103).

- Hash layers placed on later decoder layers work better than earlier ones.
- Clustered hashing (putting similar tokens together) performs worse than random hashing, suggesting that fine distinctions between similar tokens benefit from being routed to different experts.
- Multi-hashing (splitting parameters across multiple hash functions and concatenating) further improves performance.
- Hash Layers work well on downstream fine-tuning tasks, retaining the pre-training performance ordering.

URL: https://www.cerebras.ai/blog/moe-guide-router

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post, published on August 4, 2025, by Cerebras, examines Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing strategies, arguing that the router is the most critical component of an MoE model and can destroy performance if poorly implemented. It covers three fundamental routing approaches:

1. **Hash Routing (Roller et al., 2021):** Deterministic, perfect load balancing, but ignores token context, leading to low expert specialization. With 16 experts, it yields only ~1.5% loss improvement over dense models.

2. **Learned Routing (Shazeer et al., 2017):** The industry standard, used by DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, etc. Uses a learned linear layer with auxiliary loss to balance load. Delivers ~4% loss improvement with 16 experts (nearly 3x hash routing). However, suffers from "router collapse" in early and late layers where most tokens funnel to 1-2 experts.

3. **Sinkhorn Routing (Clark et al., 2022):** Achieves hash-level load balancing with learned routing-level performance by iteratively normalizing per-layer distributions. However, it limits expert specialization compared to learned routing and is hard to scale in practice due to implementation complexities (gradient detachment issues).

The post notes that modern production MoE methods (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3) are all built on core learned routing with engineering tricks like shared experts, capacity factors, and adaptive auxiliary loss layered on top. It concludes that no current routing method simultaneously improves both expert utilization and specialization, and directs readers to a follow-up guide on debugging MoE training issues.

URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.17952v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces SoftMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture for large language models that replaces the standard hard top-k routing with a differentiable soft top-k routing mechanism based on the LapSum relaxation. The key innovation is that SoftMoE enables gradient-based optimization of expert selection, unlike standard sparse MoE where the discrete top-k operator is non-differentiable. 

SoftMoE addresses three fundamental limitations of sparse MoE: (1) non-differentiability of discrete expert selection, (2) fixed number of active experts per input, and (3) inability to learn expert allocation across layers. The proposed method uses a truncated soft top-k LapSum relaxation that allows the model to learn how many experts to activate in each layer under a global budget constraint.

The routing mechanism processes each token independently and remains fully compatible with autoregressive language modeling. The authors introduce learnable per-layer expert allocation parameters (k_l) with a global budget constraint (sum of k_l = K), enabling the model to redistribute computational capacity between layers. This is achieved through an unconstrained reparameterization using softmax of auxiliary parameters.

The method was evaluated on language modeling using C4 and OpenWebText datasets, as well as downstream benchmarks (PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC-E). Experiments used a 1.63B parameter decoder-only GPT-2 architecture with 10 transformer blocks and 32 experts per block. Results show SoftMoE consistently matches or outperforms standard sparse MoE while activating significantly fewer experts on average. For example, SoftMoE* with k=1.5 on C4 activated 17% fewer experts while achieving lower perplexity than sparse MoE with k=2.

The learned allocation patterns are highly non-uniform, with later layers consistently activating more experts. Under a global budget constraint, the top 3 transformer layers absorbed approximately 50% of the total expert budget. This suggests depth-aware allocation may be more appropriate than the uniform expert allocation used in current MoE architectures.

The paper concludes that differentiable top-k routing constitutes a viable and scalable alternative to hard expert selection, enabling further research into adaptive conditional computation. Limitations include evaluation only on English text corpora, lack of multimodal experiments, and validation on a 1.63B parameter architecture rather than larger models.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# MegaBlocks: Efficient Sparse Training with Mixture-of-Experts

A guest presentation by Trevor Gale (Google DeepMind, PhD from Stanford) for the CMSC828G course at the University of Maryland (Spring 2025). The talk focuses on the MegaBlocks system for efficiently training Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models.

## Key Problem
Standard MoE implementations require a fixed "expert capacity" hyperparameter, forcing tokens to be dropped or padded when experts receive imbalanced token assignments. This creates a trade-off between model quality and speed, often wasting compute resources tuning the capacity factor.

## MegaBlocks Solution
MegaBlocks reformulates expert computation as a block-sparse matrix multiplication problem, allowing variable-sized blocks (load-imbalanced token-to-expert assignments). The approach partitions larger variable-size blocks into smaller fixed-size blocks, using a hybrid sparse matrix encoding (blocked CSR, block COO, transpose index) to handle different operations efficiently.

## Kernels
Custom block-sparse GPU kernels achieve ~99% of the throughput of cuBLAS batched matrix multiplication on A100 GPUs, supporting large block sizes (128x128), transposition of both inputs, load imbalance, and cheap sparse matrix construction.

## Results
- MegaBlocks trains 20-40% faster than state-of-the-art implementations (e.g., Microsoft's Tutel)
- 1.2-1.4x faster end-to-end vs. best-performing MoE for a given model quality
- 1.8-2.4x faster than dense transformers of equivalent quality
- Trains at the speed of capacity factor 1.0 MoE but with the quality of infinite-capacity MoE

## Industry Adoption
- Mosaic/Databricks adopted MegaBlocks to train DBRX (March 2023, state-of-the-art LLM at the time)
- Mistral's Mixtral 8x7B released with a MegaBlocks reference implementation
- JetMoE trained with MegaBlocks
- Open-source TPU implementation (using Pallas) for Google's MaxText library and PyTorch on TPUs

## Architecture
Built on NVIDIA's Megatron-LM and PyTorch. Uses 64-expert layers with top-1 routing, trained on 10B tokens from The Pile across 8 A100 GPUs with data parallelism and 8-way expert model parallelism.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive technical guide to Mixture of Experts (MoE) neural networks, published by IntuitionLabs and updated February 19, 2026. The article covers the theoretical foundations, architecture, training methods, practical challenges, and comparisons to dense transformers, along with real-world implementations including DeepSeek-V3, Llama 4, Mixtral, and other frontier MoE systems.

**Theoretical Foundation:** MoE models divide computation across multiple specialized sub-models ("experts") using a gating mechanism to select which experts to invoke per input. Originally introduced in the 1990s, MoE was revived by Shazeer et al. (2017) using sparsely-gated layers, followed by Google's GShard (600B parameters, 2048 experts) and Switch Transformer (first trillion-parameter model). The key advantage is increasing model capacity sub-linearly with respect to computation.

**Architecture:** An MoE model consists of N expert networks (typically feed-forward networks) and a gating network (router) that outputs a probability distribution over experts. Modern MoEs use sparse gating—selecting only top-k experts (usually k=1 or 2) per input. In transformer-based MoEs, the MoE layer replaces the dense feed-forward layer. The gating network is typically a simple feed-forward layer with softmax. Routing strategies include noisy top-k gating, random routing (GShard), and Expert-Choice routing.

**Training:** Key challenges include ensuring all experts receive learning signal and preventing "expert collapse." Standard techniques include: (1) auxiliary load balancing loss to encourage even token distribution across experts; (2) expert capacity limits to prevent bottlenecks; (3) noisy gating for exploration; (4) expert dropout and router z-loss regularization. The gating network is trained via backpropagation with straight-through estimation for the non-differentiable top-k selection.

**Practical Challenges:** (1) Load imbalance and communication overhead requiring all-to-all token shuffling across devices; (2) inference complexity due to large memory footprint (all experts must reside in memory); (3) expert collapse and training instability; (4) memory and infrastructure constraints; (5) routing inefficiencies. Solutions include Microsoft's Tutel library (2.5-5.9× speedup), DeepSpeed-MoE, NVIDIA's Blackwell platform (10× reduction in cost per token), and frameworks like vLLM and TensorRT-LLM.

**MoE vs. Dense Transformers:** MoEs are preferred when maximizing capacity under limited compute, handling heterogeneous data/tasks, or when inference FLOPs per token must be minimized. Dense models are preferred when model size is constrained or simplicity is paramount. Example: Google's GLaM (1.2T params, 64 experts, top-2 gating) achieved better zero-shot performance than dense 175B GPT-3 while using half the inference FLOPs. As of 2025-2026, nearly all frontier models (DeepSeek-V3/R1, Llama 4, Mistral Large 3, Gemini, likely GPT-4) use MoE architectures.

**Applications:** Primarily NLP—large language models, machine translation, and multitask benchmarks. Meta's NLLB project found 128-expert MoE significantly outperformed dense models for low-resource languages.
</summary>

Common pitfalls include treating overflow as minor, assuming routing self-fixes, and underestimating communication/batching constraints.

This Hugging Face blog post (published 2023) provides a comprehensive overview of Mixture of Experts (MoE) in transformer models, with a focus on the Mixtral 8x7B release. Key points:

**What is MoE?** MoE replaces every Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layer in transformers with an MoE layer consisting of a gate network and multiple "experts." Only a subset of experts is activated per input (sparsity), enabling models to be pretrained with far less compute while achieving similar quality to dense counterparts.

**Key Concepts:**
- **Sparsity**: Uses conditional computation - only parts of the network activate per example. Top-K gating (e.g., top-2) selects which experts to use.
- **Load Balancing**: An auxiliary loss encourages equal use of all experts, preventing tokens from being routed to just a few popular experts.
- **Expert Capacity**: (tokens per batch / number of experts) × capacity factor. A buffer for imbalanced token distribution.

**History & Research:**
- Originated from 1991 paper "Adaptive Mixture of Local Experts"
- Shazeer et al. (2017) scaled to 137B LSTM with sparsity
- GShard scaled transformers beyond 600B parameters, replacing every other FFN with MoE
- Switch Transformers (2021) achieved 4x pre-train speedup over T5-XXL, using simplified single-expert strategy
- ST-MoE introduced router Z-loss for training stability

- MoE models are more prone to overfitting during fine-tuning; higher regularization (dropout) is recommended
- Fine-tuning MoE parameters alone doesn't work well; freezing MoE layers while updating others works almost as well as full fine-tuning
- MoEs benefit more from instruction tuning than dense models
- MoE inference: a 47B model with 8 experts runs with compute of a ~12B dense model (top-2)
- More experts improve sample efficiency but with diminishing returns (especially after 256-512), and require more VRAM for inference

**Serving & Efficiency:**
- Expert parallelism places experts on different workers
- Capacity factor affects quality vs. communication costs tradeoff
- Techniques like FasterMoE, Megablocks, and quantization (QMoE) improve efficiency
- Open source MoEs include Mixtral 8x7B, Switch Transformers, and NLLB-MoE

## 1. Model Selection / Routing Between Different Model Sizes or Families

### 1.1 FrugalGPT

**Full Title:** FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance  
**Authors:** Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou  
**Venue & Year:** Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), May 2023  
**Link:** [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/FrugalGPT%3A-How-to-Use-Large-Language-Models-While-Chen-Zaharia/585f8b9725f5f5e5495c3508d39f70d1c053e190](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/FrugalGPT%3A-How-to-Use-Large-Language-Models-While-Chen-Zaharia/585f8b9725f5f5e5495c3508d39f70d1c053e190)

**Findings:**
FrugalGPT proposes a simple yet flexible instantiation of an LLM cascade which learns which combinations of LLMs to use for different queries in order to reduce cost and improve accuracy, laying a foundation for using LLMs sustainably and efficiently [1][2]. FrugalGPT revolves around three key techniques:
1. **Prompt Adaptation:** Using concise, optimized prompts to minimize token costs (e.g., selecting top k similar examples instead of all examples reduced costs by 70%, and combining similar requests reduced costs by 50%).
2. **LLM Approximation:** Utilizing caches and model fine-tuning to avoid repeated expensive queries (simple caching yields ~8% cache hits with 99% cost savings, semantic caching yields ~21% cache hits with 95% cost reduction, and fine-tuning smaller models can achieve up to 94% cost reduction).
3. **LLM Cascade:** Dynamically selecting the optimal sequence of LLMs to query based on confidence scoring, which can match GPT-4 performance with up to 98% cost reduction.

Key results: "FrugalGPT can match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction or improve the accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% with the same cost." [1] Additional techniques include converting zero-shot prompts for larger models into few-shot prompts for smaller models (up to 98.5% cost reduction with 78% speed improvement) and prompt compression using LLMLingua (2.5x-5x compression ratios). The paper has 874 citations and 57 references [2]. It has spawned significant follow-up work including MetaLLM, OptLLM, ThriftLLM, and other frameworks focused on cost-effective LLM routing, selection, and query allocation [2].

### 1.2 RouteLLM

**Full Title:** RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data  
**Authors:** Isaac Ong, Amjad Almahairi, et al. (UC Berkeley)  
**Venue & Year:** ICLR 2025 (peer-reviewed at ICLR 2025; also listed as ICLR 2024 in some sources)  
**Link:** [https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm) (Open-source framework page; paper on alphaxiv: [https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2406.18665](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2406.18665))

**Findings:**
RouteLLM introduces a training framework for learning efficient router models that dynamically select between a stronger (expensive) and weaker (cheaper) LLM during inference to balance performance and cost [3][4]. The framework leverages human preference data from Chatbot Arena (80k battles) and employs data augmentation techniques (golden-labeled data from MMLU and LLM-judge-labeled data from GPT-4). The authors evaluate several router architectures: Similarity-weighted (SW) ranking, Matrix Factorization, BERT classifier, and Causal LLM classifier (Llama 3 8B).

Key results show that routers can reduce costs by over 2x (up to 3.66x) without sacrificing response quality [3]. On MT Bench, the best routers (trained on augmented data) achieve APGR improvements of 50-60% over random baselines. The matrix factorization router required half the GPT-4 calls of random to achieve 50% performance gap recovery. Routers also demonstrate strong generalization to unseen model pairs (Claude 3 Opus/Sonnet and Llama 3.1 70B/8B) without retraining [3]. The paper finds that data augmentation is critical—routers trained solely on Arena data perform poorly on out-of-distribution benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K, but augmentation with as little as 1500 in-domain samples significantly improves performance [3][4].

Specific cost savings: "cost reductions of over 85% on MT Bench, 45% on MMLU, and 35% on GSM8K as compared to using only GPT-4, while still achieving 95% of GPT-4's performance." [4] "matrix factorization is able to achieve 95% of GPT-4 performance using 26% GPT-4 calls, which is approximately 48% cheaper as compared to the random baseline." [4] RouteLLM outperforms commercial offerings (Martian and Unify AI) by achieving the same performance while being over 40% cheaper [4].

The key innovation lies in "framing LLM routing as a preference learning problem. Rather than relying on synthetic metrics or fixed routing rules, ROUTELLM learns from human preference data to predict when a strong model will outperform a weak model for a given query." [3]

### 1.3 A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs (Cascade Routing)

**Full Title:** A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs  
**Authors:** Jasper Dekoninck, Maximilian Baader, Martin Vechev  
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2025  
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46183](https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46183)

**Findings:**
This research addresses model selection strategies for large language models. It identifies three key limitations in existing approaches (routing and cascading): lack of formal optimality proofs, failure to identify conditions for effectiveness, and inability to combine both paradigms [5]. The authors derive a novel optimal strategy for cascading and prove the optimality of an existing routing strategy. They propose "cascade routing," a unified framework that integrates routing and cascading into a theoretically optimal strategy [5]. The work identifies good quality estimators as critical for model selection success. Experiments show cascade routing consistently outperforms individual approaches by a large margin (up to 14% improvement). "Instead of always running models in a fixed sequence or sticking to just one, cascade routing iteratively picks the best model, and thus can skip models, reorder them, or running only as few as needed." [5]

### 1.4 Router-R1

**Full Title:** Router-R1: Teaching LLMs Multi-Round Routing and Aggregation via Reinforcement Learning  
**Authors:** Haozhen Zhang, Tao Feng, Jiaxuan You  
**Venue & Year:** NeurIPS 2025  
**Link:** [https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/119214](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/119214)

**Findings:**
Router-R1 presents a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that formulates multi-LLM routing and aggregation as a sequential decision process [6]. Unlike existing LLM routers that perform single-round, one-to-one mapping, Router-R1 instantiates the router as a capable LLM, leveraging its reasoning ability to interleave "think" actions (internal deliberation) with "route" actions (dynamic model invocation). It uses a lightweight rule-based reward system comprising format rewards, final outcome rewards, and a cost reward to optimize the balance between performance and cost. The system conditions only on simple model descriptors (pricing, latency, example performance), enabling generalization to unseen model selection. Experiments on seven general and multi-hop QA benchmarks show Router-R1 outperforms several strong baselines, achieving superior performance while maintaining robust generalization and cost management [6].

### 1.23 SELECT-THEN-ROUTE (StR)

**Full Title:** SELECT-THEN-ROUTE: Taxonomy guided Routing for LLMs
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** EMNLP 2025 Industry Track
**Link:** [https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-industry.28.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-industry.28.pdf)

**Findings:**
SELECT-THEN-ROUTE (StR) is a two-stage framework that first selects a small, task-appropriate pool of LLMs and then routes each query within that pool through an adaptive cascade [9]. The first stage uses a taxonomy-guided classifier (combining both slow LLM-based and fast embedding-based approaches) to map each query to a semantic class (e.g., reasoning, code, summarization) and selects a small, task-appropriat pool of candidate models. The second stage employs a confidence-based cascade (CASCADE), starting with the cheapest model in the pool and escalating only when a multi-judge agreement test (combining logit-based confidence, reward model score, domain-specific verifier, and LLM-judge score) signals low reliability.

Key results: StR achieves 94.3% accuracy (compared to 91.7% for the best single model, O3 Mini) while reducing inference cost by 4x ($5.21 vs. $16.29 per 1000 prompt samples). The taxonomy router shows high performance in structured tasks (98.21% for classification, 95.93% for arithmetic) but lower performance in open-ended reasoning (82.00% for causal reasoning) [9]. A two-stage cascade yields 89.2% routing accuracy vs. 80.3% for the base router alone [9]. The system also demonstrates 35% cost savings and 30% latency improvement over GPT-4o on enterprise data [9].
