## 2. Routing Between Different Adaptation Methods (ICL, PEFT Adapters, Fine-tuned Models, RLHF-tuned Models)

### 2.1 L2R: Dynamic Adapter Routing in Continual Learning of Language Models

**Full Title:** Dynamic Adapter Routing in Continual Learning of Language Models
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2025
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46753](https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46753)

**Findings:**
L2R introduces a strategy for continual learning (CL) in pre-trained language models (PLMs) using parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques [10]. Tradicional PEFT-based CL methods face two issues: interference with previously trained modules and suboptimal module composition [10]. L2R addresses these by isolating the training of new PEFT modules to ensure task-specific specialization, and then learning to combine these modules by training a router network that leverages a small memory of prior task examples [10]. The approach was evaluated in two CL setups across various benchmarks, and results show that L2R effectively composes PEFT modules, leading to improved generalization and performance compared to other methods [10].

### 2.2 PERFT: Parameter-Efficient Routed Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Expert Model

**Full Title:** PERFT: Parameter-Efficient Routed Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Expert Model
**Authors:** Yilun Liu, Yunpu Ma, Shuo Chen, Zifeng Ding, Bailan He, Zhen Han, Volker Tresp
**Venue & Year:** ICLR 2025 (submission)
**Link:** [https://openreview.net/froum?id=PPjpGTPG5K&noteId=dlI6oh4zSl](https://openreview.net/froum?id=PPjpGTPG5K&noteId=dlI6oh4zSl)

**Findings:**
PERFT presents a unified framework for integrating parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) modules into Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models [11]. It introduces PERFT (Parameter-Efficient Routed Fine-Tuning), a flexible family of PEFT strategies tailored for MoE LLMs [11]. The framework covers various design dimensions including functional and composition strategies [11]. Extensive experiments adapting OLMoE-1B-7B and Mixtral-8x7B for commonsense and arithmetic reasoning tasks demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and dynamics of PERFT [11].

### 2.5 LoRAMoE / MOELoRA / HydraLoRA / MixLoRA

Several methods combine PEFT with mixture-of-experts, enabling routing among LoRa experts: LoRAMoE, MOELoRA, HydraLoRA, MixLoRA. These are categorized under "PEFT with Other Technologies" in the survey. (Source: Awesome-PEFT repository [12]; also mentioned in the IJSRT review [13])

### 2.6 Efficient Large Language Models: A Survey

**Full Title:** Efficient Large Language Models: A Survey
**Authors:** Researchers from The Ohio State University, Imperial College London, University of Michigan, Amazon AWS AI, Google Research, and Microsoft Research Asia
**Venue & Year:** Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), May 2024
**Link:** [https://github.com/AIoT-MLSys-Lab/Efficient-LLMs-Survey/blob/main/README.md](https://github.com/AIoT-MLSys-Lab/Efficient-LLMs-Survey/blob/main/README.md)

**Findings:**
This comprehensive survey provides a systematic review of efficiency techniques for LLMs, organized into three main categories: (1) Model-Centric Methods, covering model compression (quantization, pruning, low-rank approximation, knowledge distillation, parameter sharing), efficient pre-training, fine-tuning, inference (parallel/speculative decoding, KV-cache optimization), and efficient architecture (attention mechanisms, Mixture of Experts, long-context LLMs, transformer alternatives like State Space Models); (2) Data-Centric Methods, covering data selection and prompt engineering (few-shot prompting, prompt compression/generation); and (3) System-Level Efficiency Optimization and LLM Frameworks [14]. The survey emphasizes the critical need for efficiency, showing that while larger models like LLaMA achieve better performance, training GPU hours grow exponentially with scale, and inference throughput degrades [14]. It highlights Mistral-7B's success using grouped-quey attention and sliding window attention as a proof point for the feasibility of efficient LLM design [14].

### 3.1 Adaptve-RAG

**Full Title:** Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
**Authors:** Soyeong Jeon, Jinheon Baek, Sukmin Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Jong C. Park (KAIST)
**Venue & Year:** NAACL 2024
**Link:** [https://aclanthologyorg/2024.naacl-long.389.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.389.pdf) | [https://pure.kaist.ac.kr/en/publications/adaptive-rag-learning-to-adapt-retrieval-augmented-large-language](https://pure.kaist.ac.kr/en/publications/adaptive-rag-learning-to-adapt-retrieval-augmented-large-language)

**Findings:**
Adaptive-RAG proposes a novel adaptive QA framework that can dynamically select the most suitable retrieval-augmented strategy for LLMs from the simplest to the most sophisticated ones based on query complexity [15][16]. The framework uses a trained classifier (a smaller LM) to categorize queries into three complexity levels: 'A' (straightforward, answerable by LLM alone), 'B' (moderate complexity, requiring single-step retrieval), and 'C' (complex, requiring multi-step iterative retrieval) [15]. The classifier is trained on automatically labeled data derived from model prediction outcomes and inductive biases from existing datasets (single-hop vs multi-hop QA datasets) [15].

The framework is validated on open-domain QA datasets including single-hop (SQuAD, Natural Questions, TriviaQA) and multi-hop (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) queries, using FLAN-T5 (3B and 11B) and GPT-3.5 models [15]. Results show Adaptive-RAG improves both accuracy and efficiency compared to baselines including Adaptive Retrieval and Self-RAG. For example, with FLAN-T5-XL (3B), Adaptive-RAG achieves 46.94 F1 and 2.17 steps per query, compared to the multi-step approach's 48.85 F1 but 4.69 steps, and no retrieval's 21.12 F1 and 0 steps [15]. The oracle classifier demonstrates potential for further improvement. The classifier effectively categorizes queries (54.52% overall accuracy), with 8.6% classified as no retrieval, 53.33% as single-step, and 38.07% as multi-step [15].

## 4. Routing Between Decoding Strategies / Prompting Strategies (e.g., Selecting CoT vs Direct Answer, Routing to Different Prompting Techniques)

### 4.1 Pattern-CoT

**Full Title:** Enhancing Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models via Pattern-Based Demonstration Selection
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** AAAI (year not specified in source; likely 2024 or 2025)
**Link:** [https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34793/36948](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34793/36948)

**Findings:**
Pattern-CoT is a method for enhancing Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting in Large Language Models (LLMs) by selecting demonstrations based on reasoning patterns rather than semantic features [23]. The authors argue that existing unsupervised CoT methods suffer from noise and lack interpretability because they rely on semantic similarity of questions [23]. Pattern-CoT addresses this by: (1) constructing task-specific reasoning pattern sets (e.g., operation tokens like +, -, ×, / for arithmetic tasks), (2) extracting patterns from rationales, (3) clustering similar patterns, and (4) selecting diverse demonstrations from each cluster [23].

The approach was tested on eight reasoning datasets (MultiArith, GSM8K, AddSub, AQuA, SingleEq, SVAMP, Coin-Flip, Date Understanding) using LLaMA-2 (7B and 13B), GPT-3.5, and Qwen models [23]. Results show Pattern-CoT consistently outperforms baselines including Zero-Shot-CoT, Random-CoT, and Auto-CoT [23]. Key findings include: greater improvements on arithmetic problems with limited operation tokens; effective even when demonstrations contain errors (e.g., 100% error rate on AQuA still yielded improvements); and enhanced interpretability through feature attribution analysis [23].

### 4.2 RoutingGen: Intention Chain-of-Thought Prompting with Dynamic Routing for Code Generation

**Full Title:** Intention Chain-of-Thought Prompting with Dynamic Routing for Code Generation
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** AAAI 2025
**Link:** [https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/37030/40992](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/37030/40992)

**Findings:**
RoutingGen is a difficulty-aware dynamic routing framework for code generation using large language models [24]. It addresses two key limitations of existing chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting methods: (1) overthinking on simple tasks due to uniform application of structured prompting, and (2) lack of intention abstraction (e.g., core algorithmic logic and time complexity modeling) in code generation [24].

Inspired by dual-process theory of human cognition (System 1 for intuitive responses, System 2 for deliberate reasoning), RoutingGen uses a difficulty classifier (Qwen3-8B) to estimate problem complexity [24]. For simple tasks, it employs direct few-shot prompting; for complex tasks, it invokes a novel structured reasoning strategy called Intention Chain-of-Thought (ICoT), which comprises two stages: Specification (defining input-output constraints) and Idea (capturing core algorithmic logic and time complexity) [24].

Key Results: RoutingGen achieves state-of-the-art Pass@1 performance across three models (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3-671B) and six benchmarks (HumanEval, HumanEval-ET, MBPP-sanitized, MBPP-ET, OpenEval, McEval) [24]. RoutingGen reduces total token usage by 46.37% on average across all settings [24]. ICoT consistently outperforms six prompting baselines (Zero-shot, Few-shot, Self-CoT, ZS-CoT, Self-Planning, SCoT) on challenging benchmarks [24]. On DeepSeek-V3-671B, RoutingGen achieves 91.83% on HumanEval and 90.21% on MBPP-sanitized [24]. On MBPP-sanitized (64.40% classified as Simple), RoutingGen achieves a 59.22% token reduction and 4.60 percentage point accuracy improvement over SCoT [24]. Ablation studies confirm both Specification and Idea stages contribute to ICoT's effectiveness, and RoutingGen is robust to variations in difficulty classifier models (Qwen3-8B vs. GPT-4o) [24].

### 4.3 DCoT: Fine-Tuning on Diverse Reasoning Chains Drives Within-Inference CoT Refinement in LLMs

**Full Title:** Fine-Tuning on Diverse Reasoning Chains Drives Within-Inference CoT Refinement in LLMs
**Authors:** UKPLab
**Venue & Year:** ACL 2025
**Link:** [https://github.com/UKPLab/acl2025-diverse-cot](https://github.com/UKPLab/acl2025-diverse-cot)

**Findings:**
DCoT introduces an approach where LLMs are fine-tuned to generate a sequence of Diverse Chains of Thought (DCoT) within a single inference step, enabling within-inference refinement of reasoning chains without external feedback [25]. Experiments spanning multiple reasoning tasks and model families (1.3B to 70B parameters) show DCoT improves performance over standard CoT baselines, particularly for tasks with large result state spaces like numeric answers [25]. The approach is distinct from prior work that uses parallel CoT generations with ensembling — DCoT generates multiple reasoning chains sequentially within one inference, and gains come from the model's ability to refine an initial reasoning chain by generating a second, improved chain in the same inference step [25].

### 4.4 Cross-lingual Prompting (CLP) for Zero-shot CoT

**Full Title:** Improving Zero-shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning across Languages
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** EMNLP 2023
**Link:** [https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.163.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.163.pdf)

**Findings:**
CLP (Cross-lingual Prompting) improves zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning across languages [26]. Traditional zero-shot CoT uses the prompt "Let's think step by step!" but is limited to single languages. CLP consists of two components: (1) Cross-lingual Alignment Prompting, which uses "Let's understand the task in English step-by-step!" to align representations across languages, and (2) Task-specific Solver Prompting, which uses "Let's resolve the task you understand above step-by-step!" to generate the final reasoning path [26]. The authors also propose Cross-lingual Self-consistent Prompting (CLSP) to ensemble reasoning paths across different languages via a voting mechanism [26].

Key findings on the MGSM benchmark (10 languages) using GPT-3.5: CLP achieves 70.6% average accuracy, outperforming Translate-En (68.4%), En-CoT (57.8%), and Native-CoT (51.0%) [26]. CLSP further improves to 76.7% average accuracy. Experiments on XCOPA (commonsense reasoning) show CLP achieves 85.3% and CLSP 92.7% average accuracy [26].

## 6. Cost-Performance Trade-offs in Routing Decisions

The cost-performance trade-off is a central theme across many of the papers already covered above. Below is a consolidated summary of the key cost-performance findings:

### From FrugalGPT [1][2]:
- LLM Cascade can match GPT-4 performance with up to 98% cost reduction
- Simple caching yields ~8% cache hits with 99% cost savings
- Semantic caching yields ~21% cache hits with 95% cost reduction
- Fine-tuning smaller models can achieve up to 94% cost reduction
- Converting zero-shot prompts to few-shot: up to 98.5% cost reduction with 78% speed improvement

### From RouteLLM [3][4]:
- Cost reduction of over 2x (up to 3.66x) without sacrificing response quality
- 85% cost savings on MT Bench at 95% of GPT-4 performance
- Matrix factorization router: 26% GPT-4 calls needed to achieve 95% GPT-4 performance (48% cheaper than random)
- RouteLLM outperforms commercial routers (Martian, Unify AI) by being over 40% cheaper at same performance

### From SELECT-THEN-ROUTE [9]:
- Achieves 94.3% accuracy vs 91.7% for best single model (O3 Mini) while reducing cost by 4x ($5.21 vs $16.29 per 1000 prompts)
- 35% cost savings and 30% latency improvement over GPT-4o on enterprise data

### From Cascade Routing (ICML 2025) [5]:
- Cascade routing outperforms individual approaches by up to 14%

### From RoutingGen (AAAI 2025) [24]:
- Reduces total token usage by 46.37% on average across all settings
- On MBPP-sanitized: 59.22% token reduction and 4.60 percentage point accuracy improvement

### Economic Case (from industry analysis [31]):
- Price spread between cheapest and most capable models is ~100x (DeepSeek V4 at ~$0.44/M input tokens to GPT-5.5-pro at $30/$180 per M)
- Teams report bill reductions of 40-85% with tuned routing layers
- Savings compound when cheap-model traffic share crosses 50%
- Router overhead is negligible vs. inference time: rule-based <1ms, embeddings ~5ms, ML classifiers 50-100ms—against LLM responses of 500-2,000ms

## 7. Benchmarking and Evaluation Frameworks for Routing

### 7.1 RouterBench

**Full Title:** RouterBench: A Benchmark for Multi-LLM Routing System
**Authors:** Qitian Hu, Jacob Bieker, Xiuyu Li, Nan Jiang, Benjamin Keigwin, Gaurav Ranganath, Kurt Keutzer, Shriyash Upadhyay
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2024 (Agentic Markets Workshop)
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2024/39041](https://icml.cc/virtual/2024/39041)

**Findings:**
RouterBench is a benchmark and dataset designed to systematically assess multi-LLM routing systems, providing over 405k precomputed inference records, standardized evaluation metrics, and a formal evaluation framework [32][33]. It addresses the need for a unified benchmark for routing strategies that dispatch user prompts to optimal LLMs [32]. It covers diverse application domains including commonsense reasoning, knowledge QA, conversation, math, coding, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [32].

**Data Collection:** The dataset comprises 405,467 inference records from 11 LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude-v1/v2, Llama-70B-chat, Mixtral-8x7B, Yi-34B-chat, Code-Llama-34B, Mistral-7B, WizardLM-13B, You.com API, sonar-small/medium-online) [32]. Domains include HellaSwag, Winogrande, ARC-Challenge, MMLU, MT-Bench, GSM8K, MBPP, and an in-house RAG set [32]. Each record includes sample_id, model name, prompt, response, true label, performance score, and cost estimate, stored in JSON Lines format [32].

**Evaluation Framework:** Uses cost–quality analysis, non-decreasing convex hull (NDCH) for Pareto envelope, and the Average Improvement in Quality (AIQ) metric for comparing routing policies without real-time compute costs [32].

**Key Statistics:** Per-model accuracy ranges from ~38% (Claude-instant) to ~83% (GPT-4); per-model mean cost from $0.08 (Mistral-7B) to $4.09 (GPT-4); oracle router achieves ~0.96 mean performance at ~$0.30 mean cost [32]. Cost–quality correlation is ρ≈0.7 [32].

**Limitations:** No latency or throughput metrics; only 11 LLMs covered; limited to general benchmarks (no niche domains); RAG set only 800 queries; GPT-4 judging may introduce systematic bias [32].

**Applications:** Training predictive routers (KNN, MLP, transformers), evaluating non-predictive strategies (cascades, rule-based), and benchmarking novel routing methodologies against theoretical bounds [32].

**Findings:**
This comprehensive survey addresses the inefficiency of monolithic, static LLM architectures that use a single general-purpose model for all queries [35]. Critical challenges include ensuring complementary LLMs for routing, avoiding over-reliance on the largest model, and the need for diverse training data for clustering approaches [8].

### 7.5 Dynamic Model Routing and Cascading for Efficient LLM Inference: A Survey

This survey (found on arXiv) organizes methods into six paradigms: difficulty-aware routing, human preference-aligned routing, clustering-based routing, reinforcement learning routing, uncertainty-based routing, and cascading. It introduces a three-dimensional framework for characterizing routing systems (when decisions are made, what information is used, how decisions are computed). Since it is an arXiv preprint, it is excluded as a source but its taxonomy is useful context.

---

### Additional Context: Broader Surveys and Taxonomies

The Awesome-Routing-LLMs GitHub repository [7] provides a comprehensive taxonomy of routing methods organized into:
1. **Pre-judgment Routing** (routing decisions made before generation): Constrained Optimization (30+ papers including IRT-Router at ACL 2025, OmniRouter at KDD 2025), Feature Matching (15+ papers including EmbedLLM at ICLR 2025, RouterDC at NeurIPS 2024, RadialRouter at EMNLP 2025, The Avengers at AAAI 2025), Predictive Scoring (30+ papers including RouteLLM at ICLR 2024, BEST-Route at ICML 2025, Zooter at NAACL 2024, ICL-Router at AAAI 2025).
2. **Verification Routing** (routing that considers intermediate states): Collaborative Generation (16 papers including Mixture of Thoughts at ICLR 2026, Router-R1 at NeurIPS 2025, FusionRoute at ICML 2026, STEER at AAAI 2026), Self-Assessment (14 papers including AutoMix at NeurIPS 2024, Self-REF at ICML 2025, SATER at EMNLP 2025, X-Router at Findings of ACL 2026).
3. **Memory-based Routing**: Retrieval (10 papers including Eagle at NeurIPS 2024 Workshop, PORT at NeurIPS 2025 Workshop, SCOPE at ICML 2026), Structured (2 papers including GraphRouter at ICLR 2025).
4. **System Analysis**: Theoretical Modeling (4 papers), Benchmark and Evaluation (19 papers including RouterBench, RouterEval, RouterArena, MMR-Bench, VL-RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, AgentSelect), Safety Analysis (4 papers including Rerouting LLM Routers at COLM 2025, R2A Attack at ACL 2026).

The Awesome-LLM-Agent-Orchestration repository [36] provides a taxonomy of agent orchestration covering: Model Routing, Agent Routing & Team Formation, Workflow Graph Optimization, Runtime Scheduling, Memory & Skill Reuse, and Evaluation. It includes key frameworks: AutoGen, LangGraph, CrewAI, MetaGPT, and GPTSwarm [36].

---

## 1. Model Selection / Routing Between Different Model Sizes or Families

### 1.1 FrugalGPT

**Full Title:** FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance  
**Authors:** Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou  
**Venue & Year:** Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), May 2023  
**Link:** [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/FrugalGPT%3A-How-to-Use-Large-Language-Models-While-Chen-Zaharia/585f8b9725f5f5e5495c3508d39f70d1c053e190](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/FrugalGPT%3A-How-to-Use-Large-Language-Models-While-Chen-Zaharia/585f8b9725f5f5e5495c3508d39f70d1c053e190)

**Findings:**
FrugalGPT proposes a simple yet flexible instantiation of an LLM cascade which learns which combinations of LLMs to use for different queries in order to reduce cost and improve accuracy, laying a foundation for using LLMs sustainably and efficiently [1][2]. FrugalGPT revolves around three key techniques:
1. **Prompt Adaptation:** Using concise, optimized prompts to minimize token costs (e.g., selecting top k similar examples instead of all examples reduced costs by 70%, and combining similar requests reduced costs by 50%).
2. **LLM Approximation:** Utilizing caches and model fine-tuning to avoid repeated expensive queries (simple caching yields ~8% cache hits with 99% cost savings, semantic caching yields ~21% cache hits with 95% cost reduction, and fine-tuning smaller models can achieve up to 94% cost reduction).
3. **LLM Cascade:** Dynamically selecting the optimal sequence of LLMs to query based on confidence scoring, which can match GPT-4 performance with up to 98% cost reduction.

Key results: "FrugalGPT can match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction or improve the accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% with the same cost." [1] Additional techniques include converting zero-shot prompts for larger models into few-shot prompts for smaller models (up to 98.5% cost reduction with 78% speed improvement) and prompt compression using LLMLingua (2.5x-5x compression ratios). The paper has 874 citations and 57 references [2]. It has spawned significant follow-up work including MetaLLM, OptLLM, ThriftLLM, and other frameworks focused on cost-effective LLM routing, selection, and query allocation [2].

### 1.2 RouteLLM

**Full Title:** RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data  
**Authors:** Isaac Ong, Amjad Almahairi, et al. (UC Berkeley)  
**Venue & Year:** ICLR 2025 (peer-reviewed at ICLR 2025; also listed as ICLR 2024 in some sources)  
**Link:** [https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm) (Open-source framework page; paper on alphaxiv: [https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2406.18665](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2406.18665))

**Findings:**
RouteLLM introduces a training framework for learning efficient router models that dynamically select between a stronger (expensive) and weaker (cheaper) LLM during inference to balance performance and cost [3][4]. The framework leverages human preference data from Chatbot Arena (80k battles) and employs data augmentation techniques (golden-labeled data from MMLU and LLM-judge-labeled data from GPT-4). The authors evaluate several router architectures: Similarity-weighted (SW) ranking, Matrix Factorization, BERT classifier, and Causal LLM classifier (Llama 3 8B).

Key results show that routers can reduce costs by over 2x (up to 3.66x) without sacrificing response quality [3]. On MT Bench, the best routers (trained on augmented data) achieve APGR improvements of 50-60% over random baselines. The matrix factorization router required half the GPT-4 calls of random to achieve 50% performance gap recovery. Routers also demonstrate strong generalization to unseen model pairs (Claude 3 Opus/Sonnet and Llama 3.1 70B/8B) without retraining [3]. The paper finds that data augmentation is critical—routers trained solely on Arena data perform poorly on out-of-distribution benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K, but augmentation with as little as 1500 in-domain samples significantly improves performance [3][4].

Specific cost savings: "cost reductions of over 85% on MT Bench, 45% on MMLU, and 35% on GSM8K as compared to using only GPT-4, while still achieving 95% of GPT-4's performance." [4] "matrix factorization is able to achieve 95% of GPT-4 performance using 26% GPT-4 calls, which is approximately 48% cheaper as compared to the random baseline." [4] RouteLLM outperforms commercial offerings (Martian and Unify AI) by achieving the same performance while being over 40% cheaper [4].

The key innovation lies in "framing LLM routing as a preference learning problem. Rather than relying on synthetic metrics or fixed routing rules, ROUTELLM learns from human preference data to predict when a strong model will outperform a weak model for a given query." [3]

### 1.3 A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs (Cascade Routing)

**Full Title:** A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs  
**Authors:** Jasper Dekoninck, Maximilian Baader, Martin Vechev  
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2025  
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46183](https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46183)

**Findings:**
This research addresses model selection strategies for large language models. It identifies three key limitations in existing approaches (routing and cascading): lack of formal optimality proofs, failure to identify conditions for effectiveness, and inability to combine both paradigms [5]. The authors derive a novel optimal strategy for cascading and prove the optimality of an existing routing strategy. They propose "cascade routing," a unified framework that integrates routing and cascading into a theoretically optimal strategy [5]. The work identifies good quality estimators as critical for model selection success. Experiments show cascade routing consistently outperforms individual approaches by a large margin (up to 14% improvement). "Instead of always running models in a fixed sequence or sticking to just one, cascade routing iteratively picks the best model, and thus can skip models, reorder them, or running only as few as needed." [5]

### 1.4 Router-R1

**Full Title:** Router-R1: Teaching LLMs Multi-Round Routing and Aggregation via Reinforcement Learning  
**Authors:** Haozhen Zhang, Tao Feng, Jiaxuan You  
**Venue & Year:** NeurIPS 2025  
**Link:** [https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/119214](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/119214)

**Findings:**
Router-R1 presents a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that formulates multi-LLM routing and aggregation as a sequential decision process [6]. Unlike existing LLM routers that perform single-round, one-to-one mapping, Router-R1 instantiates the router as a capable LLM, leveraging its reasoning ability to interleave "think" actions (internal deliberation) with "route" actions (dynamic model invocation). It uses a lightweight rule-based reward system comprising format rewards, final outcome rewards, and a cost reward to optimize the balance between performance and cost. The system conditions only on simple model descriptors (pricing, latency, example performance), enabling generalization to unseen model selection. Experiments on seven general and multi-hop QA benchmarks show Router-R1 outperforms several strong baselines, achieving superior performance while maintaining robust generalization and cost management [6].

### 1.5 BEST-Route

**Full Title:** Listed as BEST-Route (full details not retrieved)

**Venue & Year:** ICML 2025  
**Link:** Not retrieved (cited in survey sources)

### 1.7 RouterDC

### 1.23 SELECT-THEN-ROUTE (StR)

**Full Title:** SELECT-THEN-ROUTE: Taxonomy guided Routing for LLMs
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** EMNLP 2025 Industry Track
**Link:** [https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-industry.28.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-industry.28.pdf)

**Findings:**
SELECT-THEN-ROUTE (StR) is a two-stage framework that first selects a small, task-appropriate pool of LLMs and then routes each query within that pool through an adaptive cascade [9]. The first stage uses a taxonomy-guided classifier (combining both slow LLM-based and fast embedding-based approaches) to map each query to a semantic class (e.g., reasoning, code, summarization) and selects a small, task-appropriat pool of candidate models. The second stage employs a confidence-based cascade (CASCADE), starting with the cheapest model in the pool and escalating only when a multi-judge agreement test (combining logit-based confidence, reward model score, domain-specific verifier, and LLM-judge score) signals low reliability.

Key results: StR achieves 94.3% accuracy (compared to 91.7% for the best single model, O3 Mini) while reducing inference cost by 4x ($5.21 vs. $16.29 per 1000 prompt samples). The taxonomy router shows high performance in structured tasks (98.21% for classification, 95.93% for arithmetic) but lower performance in open-ended reasoning (82.00% for causal reasoning) [9]. A two-stage cascade yields 89.2% routing accuracy vs. 80.3% for the base router alone [9]. The system also demonstrates 35% cost savings and 30% latency improvement over GPT-4o on enterprise data [9].

### 2.1 L2R: Dynamic Adapter Routing in Continual Learning of Language Models

**Full Title:** Dynamic Adapter Routing in Continual Learning of Language Models
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2025
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46753](https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46753)

**Findings:**
L2R introduces a strategy for continual learning (CL) in pre-trained language models (PLMs) using parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques [10]. Tradicional PEFT-based CL methods face two issues: interference with previously trained modules and suboptimal module composition [10]. L2R addresses these by isolating the training of new PEFT modules to ensure task-specific specialization, and then learning to combine these modules by training a router network that leverages a small memory of prior task examples [10]. The approach was evaluated in two CL setups across various benchmarks, and results show that L2R effectively composes PEFT modules, leading to improved generalization and performance compared to other methods [10].

## 3. Routing to Different Retrieval Depths for RAG (Adaptive Retrieval, Multi-hop Retrieval Routing)

### 3.1 Adaptve-RAG

**Full Title:** Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
**Authors:** Soyeong Jeon, Jinheon Baek, Sukmin Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Jong C. Park (KAIST)
**Venue & Year:** NAACL 2024
**Link:** [https://aclanthologyorg/2024.naacl-long.389.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.389.pdf) | [https://pure.kaist.ac.kr/en/publications/adaptive-rag-learning-to-adapt-retrieval-augmented-large-language](https://pure.kaist.ac.kr/en/publications/adaptive-rag-learning-to-adapt-retrieval-augmented-large-language)

**Findings:**
Adaptive-RAG proposes a novel adaptive QA framework that can dynamically select the most suitable retrieval-augmented strategy for LLMs from the simplest to the most sophisticated ones based on query complexity [15][16]. The framework uses a trained classifier (a smaller LM) to categorize queries into three complexity levels: 'A' (straightforward, answerable by LLM alone), 'B' (moderate complexity, requiring single-step retrieval), and 'C' (complex, requiring multi-step iterative retrieval) [15]. The classifier is trained on automatically labeled data derived from model prediction outcomes and inductive biases from existing datasets (single-hop vs multi-hop QA datasets) [15].

The framework is validated on open-domain QA datasets including single-hop (SQuAD, Natural Questions, TriviaQA) and multi-hop (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) queries, using FLAN-T5 (3B and 11B) and GPT-3.5 models [15]. Results show Adaptive-RAG improves both accuracy and efficiency compared to baselines including Adaptive Retrieval and Self-RAG. For example, with FLAN-T5-XL (3B), Adaptive-RAG achieves 46.94 F1 and 2.17 steps per query, compared to the multi-step approach's 48.85 F1 but 4.69 steps, and no retrieval's 21.12 F1 and 0 steps [15]. The oracle classifier demonstrates potential for further improvement. The classifier effectively categorizes queries (54.52% overall accuracy), with 8.6% classified as no retrieval, 53.33% as single-step, and 38.07% as multi-step [15].

### 3.3 CA-RAG (Cost-Aware RAG)

**Findings (from source [18]**):
CA-RAG is a routing framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems that dynamically selects a retrieval strategy per query from a fixed set of four options (direct_llm, light_rag, medium_rag, heavy_rag) to balance answer quality, latency, and token cost [18]. The framework uses a utility scoring formula with operator-adjustable weights to select the best strategy for each query without requiring model retraining [18].

Key contributions include: a concrete utility formulation and discrete bundle catalog (4 bundles: no retrieval, top-3, top-5, top-10) for operational RAG routing; uses FAISS for retrieval, OpenAI gpt-4o-mini for generation, and text-embedding-3-small for embeddings [18]. The router selects bundles by maximizing a weighted score combining estimated answer quality, predicted latency, and token cost [18].

Key findings: "CA-RAG selects the most suitable retrieval strategy from a fixed menu of four options, ranging from no retrieval to fetching the top most-relevant documents." [18] "The router assigns different strategies to different queries, achieving 26% fewer billed tokens compared to always using heavy retrieval and 34% lower response time compared to always answering without retrieval, while maintaining answer-quality parity in both cases." [18]

CA-RAG's design point is explicitly differentiated from prior systems (Self-RAG, Adaptive-RAG, CRAG, RAGRouter) noting it is training-free, pre-retrieval, cost-zero at routing time, and operator-adjustable via numeric weights [18]. ### 3.4 R3AG: Retriever Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

**Findings (from survey source [19]**):
R3AG is a novel retriever routing framework for RAG that proposes dynamically routing queries to the most suitable retriever by explicitly modeling retriever capability into two learnable dimensions: retrieval quality and generation utility [19]. The framework employs dual-encoder capability modeling (retrieval quality encoder and generation utility encoder), a multi-head attention mechanism for query-conditioned capabilitiy fusion, and similarity-based routing [19]. It undergoes two-stage optimization: first training the capability encoders with contrastive learning, then optimizing the fusion mechanism [19].

Experiments were conducted on three knowledge-intensive benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, and HotpotQA) using LLaMA3-8B-Instruct as the generator and eight candidate retrievers (BM25 + seven dense retrievers) [19]. Results show R3AG consistently outperforms both the best individual retrievers (achieving 43.06 average EM and 53.86 average F1 vs. 41.31/51.81 for the best single retriever) and state-of-the-art static routing methods (RouterRetriver at 38.08/48.34 and LTRR at 39.14/48.85) [19]. R0 (no-retrieval) selection rates of 37.82% on TriviaQA, 15.23% on NQ, and 9.52% on HotpotQA, indicating that a non-trivial portion of queries can be handled without retrieval [19]. (Note: This paper appears to be an arXiv preprint and may not be published at a top conference yet.)

### 3.5 ARK: Adaptive Retriever of Knowledge

**Full Title:** ARK: Adaptive Retriever of Knowledge
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** ACL 2026 (outside the 2022-2025 range but included for completeness)
**Link:** [https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.714.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.714.pdf)

**Findings:**
ARK introduces a training-free, tool-using knowledge graph (KG) retriever that gives a language model control over the breadth-depth tradeoff in evidence retrieval [20]. ARK uses a minimal two-tool interface: (1) Global Search for broad lexical retrieval over node descriptors, and (2) Neighborhood Exploration for one-hop traversal that composes into multi-hop paths [20]. Unlike prior methods, ARK does not require seed node selection, preset hop depth, or task-specific training [20].

Key results: On the STaRK benchmark, ARK achieves 59.1% average Hot@1 and 67.4 average MRR, improving average Hit@1 by up to 31.4% and average MRR by up to 28.0% over training-free retrieval and agent-based methods [20]. ARK adapts tool use to query type—using global search for text-heavy queries (87.7% on AMAZON) and neighborhood exploration for relation-heavy queries (65.3% on MAG, 52.3% on PRIME) [20]. The authors also distill ARK's tool-use trajectories from a GPT-4.1 teacher into an 8B Qwen3-8B model via label-free imitation learning, improving Hit@1 by +7.0, +26.6, and +13.5 absolute points over the base model on AMAZON, MAG, and PRIME respectively, while retaining up to 98.5% of teacher performance [20].

## 4. Routing Between Decoding Strategies / Prompting Strategies (e.g., Selecting CoT vs Direct Answer, Routing to Different Prompting Techniques)

### 4.1 Pattern-CoT

**Full Title:** Enhancing Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models via Pattern-Based Demonstration Selection
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** AAAI (year not specified in source; likely 2024 or 2025)
**Link:** [https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34793/36948](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34793/36948)

**Findings:**
Pattern-CoT is a method for enhancing Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting in Large Language Models (LLMs) by selecting demonstrations based on reasoning patterns rather than semantic features [23]. The authors argue that existing unsupervised CoT methods suffer from noise and lack interpretability because they rely on semantic similarity of questions [23]. Pattern-CoT addresses this by: (1) constructing task-specific reasoning pattern sets (e.g., operation tokens like +, -, ×, / for arithmetic tasks), (2) extracting patterns from rationales, (3) clustering similar patterns, and (4) selecting diverse demonstrations from each cluster [23].

The approach was tested on eight reasoning datasets (MultiArith, GSM8K, AddSub, AQuA, SingleEq, SVAMP, Coin-Flip, Date Understanding) using LLaMA-2 (7B and 13B), GPT-3.5, and Qwen models [23]. Results show Pattern-CoT consistently outperforms baselines including Zero-Shot-CoT, Random-CoT, and Auto-CoT [23]. Key findings include: greater improvements on arithmetic problems with limited operation tokens; effective even when demonstrations contain errors (e.g., 100% error rate on AQuA still yielded improvements); and enhanced interpretability through feature attribution analysis [23].

### 4.2 RoutingGen: Intention Chain-of-Thought Prompting with Dynamic Routing for Code Generation

**Full Title:** Intention Chain-of-Thought Prompting with Dynamic Routing for Code Generation
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** AAAI 2025
**Link:** [https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/37030/40992](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/37030/40992)

**Findings:**
RoutingGen is a difficulty-aware dynamic routing framework for code generation using large language models [24]. It addresses two key limitations of existing chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting methods: (1) overthinking on simple tasks due to uniform application of structured prompting, and (2) lack of intention abstraction (e.g., core algorithmic logic and time complexity modeling) in code generation [24].

Inspired by dual-process theory of human cognition (System 1 for intuitive responses, System 2 for deliberate reasoning), RoutingGen uses a difficulty classifier (Qwen3-8B) to estimate problem complexity [24]. For simple tasks, it employs direct few-shot prompting; for complex tasks, it invokes a novel structured reasoning strategy called Intention Chain-of-Thought (ICoT), which comprises two stages: Specification (defining input-output constraints) and Idea (capturing core algorithmic logic and time complexity) [24].

Key Results: RoutingGen achieves state-of-the-art Pass@1 performance across three models (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3-671B) and six benchmarks (HumanEval, HumanEval-ET, MBPP-sanitized, MBPP-ET, OpenEval, McEval) [24]. RoutingGen reduces total token usage by 46.37% on average across all settings [24]. ICoT consistently outperforms six prompting baselines (Zero-shot, Few-shot, Self-CoT, ZS-CoT, Self-Planning, SCoT) on challenging benchmarks [24]. On DeepSeek-V3-671B, RoutingGen achieves 91.83% on HumanEval and 90.21% on MBPP-sanitized [24]. On MBPP-sanitized (64.40% classified as Simple), RoutingGen achieves a 59.22% token reduction and 4.60 percentage point accuracy improvement over SCoT [24]. Ablation studies confirm both Specification and Idea stages contribute to ICoT's effectiveness, and RoutingGen is robust to variations in difficulty classifier models (Qwen3-8B vs. GPT-4o) [24].

### 4.3 DCoT: Fine-Tuning on Diverse Reasoning Chains Drives Within-Inference CoT Refinement in LLMs

**Full Title:** Fine-Tuning on Diverse Reasoning Chains Drives Within-Inference CoT Refinement in LLMs
**Authors:** UKPLab
**Venue & Year:** ACL 2025
**Link:** [https://github.com/UKPLab/acl2025-diverse-cot](https://github.com/UKPLab/acl2025-diverse-cot)

**Findings:**
DCoT introduces an approach where LLMs are fine-tuned to generate a sequence of Diverse Chains of Thought (DCoT) within a single inference step, enabling within-inference refinement of reasoning chains without external feedback [25]. Experiments spanning multiple reasoning tasks and model families (1.3B to 70B parameters) show DCoT improves performance over standard CoT baselines, particularly for tasks with large result state spaces like numeric answers [25]. The approach is distinct from prior work that uses parallel CoT generations with ensembling — DCoT generates multiple reasoning chains sequentially within one inference, and gains come from the model's ability to refine an initial reasoning chain by generating a second, improved chain in the same inference step [25].

### 4.4 Cross-lingual Prompting (CLP) for Zero-shot CoT

**Full Title:** Improving Zero-shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning across Languages
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** EMNLP 2023
**Link:** [https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.163.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.163.pdf)

**Findings:**
CLP (Cross-lingual Prompting) improves zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning across languages [26]. Traditional zero-shot CoT uses the prompt "Let's think step by step!" but is limited to single languages. CLP consists of two components: (1) Cross-lingual Alignment Prompting, which uses "Let's understand the task in English step-by-step!" to align representations across languages, and (2) Task-specific Solver Prompting, which uses "Let's resolve the task you understand above step-by-step!" to generate the final reasoning path [26]. The authors also propose Cross-lingual Self-consistent Prompting (CLSP) to ensemble reasoning paths across different languages via a voting mechanism [26].

Key findings on the MGSM benchmark (10 languages) using GPT-3.5: CLP achieves 70.6% average accuracy, outperforming Translate-En (68.4%), En-CoT (57.8%), and Native-CoT (51.0%) [26]. CLSP further improves to 76.7% average accuracy. Experiments on XCOPA (commonsense reasoning) show CLP achieves 85.3% and CLSP 92.7% average accuracy [26].

**Link:** [https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/115584](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/115584)

**Findings:**
AgentNet proposes a decentralized, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems [27]. Unlike traditional centralized multi-agent systems, AgentNet uses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)-structured network where agents autonomously evolve, specialize, and coordinate without a central orchestrator [27]. The framework features three key innovations: (1) a fully decentralized paradigm for fault tolerance and emergent collective intelligence, (2) dynamically evolving graph topology for real-time adaptation of agent connections, and (3) adaptive learning for expertise refinement via a retrieval-based memory system [27]. Experimental results show AgentNet outperforms traditional centralized systems in efficiency, adaptability, and scalability, while enabling privacy-preserving cross-organizational collaboration [27].

### 5.2 AgentMaster

**Full Title:** AgentMaster: A Modular Multi-Agent Framework with A2A and MCP Protocols via a Unified Conversational Interface
**Authors:** Callie Liao, Duoduo Liao, Sai Gadiraju
**Venue & Year:** NeurIPS 2025 Workshop (LAW 2025)
**Link:** [https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/137154](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/137154)

**Findings:**
AgentMaster is a novel modular multi-agent framework that integrates both Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google's Agent-to-Agent (A2A) communication protocol within a single unified conversational interface [28]. The framework enables dynamic coordination across agent-to-agent, agent-to-tool, and agent-to-resource channels, supporting natural language interaction and multimodal queries (information retrieval, QA, image analysis) [28]. Evaluation using BERTScore F1 and G-Eval (LLM-as-a-Judge) achieved 96.3% and 87.1% respectively, demonstrating robust inter-agent coordination, query decomposition, and dynamic routing [28].

### 5.3 Lessons Learned: A Multi-Agent Framework for Code LLMs

**Full Title:** Lessons Learned: A Multi-Agent Framework for Code LLMs to Learn and Improve
**Authors:** Yuanzhe Liu, Ryan Deng, Tim Kaler, Xuhao Chen, Charles Leiserson, Yao Ma, Jie Chen
**Venue & Year:** NeurIPS 2025
**Link:** [https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/115952](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/115952)

**Findings:**
This paper addresses the observation that code LLMs have varied performance across different optimization tasks, with no single model dominating [29]. The authors propose a lesson-based collaboration framework where multiple LLM agents share knowledge (lessons) through a solicitation-banking-selection mechanism [29]. Key finding: "a team of small LLMs using this 'lessons learned' approach can outperform a much larger LLM and other multi-LLM collaboration methods" [29].

### 5.4 Large Language Models Miss the Multi-agent Mark (Position Paper)

**Full Title:** Large Language Models Miss the Multi-agent Mark
**Venue & Year:** NeurIPS 2025
**Link:** [https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/121946](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/121946)

**Findings:**
This position paper critically examines the current state of Multi-Agent Systems of Large Language Models (MAS LLMs) [30]. The authors argue that despite growing interest in using multiple LLMs to tackle complex tasks, many implementations misuse MAS terminology without engaging with the field's foundational principles [30]. The paper identifies four key areas of discrepancy between traditional MAS theory and current MAS LLMs implementations: (1) the social aspect of agency, (2) environment design, (3) coordination and communication protocols, and (4) measuring emergent behaviors [30]. The authors contend that many MAS LLMs lack essential multi-agent characteristics such as autonomy, social interaction, and structured environments, often relying on oversimplified, LLM-centric architectures [30].

### 5.5 AgentAsk

**Full Title:** AgentAsk: Multi-Agent Systems Need to Ask
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** Not identified at a top conference (found on arXiv)
**Link:** [https://arxiv.org/html/2510.07593v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.07593v1)

**Findings (included for context but excluded from sources due to arXiv-only status):**
AgentAsk is a lightweight, plug-and-play clarification module for LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) that addresses edge-level error cascades. The authors propose a taxonomy of four core error types: Data Gap (DG) 29.1%, Referential Drift (RD) 27.3%, Signal Corruption (SC) 36.8%, and Capability Gap (CG) 6.8%, based on auditing 824 execution logs. This paper is not included as a source due to being arXiv-only.

---

## 6. Cost-Performance Trade-offs in Routing Decisions

The cost-performance trade-off is a central theme across many of the papers already covered above. Below is a consolidated summary of the key cost-performance findings:

### From FrugalGPT [1][2]:
- LLM Cascade can match GPT-4 performance with up to 98% cost reduction
- Simple caching yields ~8% cache hits with 99% cost savings
- Semantic caching yields ~21% cache hits with 95% cost reduction
- Fine-tuning smaller models can achieve up to 94% cost reduction
- Converting zero-shot prompts to few-shot: up to 98.5% cost reduction with 78% speed improvement

### From RouteLLM [3][4]:
- Cost reduction of over 2x (up to 3.66x) without sacrificing response quality
- 85% cost savings on MT Bench at 95% of GPT-4 performance
- Matrix factorization router: 26% GPT-4 calls needed to achieve 95% GPT-4 performance (48% cheaper than random)
- RouteLLM outperforms commercial routers (Martian, Unify AI) by being over 40% cheaper at same performance

### From SELECT-THEN-ROUTE [9]:
- Achieves 94.3% accuracy vs 91.7% for best single model (O3 Mini) while reducing cost by 4x ($5.21 vs $16.29 per 1000 prompts)
- 35% cost savings and 30% latency improvement over GPT-4o on enterprise data

### From Cascade Routing (ICML 2025) [5]:
- Cascade routing outperforms individual approaches by up to 14%

### From RoutingGen (AAAI 2025) [24]:
- Reduces total token usage by 46.37% on average across all settings
- On MBPP-sanitized: 59.22% token reduction and 4.60 percentage point accuracy improvement

### Economic Case (from industry analysis [31]):
- Price spread between cheapest and most capable models is ~100x (DeepSeek V4 at ~$0.44/M input tokens to GPT-5.5-pro at $30/$180 per M)
- Teams report bill reductions of 40-85% with tuned routing layers
- Savings compound when cheap-model traffic share crosses 50%
- Router overhead is negligible vs. inference time: rule-based <1ms, embeddings ~5ms, ML classifiers 50-100ms—against LLM responses of 500-2,000ms

---

## 7. Benchmarking and Evaluation Frameworks for Routing

### 7.1 RouterBench

**Full Title:** RouterBench: A Benchmark for Multi-LLM Routing System
**Authors:** Qitian Hu, Jacob Bieker, Xiuyu Li, Nan Jiang, Benjamin Keigwin, Gaurav Ranganath, Kurt Keutzer, Shriyash Upadhyay
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2024 (Agentic Markets Workshop)
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2024/39041](https://icml.cc/virtual/2024/39041)

**Findings:**
RouterBench is a benchmark and dataset designed to systematically assess multi-LLM routing systems, providing over 405k precomputed inference records, standardized evaluation metrics, and a formal evaluation framework [32][33]. It addresses the need for a unified benchmark for routing strategies that dispatch user prompts to optimal LLMs [32]. It covers diverse application domains including commonsense reasoning, knowledge QA, conversation, math, coding, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [32].

**Data Collection:** The dataset comprises 405,467 inference records from 11 LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude-v1/v2, Llama-70B-chat, Mixtral-8x7B, Yi-34B-chat, Code-Llama-34B, Mistral-7B, WizardLM-13B, You.com API, sonar-small/medium-online) [32]. Domains include HellaSwag, Winogrande, ARC-Challenge, MMLU, MT-Bench, GSM8K, MBPP, and an in-house RAG set [32]. Each record includes sample_id, model name, prompt, response, true label, performance score, and cost estimate, stored in JSON Lines format [32].

**Evaluation Framework:** Uses cost–quality analysis, non-decreasing convex hull (NDCH) for Pareto envelope, and the Average Improvement in Quality (AIQ) metric for comparing routing policies without real-time compute costs [32].

**Key Statistics:** Per-model accuracy ranges from ~38% (Claude-instant) to ~83% (GPT-4); per-model mean cost from $0.08 (Mistral-7B) to $4.09 (GPT-4); oracle router achieves ~0.96 mean performance at ~$0.30 mean cost [32]. Cost–quality correlation is ρ≈0.7 [32].

**Limitations:** No latency or throughput metrics; only 11 LLMs covered; limited to general benchmarks (no niche domains); RAG set only 800 queries; GPT-4 judging may introduce systematic bias [32].

**Applications:** Training predictive routers (KNN, MLP, transformers), evaluating non-predictive strategies (cascades, rule-based), and benchmarking novel routing methodologies against theoretical bounds [32].

### 7.2 RouterXBench

**Full Title:** Towards Fair and Comprehensive Evaluation of Routers in Collaborative LLM Systems
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** Not identified at a top conference (found on arXiv)
**Link:** [https://arxiv.org/html/2602.11877v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.11877v1)

**Findings (excluded from sources due to arXiv-only):**
RouterXBench is a systematic evaluation framework for routers in collaborative LLM systems, evaluating across three dimensions: (1) Router Ability (measured by AUROC), (2) Scenario Alignment (using LPM, MPM, and HCR metrics for low-cost, balanced, and high-accuracy deployment regimes), and (3) Cross-Domain Robustness (across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks) [34].

### 7.3 Other Benchmark and Evaluation Works (from Awesome-Routing-LLMs [7])

The Awesome-Routing-LLMs repository lists 19 papers under "Benchmark and Evaluation" including:
- RouterBench
- RouterEval
- RouterArena
- MMR-Bench (Multimodal Routing Benchmark)
- VL-RouterBench (Vision-Language Router Benchmark)
- LLMRouterBench
- AgentSelect

These are cited as existing works in the field but full details (authors, venues, years) were not retrieved for each.

### 7.4 Doing More with Less – Implementing Routing Strategies in Large Language Model-Based Systems: An Extended Survey

**Full Title:** Doing More with Less – Implementing Routing Strategies in Large Language Model-Based Systems: An Extended Survey
**Authors:** Clovis Varangot-Reille, Christophe Bouvard, Mathieu Ciancone, Antoine Gourru, Marion Schaeffer, François Jacquenet
**Venue & Year:** Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research (JAIR), June 30, 2026 (outside 2022-2025 range)
**Link:** [https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/19801](https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/19801)

**Findings:**
This comprehensive survey addresses the inefficiency of monolithic, static LLM architectures that use a single general-purpose model for all queries [35]. It argues that routing mechanisms can direct queries to more appropriate components (e.g., smaller or specialized models) to optimize resource consumption [35]. The paper formalizes routing as a performance–cost optimization problem [35]. It covers high-resource strategies (supervised routing, generative-based routing, code execution) and low-resource strategies (similarity-based routing, supervised routing with matrix factorization) [8]. Key findings: FrugalGPT could save between 59% and 98% of costs while maintaining similar accuracy to larger models like GPT-4 [8]; Routoo achieved 75.9% on MMLU vs 69.9% for Llama2-70B at similar or lower costs [8]; Self-Route reduced token usage by 61% on average for GPT-4o while maintaining comparable performance [8]; RouterDC outperformed standalone LLMs and other routing methods across out-of-distribution datasets [8]. Critical challenges include ensuring complementary LLMs for routing, avoiding over-reliance on the largest model, and the need for diverse training data for clustering approaches [8].

### 7.5 Dynamic Model Routing and Cascading for Efficient LLM Inference: A Survey

This survey (found on arXiv) organizes methods into six paradigms: difficulty-aware routing, human preference-aligned routing, clustering-based routing, reinforcement learning routing, uncertainty-based routing, and cascading. It introduces a three-dimensional framework for characterizing routing systems (when decisions are made, what information is used, how decisions are computed). Since it is an arXiv preprint, it is excluded as a source but its taxonomy is useful context.

---

### Additional Context: Broader Surveys and Taxonomies

The Awesome-Routing-LLMs GitHub repository [7] provides a comprehensive taxonomy of routing methods organized into:
1. **Pre-judgment Routing** (routing decisions made before generation): Constrained Optimization (30+ papers including IRT-Router at ACL 2025, OmniRouter at KDD 2025), Feature Matching (15+ papers including EmbedLLM at ICLR 2025, RouterDC at NeurIPS 2024, RadialRouter at EMNLP 2025, The Avengers at AAAI 2025), Predictive Scoring (30+ papers including RouteLLM at ICLR 2024, BEST-Route at ICML 2025, Zooter at NAACL 2024, ICL-Router at AAAI 2025).
2. **Verification Routing** (routing that considers intermediate states): Collaborative Generation (16 papers including Mixture of Thoughts at ICLR 2026, Router-R1 at NeurIPS 2025, FusionRoute at ICML 2026, STEER at AAAI 2026), Self-Assessment (14 papers including AutoMix at NeurIPS 2024, Self-REF at ICML 2025, SATER at EMNLP 2025, X-Router at Findings of ACL 2026).
3. **Memory-based Routing**: Retrieval (10 papers including Eagle at NeurIPS 2024 Workshop, PORT at NeurIPS 2025 Workshop, SCOPE at ICML 2026), Structured (2 papers including GraphRouter at ICLR 2025).
4. **System Analysis**: Theoretical Modeling (4 papers), Benchmark and Evaluation (19 papers including RouterBench, RouterEval, RouterArena, MMR-Bench, VL-RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, AgentSelect), Safety Analysis (4 papers including Rerouting LLM Routers at COLM 2025, R2A Attack at ACL 2026).

The Awesome-LLM-Agent-Orchestration repository [36] provides a taxonomy of agent orchestration covering: Model Routing, Agent Routing & Team Formation, Workflow Graph Optimization, Runtime Scheduling, Memory & Skill Reuse, and Evaluation. It includes key frameworks: AutoGen, LangGraph, CrewAI, MetaGPT, and GPTSwarm [36].

## 1. Model Selection / Routing Between Different Model Sizes or Families

### 1.1 FrugalGPT

**Full Title:** FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance  
**Authors:** Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou  
**Venue & Year:** Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), May 2023  
**Link:** [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/FrugalGPT%3A-How-to-Use-Large-Language-Models-While-Chen-Zaharia/585f8b9725f5f5e5495c3508d39f70d1c053e190](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/FrugalGPT%3A-How-to-Use-Large-Language-Models-While-Chen-Zaharia/585f8b9725f5f5e5495c3508d39f70d1c053e190)

**Findings:**
FrugalGPT proposes a simple yet flexible instantiation of an LLM cascade which learns which combinations of LLMs to use for different queries in order to reduce cost and improve accuracy, laying a foundation for using LLMs sustainably and efficiently [1][2]. FrugalGPT revolves around three key techniques:
1. **Prompt Adaptation:** Using concise, optimized prompts to minimize token costs (e.g., selecting top k similar examples instead of all examples reduced costs by 70%, and combining similar requests reduced costs by 50%).
2. **LLM Approximation:** Utilizing caches and model fine-tuning to avoid repeated expensive queries (simple caching yields ~8% cache hits with 99% cost savings, semantic caching yields ~21% cache hits with 95% cost reduction, and fine-tuning smaller models can achieve up to 94% cost reduction).
3. **LLM Cascade:** Dynamically selecting the optimal sequence of LLMs to query based on confidence scoring, which can match GPT-4 performance with up to 98% cost reduction.

Key results: "FrugalGPT can match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction or improve the accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% with the same cost." [1] Additional techniques include converting zero-shot prompts for larger models into few-shot prompts for smaller models (up to 98.5% cost reduction with 78% speed improvement) and prompt compression using LLMLingua (2.5x-5x compression ratios). The paper has 874 citations and 57 references [2]. It has spawned significant follow-up work including MetaLLM, OptLLM, ThriftLLM, and other frameworks focused on cost-effective LLM routing, selection, and query allocation [2].

### 1.2 RouteLLM

**Full Title:** RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data  
**Authors:** Isaac Ong, Amjad Almahairi, et al. (UC Berkeley)  
**Venue & Year:** ICLR 2025 (peer-reviewed at ICLR 2025; also listed as ICLR 2024 in some sources)  
**Link:** [https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm) (Open-source framework page; paper on alphaxiv: [https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2406.18665](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2406.18665))

**Findings:**
RouteLLM introduces a training framework for learning efficient router models that dynamically select between a stronger (expensive) and weaker (cheaper) LLM during inference to balance performance and cost [3][4]. The framework leverages human preference data from Chatbot Arena (80k battles) and employs data augmentation techniques (golden-labeled data from MMLU and LLM-judge-labeled data from GPT-4). The authors evaluate several router architectures: Similarity-weighted (SW) ranking, Matrix Factorization, BERT classifier, and Causal LLM classifier (Llama 3 8B).

Key results show that routers can reduce costs by over 2x (up to 3.66x) without sacrificing response quality [3]. On MT Bench, the best routers (trained on augmented data) achieve APGR improvements of 50-60% over random baselines. The matrix factorization router required half the GPT-4 calls of random to achieve 50% performance gap recovery. Routers also demonstrate strong generalization to unseen model pairs (Claude 3 Opus/Sonnet and Llama 3.1 70B/8B) without retraining [3]. The paper finds that data augmentation is critical—routers trained solely on Arena data perform poorly on out-of-distribution benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K, but augmentation with as little as 1500 in-domain samples significantly improves performance [3][4].

Specific cost savings: "cost reductions of over 85% on MT Bench, 45% on MMLU, and 35% on GSM8K as compared to using only GPT-4, while still achieving 95% of GPT-4's performance." [4] "matrix factorization is able to achieve 95% of GPT-4 performance using 26% GPT-4 calls, which is approximately 48% cheaper as compared to the random baseline." [4] RouteLLM outperforms commercial offerings (Martian and Unify AI) by achieving the same performance while being over 40% cheaper [4].

The key innovation lies in "framing LLM routing as a preference learning problem. Rather than relying on synthetic metrics or fixed routing rules, ROUTELLM learns from human preference data to predict when a strong model will outperform a weak model for a given query." [3]

### 1.3 A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs (Cascade Routing)

**Full Title:** A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs  
**Authors:** Jasper Dekoninck, Maximilian Baader, Martin Vechev  
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2025  
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46183](https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46183)

**Findings:**
This research addresses model selection strategies for large language models. It identifies three key limitations in existing approaches (routing and cascading): lack of formal optimality proofs, failure to identify conditions for effectiveness, and inability to combine both paradigms [5]. The authors derive a novel optimal strategy for cascading and prove the optimality of an existing routing strategy. They propose "cascade routing," a unified framework that integrates routing and cascading into a theoretically optimal strategy [5]. The work identifies good quality estimators as critical for model selection success. Experiments show cascade routing consistently outperforms individual approaches by a large margin (up to 14% improvement). "Instead of always running models in a fixed sequence or sticking to just one, cascade routing iteratively picks the best model, and thus can skip models, reorder them, or running only as few as needed." [5]

### 1.4 Router-R1

**Full Title:** Router-R1: Teaching LLMs Multi-Round Routing and Aggregation via Reinforcement Learning  
**Authors:** Haozhen Zhang, Tao Feng, Jiaxuan You  
**Venue & Year:** NeurIPS 2025  
**Link:** [https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/119214](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/119214)

**Findings:**
Router-R1 presents a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that formulates multi-LLM routing and aggregation as a sequential decision process [6]. Unlike existing LLM routers that perform single-round, one-to-one mapping, Router-R1 instantiates the router as a capable LLM, leveraging its reasoning ability to interleave "think" actions (internal deliberation) with "route" actions (dynamic model invocation). It uses a lightweight rule-based reward system comprising format rewards, final outcome rewards, and a cost reward to optimize the balance between performance and cost. The system conditions only on simple model descriptors (pricing, latency, example performance), enabling generalization to unseen model selection. Experiments on seven general and multi-hop QA benchmarks show Router-R1 outperforms several strong baselines, achieving superior performance while maintaining robust generalization and cost management [6].

### 1.23 SELECT-THEN-ROUTE (StR)

**Full Title:** SELECT-THEN-ROUTE: Taxonomy guided Routing for LLMs
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** EMNLP 2025 Industry Track
**Link:** [https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-industry.28.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-industry.28.pdf)

**Findings:**
SELECT-THEN-ROUTE (StR) is a two-stage framework that first selects a small, task-appropriate pool of LLMs and then routes each query within that pool through an adaptive cascade [9]. The first stage uses a taxonomy-guided classifier (combining both slow LLM-based and fast embedding-based approaches) to map each query to a semantic class (e.g., reasoning, code, summarization) and selects a small, task-appropriat pool of candidate models. The second stage employs a confidence-based cascade (CASCADE), starting with the cheapest model in the pool and escalating only when a multi-judge agreement test (combining logit-based confidence, reward model score, domain-specific verifier, and LLM-judge score) signals low reliability.

Key results: StR achieves 94.3% accuracy (compared to 91.7% for the best single model, O3 Mini) while reducing inference cost by 4x ($5.21 vs. $16.29 per 1000 prompt samples). The taxonomy router shows high performance in structured tasks (98.21% for classification, 95.93% for arithmetic) but lower performance in open-ended reasoning (82.00% for causal reasoning) [9]. A two-stage cascade yields 89.2% routing accuracy vs. 80.3% for the base router alone [9]. The system also demonstrates 35% cost savings and 30% latency improvement over GPT-4o on enterprise data [9].

## 2. Routing Between Different Adaptation Methods (ICL, PEFT Adapters, Fine-tuned Models, RLHF-tuned Models)

### 2.1 L2R: Dynamic Adapter Routing in Continual Learning of Language Models

**Full Title:** Dynamic Adapter Routing in Continual Learning of Language Models
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** ICML 2025
**Link:** [https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46753](https://icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/46753)

**Findings:**
L2R introduces a strategy for continual learning (CL) in pre-trained language models (PLMs) using parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques [10]. Tradicional PEFT-based CL methods face two issues: interference with previously trained modules and suboptimal module composition [10]. L2R addresses these by isolating the training of new PEFT modules to ensure task-specific specialization, and then learning to combine these modules by training a router network that leverages a small memory of prior task examples [10]. The approach was evaluated in two CL setups across various benchmarks, and results show that L2R effectively composes PEFT modules, leading to improved generalization and performance compared to other methods [10].

### 2.6 Efficient Large Language Models: A Survey

**Full Title:** Efficient Large Language Models: A Survey
**Authors:** Researchers from The Ohio State University, Imperial College London, University of Michigan, Amazon AWS AI, Google Research, and Microsoft Research Asia
**Venue & Year:** Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), May 2024
**Link:** [https://github.com/AIoT-MLSys-Lab/Efficient-LLMs-Survey/blob/main/README.md](https://github.com/AIoT-MLSys-Lab/Efficient-LLMs-Survey/blob/main/README.md)

**Findings:**
This comprehensive survey provides a systematic review of efficiency techniques for LLMs, organized into three main categories: (1) Model-Centric Methods, covering model compression (quantization, pruning, low-rank approximation, knowledge distillation, parameter sharing), efficient pre-training, fine-tuning, inference (parallel/speculative decoding, KV-cache optimization), and efficient architecture (attention mechanisms, Mixture of Experts, long-context LLMs, transformer alternatives like State Space Models); (2) Data-Centric Methods, covering data selection and prompt engineering (few-shot prompting, prompt compression/generation); and (3) System-Level Efficiency Optimization and LLM Frameworks [14]. The survey emphasizes the critical need for efficiency, showing that while larger models like LLaMA achieve better performance, training GPU hours grow exponentially with scale, and inference throughput degrades [14]. It highlights Mistral-7B's success using grouped-quey attention and sliding window attention as a proof point for the feasibility of efficient LLM design [14].

## 3. Routing to Different Retrieval Depths for RAG (Adaptive Retrieval, Multi-hop Retrieval Routing)

### 3.1 Adaptve-RAG

**Full Title:** Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
**Authors:** Soyeong Jeon, Jinheon Baek, Sukmin Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Jong C. Park (KAIST)
**Venue & Year:** NAACL 2024
**Link:** [https://aclanthologyorg/2024.naacl-long.389.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.389.pdf) | [https://pure.kaist.ac.kr/en/publications/adaptive-rag-learning-to-adapt-retrieval-augmented-large-language](https://pure.kaist.ac.kr/en/publications/adaptive-rag-learning-to-adapt-retrieval-augmented-large-language)

**Findings:**
Adaptive-RAG proposes a novel adaptive QA framework that can dynamically select the most suitable retrieval-augmented strategy for LLMs from the simplest to the most sophisticated ones based on query complexity [15][16]. The framework uses a trained classifier (a smaller LM) to categorize queries into three complexity levels: 'A' (straightforward, answerable by LLM alone), 'B' (moderate complexity, requiring single-step retrieval), and 'C' (complex, requiring multi-step iterative retrieval) [15]. The classifier is trained on automatically labeled data derived from model prediction outcomes and inductive biases from existing datasets (single-hop vs multi-hop QA datasets) [15].

The framework is validated on open-domain QA datasets including single-hop (SQuAD, Natural Questions, TriviaQA) and multi-hop (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) queries, using FLAN-T5 (3B and 11B) and GPT-3.5 models [15]. Results show Adaptive-RAG improves both accuracy and efficiency compared to baselines including Adaptive Retrieval and Self-RAG. For example, with FLAN-T5-XL (3B), Adaptive-RAG achieves 46.94 F1 and 2.17 steps per query, compared to the multi-step approach's 48.85 F1 but 4.69 steps, and no retrieval's 21.12 F1 and 0 steps [15]. The oracle classifier demonstrates potential for further improvement. The classifier effectively categorizes queries (54.52% overall accuracy), with 8.6% classified as no retrieval, 53.33% as single-step, and 38.07% as multi-step [15].

### 3.3 CA-RAG (Cost-Aware RAG)

**Findings (from source [18]**):
CA-RAG is a routing framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems that dynamically selects a retrieval strategy per query from a fixed set of four options (direct_llm, light_rag, medium_rag, heavy_rag) to balance answer quality, latency, and token cost [18]. The framework uses a utility scoring formula with operator-adjustable weights to select the best strategy for each query without requiring model retraining [18].

Key contributions include: a concrete utility formulation and discrete bundle catalog (4 bundles: no retrieval, top-3, top-5, top-10) for operational RAG routing; uses FAISS for retrieval, OpenAI gpt-4o-mini for generation, and text-embedding-3-small for embeddings [18]. The router selects bundles by maximizing a weighted score combining estimated answer quality, predicted latency, and token cost [18].

Key findings: "CA-RAG selects the most suitable retrieval strategy from a fixed menu of four options, ranging from no retrieval to fetching the top most-relevant documents." [18] "The router assigns different strategies to different queries, achieving 26% fewer billed tokens compared to always using heavy retrieval and 34% lower response time compared to always answering without retrieval, while maintaining answer-quality parity in both cases." [18]

CA-RAG's design point is explicitly differentiated from prior systems (Self-RAG, Adaptive-RAG, CRAG, RAGRouter) noting it is training-free, pre-retrieval, cost-zero at routing time, and operator-adjustable via numeric weights [18]. (Note: this paper was published in MDPI AI journal, not a top conference per the user's criteria, but included for completeness with this caveat.)

### 3.4 R3AG: Retriever Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

**Findings (from survey source [19]**):
R3AG is a novel retriever routing framework for RAG that proposes dynamically routing queries to the most suitable retriever by explicitly modeling retriever capability into two learnable dimensions: retrieval quality and generation utility [19]. The framework employs dual-encoder capability modeling (retrieval quality encoder and generation utility encoder), a multi-head attention mechanism for query-conditioned capabilitiy fusion, and similarity-based routing [19]. It undergoes two-stage optimization: first training the capability encoders with contrastive learning, then optimizing the fusion mechanism [19].

Experiments were conducted on three knowledge-intensive benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, and HotpotQA) using LLaMA3-8B-Instruct as the generator and eight candidate retrievers (BM25 + seven dense retrievers) [19]. Results show R3AG consistently outperforms both the best individual retrievers (achieving 43.06 average EM and 53.86 average F1 vs. 41.31/51.81 for the best single retriever) and state-of-the-art static routing methods (RouterRetriver at 38.08/48.34 and LTRR at 39.14/48.85) [19]. R0 (no-retrieval) selection rates of 37.82% on TriviaQA, 15.23% on NQ, and 9.52% on HotpotQA, indicating that a non-trivial portion of queries can be handled without retrieval [19]. (Note: This paper appears to be an arXiv preprint and may not be published at a top conference yet.)

### 3.5 ARK: Adaptive Retriever of Knowledge

**Full Title:** ARK: Adaptive Retriever of Knowledge
**Authors:** Not retrieved
**Venue & Year:** ACL 2026 (outside the 2022-2025 range but included for completeness)
**Link:** [https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.714.pdf](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.714.pdf)

**Findings:**
ARK introduces a training-free, tool-using knowledge graph (KG) retriever that gives a language model control over the breadth-depth tradeoff in evidence retrieval [20]. ARK uses a minimal two-tool interface: (1) Global Search for broad lexical retrieval over node descriptors, and (2) Neighborhood Exploration for one-hop traversal that composes into multi-hop paths [20]. Unlike prior methods, ARK does not require seed node selection, preset hop depth, or task-specific training [20].

Key results: On the STaRK benchmark, ARK achieves 59.1% average Hot@1 and 67.4 average MRR, improving average Hit@1 by up to 31.4% and average MRR by up to 28.0% over training-free retrieval and agent-based methods [20]. ARK adapts tool use to query type—using global search for text-heavy queries (87.7% on AMAZON) and neighborhood exploration for relation-heavy queries (65.3% on MAG, 52.3% on PRIME) [20]. The authors also distill ARK's tool-use trajectories from a GPT-4.1 teacher into an 8B Qwen3-8B model via label-free imitation learning, improving Hit@1 by +7.0, +26.6, and +13.5 absolute points over the base model on AMAZON, MAG, and PRIME respectively, while retaining up to 98.5% of teacher performance [20].

### 3.6 Adaptive Hyrid Retrieval (AHR) / Tree Reasoning / Vector RAG (Cross-domain comparsion)

**Findings (from survey source [21]**:
A cross-domain experimental comparison of three retrieval architectures—Vector RAG, Tree Reasoning, and a proposed Adaptive Hybrid Retrieval (AHR)—across financial, legal, and medical documents [21]. It introduces a four-tier query complexity benchmark (single-fact lookup, multi-section reasoning, cross-reference, and multi-document synthesis) and uses GPT-4-powered LLM-as-judge evaluation [21].

Key findings: Tree Reasoning achieves the highest overall quality score (0.900) on the controlled corpus, but no single paradigm dominates across all tiers [21]. Vector RAG leads on multi-document synthesis (Tier 4, 0.900) and financial documents (0.910). Tree Reasoning excels on legal (0.883) and medical (0.933) domains and information extraction [21]. The Hybrid AHR achieves best performance on cross-reference (0.850) and multi-section queries (0.929) [21]. Cross-reference recall reaches 100% for tree-based and hybrid approaches versus 91.7% for vector search [21]. Validation on FinanceBench confirms: Tree Reasoning scores 0.938, Hybrid AHR 0.901, and Vector RAG 0.821 [21]. (Note: This appears to be an arXiv preprint, not a top conference paper.)
